shelves.title: Vitamin D and respiratory infection in adults Deposit #3 · Oct 23, 2026
shelves.question: Does vitamin D prevent or soften infections in adults — respiratory, tuberculosis, COVID-19, critical illness?
shelves.balance: The newest and largest synthesis (Jolliffe 2025) finds vitamin D’s overall effect on acute respiratory infection borderline and not significant (OR 0.94, p=0.057), with a residual signal in daily dosing (0.84) — while the dramatic 2017 benefit in the severely deficient (aOR 0.30) did not survive as effect modification in the update. Tuberculosis prevention shows no benefit; a critical-illness mortality signal (RR 0.78) rests on small trials and a route subgroup. Correcting deficiency remains sensible care; vitamin D is not a proven shield against infection in adults. The children evidence now lives on its own shelf, #37.

cards.headline: Does vitamin D reduce acute respiratory infection? (2025 meta-analysis, newest & largest)
cards.summary: Any vitamin D vs placebo: OR 0.94 (0.88–1.00) , p=0.057; children 1–15 OR 0.74 ; daily dosing OR 0.84 ; no effect modification — 40 studies, 61,589 in the primary comparison.
cards.type: Systematic review & meta-analysis of RCTs (updated), Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2025
cards.people: 40 studies, 61,589 participants in the primary comparison (46 RCTs, 64,086 overall)
cards.result: OR 0.94 (0.88–1.00) , p=0.057; children 1–15 OR 0.74 ; daily dosing OR 0.84 ; no effect modification by age, baseline status, frequency or dose
cards.watchOut: The overall result just misses statistical significance, and the subgroup findings are secondary
cards.source: Jolliffe et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2025; PMID 39993397
cards.search: jolliffe 2025 vitamin d acute respiratory infection meta-analysis lancet diabetes endocrinology daily dosing children odds ratio pmid 39993397 newest largest

cards.headline: Does vitamin D prevent respiratory infection? (2017 IPD meta-analysis)
cards.summary: Overall OR 0.88 (0.81–0.96) ; baseline <25 nmol/L with daily/weekly dosing aOR 0.30 (0.17–0.53) ; bolus aOR 0.97 — 10,933 analysed.
cards.type: Individual participant data meta-analysis of RCTs, BMJ 2017
cards.people: 11,321 randomised, 10,933 analysed
cards.result: Overall OR 0.88 (0.81–0.96) ; baseline <25 nmol/L with daily/weekly dosing aOR 0.30 (0.17–0.53) ; bolus dosing aOR 0.97
cards.watchOut: The largest benefit sits in a small deficient subgroup, and the 2025 update found no significant effect modification by baseline status
cards.source: Martineau et al., BMJ 2017; PMID 28202713
cards.search: martineau 2017 vitamin d respiratory infection individual participant data meta-analysis bmj deficient bolus daily weekly pmid 28202713

cards.headline: Does the way vitamin D is given change its effect?
cards.summary: Overall RR 0.99 (0.97–1.01) ; daily dosing RR 0.92 (0.85–0.99) — 43 RCTs, 49,320 participants.
cards.type: Systematic review & meta-analysis of RCTs, Nutr J 2024
cards.people: 43 RCTs, 49,320 participants
cards.result: Overall RR 0.99 (0.97–1.01) ; daily dosing RR 0.92 (0.85–0.99)
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity is moderate and the daily-dosing signal is a subgroup finding
cards.source: Wang et al., Nutr J 2024; PMID 39143549

cards.headline: Does vitamin D prevent tuberculosis?

cards.headline: Did monthly vitamin D reduce hospitalisation for infection? (D-Health)

shelves.title: Zinc and wound healing Deposit #9 · Oct 23, 2026
shelves.question: Does zinc — in the blood, by mouth, or on the skin — change whether diabetic foot and leg ulcers heal?
shelves.balance: Low zinc is common where ulcers are — 26.9% deficient in a prospective foot-clinic cohort — and lower zinc travels with ulcer presence and slower early healing. But the one prospective healing cohort found baseline zinc did not predict who healed (HR 1.05), and giving zinc is unproven: the positive diabetic-ulcer trial carries a 2024 Expression of Concern, the combined-nutrient pilot was neutral at 12 weeks, and Cochrane’s pooled verdict for venous ulcers is no benefit. Topical zinc has older, small positive trials. On this shelf, association does most of the work.

cards.headline: Baseline zinc does not predict healing
cards.summary: Prospective cohort, 100 foot-wound patients — zinc 11.5 vs 11.1 µmol/L healed vs not (p=0.45); deficiency and time to healing HR 1.05 (NS) .
cards.type: Prospective single-center cohort, Adv Wound Care 2026
cards.people: 100 adults with active foot wounds; 91% had diabetes; 65 healed, 31 not healed or amputated, 4 lost to follow-up
cards.result: Zinc 11.5 vs 11.1 µmol/L in the healed vs not-healed groups (p = 0.45); zinc deficiency was not associated with time to healing: HR 1.05 (0.94–1.17, p = 0.38)
cards.watchOut: A single-center cohort with one baseline zinc measurement and a combined poor-outcome group
cards.source: Bechara et al., Adv Wound Care 2026; PMID 38940723
cards.search: zinc baseline healing diabetic foot wound prospective cohort bechara advances wound care 2026 micronutrients pmid 38940723

cards.headline: Lower zinc in healing failure (diabetic foot)
cards.summary: Retrospective, 39 ulcer patients — zinc 47.6 vs 62.8 µg/dL in failure vs no failure ( p=0.00003 ).
cards.type: Retrospective cohort, Int J Low Extrem Wounds 2026
cards.people: 39 patients with diabetic foot ulcer (within 319 patients overall): 21 without and 18 with wound-healing failure
cards.result: Serum zinc 47.6 µg/dL in patients with wound-healing failure vs 62.8 µg/dL without failure ( p = 0.00003 )
cards.watchOut: The diabetic-foot subgroup was small and retrospective, and the published adjusted zinc confidence interval appears internally inconsistent
cards.source: Nakamura et al., Int J Low Extrem Wounds 2026; PMID 40080868
cards.search: zinc healing failure diabetic foot ulcer retrospective nakamura international journal lower extremity wounds 2026 serum pmid 40080868

cards.headline: Low zinc and poor early healing
cards.summary: Retrospective, 112 inpatients — zinc below 101 µg/dL: adjusted OR 4.75 (1.52–14.83) for poor 2-week healing.
cards.type: Single-center retrospective cohort, Chin J Clinicians 2025
cards.people: 112 hospitalized patients with Wagner grade 2–4 diabetic foot ulcers; 56 with poor and 56 with better healing at 2 weeks
cards.result: Zinc below 101 µg/dL was present in 51/56 poor healers vs 34/56 better healers; after adjustment, low zinc remained associated with poor healing: aOR 4.75 (1.52–14.83) , p = 0.007
cards.watchOut: The zinc cutoff was high and laboratory-specific, and the endpoint was 2-week wound-area response rather than complete healing
cards.source: Cui et al., Chin J Clinicians 2025
cards.search: zinc poor early healing diabetic foot ulcer retrospective cui chinese journal clinicians 2025 wagner adjusted odds ratio

cards.headline: How common is deficiency in foot ulcers?
cards.summary: Prospective, 131 patients — zinc deficiency 26.9% ; vitamin D 55.7% ; vitamin C deficient 50.8% .
cards.people: 131 patients with diabetes and foot ulcers seen in multidisciplinary foot clinics or a vascular-surgery unit
cards.result: Zinc deficiency 26.9% ; vitamin D deficiency 55.7% ; vitamin C deficient 50.8% (suboptimal 73.0%); vitamin A deficiency 10.9%; low ferritin 5.9%
cards.watchOut: The study measured prevalence and severity associations but did not report longitudinal healing outcomes by zinc status
cards.source: Pena et al., Adv Wound Care 2020; PMID 31871826
cards.search: zinc deficiency prevalence diabetic foot ulcers prospective pena advances wound care 2020 vitamin d vitamin c micronutrient pmid 31871826

cards.headline: Minerals: ulcer vs no ulcer in diabetes
cards.summary: Case-control, 64 adults — zinc 35.2 vs 58.8 µg/dL ; HbA1c 9.42% vs 7.38% .
cards.type: Hospital-based case-control study, Biol Trace Elem Res 2020
cards.people: 64 adults: 32 with type 2 diabetes and foot ulcer, 32 with diabetes without foot ulcer
cards.result: Serum zinc 35.2 vs 58.8 µg/dL in the foot-ulcer vs diabetes-control groups; HbA1c 9.42% vs 7.38%
cards.watchOut: The cross-sectional design cannot determine whether low zinc preceded the ulcer or reflected illness severity and glycemic control
cards.source: Yadav et al., Biol Trace Elem Res 2020; PMID 31435884
cards.search: minerals zinc ulcer diabetes case-control yadav biological trace element research 2020 hba1c pmid 31435884

cards.headline: Hypozincemia in Mexican outpatients
cards.summary: Cross-sectional, 102 patients — low zinc in 70% with ulcer vs 25% without; OR 5.2 (2.14–12.65) .
cards.type: Cross-sectional analytical observational study, Cir Cir 2022
cards.people: 102 Mexican outpatients with diabetes: 48 with diabetic foot ulcer, 54 without
cards.result: Hypozincemia (serum zinc below 70 µg/dL) in 70% of patients with ulcer vs 25% without; OR 5.2 (2.14–12.65) ; ulcer area did not differ significantly by zinc status
cards.watchOut: This study addressed ulcer presence, not prospective healing of an existing ulcer
cards.source: Sánchez-Cruz et al., Cir Cir 2022; PMID 35120107
cards.search: hypozincemia mexican outpatients diabetic foot ulcer cross-sectional sanchez-cruz cirugia cirujanos 2022 mexico pmid 35120107

cards.headline: Amputation cohort — zinc measured in only 9
cards.summary: Retrospective, 48 patients — amputation 52.1% ; vitamin C and albumin lower in amputees; zinc subset mean 10.6 µmol/L (n=9) .
cards.type: Retrospective cohort, Int J Low Extrem Wounds 2020
cards.people: 48 patients with diabetic foot ulcers at a tertiary diabetic-foot center; 25 underwent amputation
cards.result: Amputation rate 52.1% ; vitamin C 15.7 vs 28.4 µmol/L (p<0.01) and albumin lower in amputees; mean zinc for the small measured subset was 10.6 µmol/L
cards.watchOut: Zinc was measured in only nine patients, so the study cannot establish a reliable zinc–amputation association
cards.source: Brookes et al., Int J Low Extrem Wounds 2020; PMID 31549527
cards.search: micronutrient amputation diabetic foot ulcer retrospective brookes international journal lower extremity wounds 2020 zinc subset pmid 31549527

cards.headline: Oral zinc in grade 3 ulcers — positive trial, integrity concern
cards.summary: RCT, 60 patients — ulcer length −1.5 vs −0.9 cm (p=0.02); complete healing NS; a 2024 Expression of Concern cites unverifiable records.
cards.type: Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial, Wound Repair Regen 2017
cards.people: 60 patients aged 40–85 with grade 3 diabetic foot ulcers; 30 received zinc and 30 placebo
cards.result: Greater reductions in ulcer length with zinc: −1.5 vs −0.9 cm (p = 0.02), and width −1.4 vs −0.8 cm (p = 0.02); complete-treatment proportions were not significantly different
cards.watchOut: A 2024 Expression of Concern cited unresolved research-integrity and reporting concerns and inability to verify clinical records
cards.source: Momen-Heravi et al., Wound Repair Regen 2017; PMID 28395131
cards.search: oral zinc grade 3 diabetic foot ulcer randomized trial momen-heravi wound repair regeneration 2017 expression of concern 2024 pmid 28395131

cards.headline: Vitamin C + A + zinc pilot — neutral at 12 weeks
cards.summary: RCT, 99 patients — wound-area reduction 65% vs 75% (p=0.42); complete healing 13/49 vs 14/50 at 12 weeks.
cards.type: Double-blind randomized placebo-controlled pilot trial, Diabetes Obes Cardiometab Care 2026
cards.people: 99 participants with nonhealing diabetes-related foot ulcers; 49 received vitamin C, vitamin A and zinc, 50 received placebo
cards.result: Median wound-area reduction at 12 weeks 65% vs 75% (p = 0.42); complete healing 13/49 vs 14/50 at 12 weeks; baseline zinc deficiency in 11/99 participants (11.1%)
cards.watchOut: A multinutrient pilot trial, and the positive 4-week healing result was post hoc while the 12-week primary outcome was neutral
cards.source: Nixon et al., Diabetes Obes Cardiometab Care 2026

cards.headline: Zinc oxide tape for necrotic ulcers
cards.summary: RCT, 42 patients — ≥50% necrotic-area improvement 14/21 vs 6/21 ( p<0.025 ).
cards.type: Open randomized controlled trial with blinded photographic assessment, Br J Dermatol 1990
cards.people: 44 patients randomized; 42 patients, 21 per arm, contributed to the primary comparison
cards.result: At 5 weeks, necrotic ulcer area improved by at least 50% in 14/21 patients treated with zinc oxide tape (MeZinc) vs 6/21 treated with hydrocolloid (DuoDerm) ( p<0.025 )
cards.watchOut: Treatment was open-label and the endpoint was necrotic-area reduction rather than complete epithelial healing

cards.headline: Zinc oxide nanoparticle dressing
cards.summary: RCT, 26 patients — closure 75% vs 71% as reported; healing time 48 vs 72 days .
cards.type: Randomized controlled clinical trial, Biomed Pharmacother 2022
cards.people: 26 patients with type 2 diabetes and foot ulcers; 16 received the nanoparticle dressing and 10 control alginate
cards.result: Wound closure 75% vs 71% as reported (p = 0.011); average healing time 48 vs 72 days
cards.watchOut: A very small trial with unequal group sizes and imprecisely described wound-closure reporting
cards.source: Loera-Valencia et al., Biomed Pharmacother 2022; PMID 36162373

cards.headline: Topical zinc oxide, arterial and venous ulcers
cards.summary: RCT, 37 patients — clinical success 83% (15/18) vs 42% (8/19) .
cards.type: Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial, Br J Dermatol 1984
cards.people: 37 geriatric patients with leg ulcers (19 arterial, 18 venous); 18 received zinc oxide compresses and 19 placebo
cards.result: Clinical success in 15/18 (83%) zinc-treated vs 8/19 (42%) placebo patients (p<0.05); by 12 weeks, 11/18 zinc-treated ulcers vs 4/19 placebo ulcers had healed
cards.watchOut: The trial mixed arterial and venous ulcers and used a composite success definition before reporting complete healing
cards.source: Strömberg & Ågren, Br J Dermatol 1984; PMID 6386033

cards.headline: Oral zinc in chronic venous ulcers (1972)
cards.summary: RCT, 36 completers — healing 3 vs 2 patients ; rate difference NS .
cards.type: Double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial, Br J Dermatol 1972
cards.people: 38 patients enrolled and 36 completed the trial; the healing-rate table reported 15 patients per arm
cards.result: Complete healing in 3 zinc-treated vs 2 placebo patients; mean linear healing rate 0.9 vs 0.6 mm/week, not significant (p>0.2)
cards.watchOut: The report is small and only 30 of 36 completers appear in the main outcome table

cards.headline: Oral zinc in venous ulcers (1972)
cards.summary: RCT, 53 patients — healed by 3 months 11/12 (zinc capsules) vs 11/19 (placebo) among evaluable patients.
cards.type: Randomized double-blind trial plus nonblinded effervescent-zinc arm, Vasa 1972
cards.people: 53 ambulatory patients: 15 zinc capsules, 17 effervescent zinc, 21 placebo; the 3-month efficacy table included 12 zinc-capsule and 19 placebo patients
cards.result: Healed by 3 months: 11/12 zinc-capsule vs 11/19 placebo patients among evaluable patients (p<0.05 as reported); all 17 patients in the effervescent-zinc group healed; residual ulcer area 1.0% vs 35.7% at day 90
cards.watchOut: Attrition reduced the double-blind comparison and the effervescent-zinc arm was not a blinded placebo comparison

cards.headline: Oral zinc in ischemic ulcers — the low-zinc subgroup
cards.summary: Controlled trial, 30 in main analysis — low-zinc: 7/7 treated healed vs 5/7 untreated; no difference when zinc normal.
cards.type: Controlled trial stratified by baseline serum zinc, Vasa 1974
cards.people: Serum zinc measured in 50 patients with ischemic leg ulcers; the main analysis included 30 (7 low-zinc untreated, 7 low-zinc treated, 9 normal-zinc untreated, 7 normal-zinc treated)
cards.result: Low-zinc group: 7/7 treated vs 5/7 untreated ulcers healed within 1 year (p<0.01 as reported); normal-zinc group: 9/9 untreated and 7/7 treated healed, no significant treatment difference
cards.watchOut: The study was small, baseline ulcer sizes were imbalanced, and treatment assignment methods were incompletely reported
cards.source: Hæger & Lanner, Vasa 1974; PMID 4460452

cards.headline: Cochrane: oral zinc for leg ulcers — no benefit
cards.summary: Meta-analysis, 6 trials, 183 people — venous healing RR 1.22 (0.88–1.68) , NS .
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials (Cochrane), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014
cards.people: 6 small trials with 183 participants (4 venous-ulcer, 1 arterial-ulcer, 1 mixed-aetiology)
cards.result: Pooling 4 venous-ulcer trials: healing RR 1.22 (0.88–1.68) , not significant; no overall evidence that oral zinc increased healing of arterial or venous leg ulcers
cards.watchOut: All included trials were small and at unclear risk of bias because of poor reporting
cards.source: Wilkinson, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014; PMID 25202988

shelves.title: Vitamin E Deposit #23 · Oct 24, 2026
shelves.question: Does vitamin E help — liver, prostate, or anything else — and at what cost?
shelves.balance: Vitamin E improves liver histology in nondiabetic NASH/MASH ( 43% vs 19% in PIVENS; 29.3% vs 14.1% at 300 mg in MASH) without improving fibrosis — but the same vitamin, at 400 IU daily for prevention in healthy men, raised prostate cancer ( HR 1.17 ). Benefit is disease-specific and biopsy-deep; harm is prevention-dose-specific. Neither generalizes to the other. On dose, the 2026 VEDS trial found 200 IU/day matched 800 IU/day for ALT reduction over 24 weeks with no safety signal — if vitamin E is used, the lowest effective dose has the best-supported risk position.

cards.headline: Sanyal 2010 (PIVENS): vitamin E for NASH
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 247 nondiabetic adults with biopsy-proven NASH — histology improved 43% vs 19% (P=0.001) with vitamin E 800 IU/day; fibrosis not improved (P=0.24).
cards.people: 247 nondiabetic adults with biopsy-proven NASH; 84 received vitamin E 800 IU/day, 80 pioglitazone, and 83 placebo for 96 weeks
cards.result: The prespecified histologic primary outcome improved in 43% with vitamin E versus 19% with placebo (P=0.001). Vitamin E improved steatosis and lobular inflammation but did not significantly improve fibrosis (P=0.24)
cards.watchOut: The endpoint was liver histology rather than clinical liver outcomes, participants did not have diabetes, and fibrosis did not improve
cards.source: Sanyal AJ et al., N Engl J Med 2010;362:1675–1685, DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa0907929, PMID 20427778
cards.search: sanyal 2010 pivens vitamin e nash steatohepatitis liver histology pioglitazone randomized trial new england journal medicine pmid 20427778

cards.headline: Song 2025: vitamin E 300 mg for MASH
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 124 nondiabetic adults with biopsy-proven MASH — histology improved 29.3% vs 14.1% with vitamin E 300 mg/day over 96 weeks.
cards.people: 124 nondiabetic adults with biopsy-proven MASH, randomized 1:1 to vitamin E 300 mg/day or placebo for 96 weeks
cards.result: In the modified intention-to-treat analysis, the primary histologic outcome improved in 29.3% with vitamin E versus 14.1% with placebo. Twelve serious adverse events occurred, and none was judged treatment-related
cards.watchOut: This was a small trial conducted entirely in China, used a biopsy surrogate, and had greater-than-expected dropout during the COVID-19 pandemic
cards.source: Song Y et al., Cell Rep Med 2025;6:101939, DOI 10.1016/j.xcrm.2025.101939, PMID 39970876
cards.search: song 2025 vitamin e 300 mg mash metabolic steatohepatitis liver histology randomized trial cell reports medicine pmid 39970876

cards.headline: Dasarathy 2026 (VEDS): 200 IU a day matched 800 IU for ALT in fatty liver disease
cards.summary: NASH Clinical Research Network multicenter RCT, 200 adults with suspected MASH — ALT fell −38% (200 IU), −36% (400 IU) and −36% (800 IU) vs −12% on placebo over 24 weeks (p ≤0.001 for all); ALT normalized in 49% , 37% and 50% vs 22% . No safety signals — adverse events were mild to moderate and similar to placebo.
cards.type: Multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial (NASH Clinical Research Network)
cards.people: 200 adults with suspected MASH (CAP >280 dB/m on elastography, ALT ≥60 U/L), randomized to natural vitamin E 200, 400, or 800 IU/day or placebo for 24 weeks
cards.result: ALT fell equally at all doses: −38% (200 IU), −36% (400 IU), −36% (800 IU) vs −12% on placebo (p ≤0.001 for all). ALT normalized in 49% , 37% , and 50% vs 22% on placebo. Adverse events were mild to moderate, there were no life-threatening events, and rates were similar between vitamin E and placebo — no safety signals. The authors concluded 200 IU/day was as effective as the higher doses
cards.watchOut: 24 weeks only, and a surrogate endpoint (ALT) — the trial supports using the lowest effective dose; it does not address the safety of years-long high-dose use, where the SELECT and mortality signals live
cards.source: Dasarathy S et al., Hepatology 2026, “Vitamin E dosing study (VEDS) in patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease with elevated aminotransferases,” DOI 10.1097/HEP.0000000000001797, PMID 42268981
cards.search: dasarathy 2026 veds vitamin e dosing study mash masld metabolic dysfunction steatotic liver alt aminotransferases hepatology nash clinical research network randomized trial dose pmid 42268981

shelves.title: Vitamin E and prostate cancer (SELECT)
shelves.question: Does vitamin E 400 IU/day raise prostate cancer risk in healthy men?
shelves.balance: SELECT’s harm arrived in two acts: the 2009 primary report showed no prevention benefit and a nonsignificant vitamin E trend (473 vs 416 cases, HR 1.13), and the supplements were stopped early for futility; extended follow-up made the harm significant — 620 vs 529 cases, HR 1.17, about 1.6 extra cancers per 1,000 person-years (Klein 2011). The harm is prevention-dose-specific: the same vitamin at treatment doses improves liver histology in MASH without this signal.

cards.headline: The first report: no prevention, supplements stopped early — and a warning trend.
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 35,533 healthy men — at median follow-up 5.46 years , no arm prevented prostate cancer: vitamin E 473 vs 416 cases, HR 1.13 (99% CI 0.95–1.35; P = .06) ; supplements stopped early for futility.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial — the SELECT primary report.
cards.people: 35,533 healthy men (age 50+ if African American, 55+ otherwise; PSA ≤4 ng/mL) in the US, Canada and Puerto Rico; vitamin E 400 IU/day, selenium 200 µg/day, both, or placebo, planned 7–12 years.
cards.result: At median follow-up 5.46 years, no arm prevented prostate cancer: vitamin E 473 cases vs 416 on placebo ( HR 1.13 ; 99% CI 0.95–1.35; P = .06); selenium 432 cases (HR 1.04); the combination 437 cases (HR 1.05). The data and safety monitoring committee stopped the supplements in 2008 for futility.
cards.watchOut: The vitamin E excess was not yet statistically significant in this report — it became significant only with extended follow-up (Reference 2). A “nonsignificant trend” in a prevention trial of healthy people is not reassurance.
cards.source: Lippman SM, Klein EA, Goodman PJ, et al. Effect of selenium and vitamin E on risk of prostate cancer and other cancers: the Selenium and Vitamin E Cancer Prevention Trial (SELECT). JAMA 2009;301(1):39–51. DOI 10.1001/jama.2008.864. PMID 19066370.
cards.search: lippman 2009 select selenium vitamin e prostate cancer primary report randomized trial jama stopped early futility pmid 19066370

cards.headline: Klein 2011 (SELECT): vitamin E and prostate cancer
cards.summary: Randomized prevention trial, 35,533 men randomized, 34,887 analyzed — prostate cancer 620 vs 529 , HR 1.17 (99% CI 1.004–1.36; P=0.008) with vitamin E 400 IU/day; absolute excess 1.6 per 1,000 person-years.
cards.type: Large randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled 2×2 factorial prevention trial with extended follow-up
cards.people: 35,533 men randomized, 34,887 in the primary analysis (8,737 vitamin E alone, 8,696 placebo)
cards.result: Vitamin E 400 IU/day: prostate cancer 620 vs 529 ( HR 1.17 , 99% CI 1.004–1.36; P=0.008); absolute excess 1.6 prostate cancers per 1,000 person-years
cards.watchOut: This harm signal applies to 400 IU/day synthetic alpha-tocopherol used for prevention in generally healthy men, not necessarily to lower doses or selected MASH treatment
cards.source: Klein EA, Thompson IM Jr, Tangen CM, et al., JAMA 2011;306:1549–1556, DOI 10.1001/jama.2011.1437, PMID 21990298
cards.search: klein 2011 select vitamin e prostate cancer supplement harm randomized trial jama synthetic alpha-tocopherol pmid 21990298

shelves.title: Annual vitamin D mega-dose and falls/fractures (Sanders)
shelves.question: Does a single annual 500,000-IU vitamin D dose prevent falls and fractures — or cause them?
shelves.balance: It caused them: falls up 15%, fractures up 26% in 2,256 older women. The finding belongs to the annual mega-dose alone and says nothing about daily replacement for deficiency.

cards.headline: Sanders 2010: annual mega-dose vitamin D, falls and fractures
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 2,256 women aged 70+ at high fracture risk — falls 2,892 vs 2,512 , RR 1.15 (1.02–1.30) ; fractures 171 vs 135 , RR 1.26 (1.00–1.59) with one annual 500,000-IU dose.
cards.people: 2,256 community-dwelling women aged at least 70 years at high fracture risk (1,131 vitamin D, 1,125 placebo)
cards.result: Single annual 500,000-IU vitamin D dose: falls 2,892 (83.4 per 100 person-years) vs 2,512 (72.7), incidence RR 1.15 (95% CI 1.02–1.30); fractures 171 vs 135 , incidence RR 1.26 (95% CI 1.00–1.59)
cards.watchOut: The finding applies to a very large annual bolus dose and should not be generalized to ordinary daily replacement for documented deficiency
cards.source: Sanders KM, Stuart AL, Williamson EJ, et al., JAMA 2010;303:1815–1822, DOI 10.1001/jama.2010.594, PMID 20460620
cards.search: sanders 2010 annual vitamin d 500000 iu falls fractures older women supplement harm randomized trial jama pmid 20460620

shelves.title: Beta-carotene, vitamin A, and lung cancer (CARET)
shelves.question: Does high-dose beta-carotene plus vitamin A prevent lung cancer in smokers?
shelves.balance: Twice tested, twice harmful: beta-carotene raised lung cancer 18% in 29,133 Finnish smokers (ATBC 1994), and the beta-carotene + vitamin A combination raised it 28% in 18,314 US smokers and asbestos-exposed workers (CARET 1996, stopped 21 months early). The harm belongs to high-dose supplements in high-risk lungs, not to carotenoids in food.

cards.headline: Omenn 1996 (CARET): beta-carotene plus vitamin A in smokers
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 18,314 smokers and asbestos-exposed adults — lung cancer RR 1.28 (1.04–1.57) ; all-cause death RR 1.17 ; lung-cancer death RR 1.46 ; stopped 21 months early.
cards.type: Multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled primary-prevention trial
cards.people: 18,314 current or former smokers and workers exposed to asbestos
cards.result: Beta-carotene 30 mg/day plus retinyl palmitate 25,000 IU/day: lung cancer RR 1.28 (95% CI 1.04–1.57); all-cause death RR 1.17 (95% CI 1.03–1.33); lung-cancer death RR 1.46 (95% CI 1.07–2.00); trial stopped 21 months early
cards.watchOut: The harm applies to this high-dose combination in smokers and asbestos-exposed adults, not to carotenoids consumed in food
cards.source: Omenn GS, Goodman GE, Thornquist MD, et al., N Engl J Med 1996;334:1150–1155, DOI 10.1056/NEJM199605023341802, PMID 8602180
cards.search: omenn 1996 caret beta carotene retinyl palmitate vitamin a lung cancer smokers asbestos supplement harm randomized trial stopped early new england journal medicine pmid 8602180

cards.headline: The first warning: beta-carotene raised lung cancer 18% in Finnish smokers.
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 29,133 male smokers in Finland — beta-carotene: lung cancer +18% (95% CI 3 to 36%), total mortality +8% ; vitamin E: no effect on lung cancer.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled primary-prevention trial (2×2 factorial)
cards.people: 29,133 male smokers aged 50–69 in southwestern Finland; beta-carotene 20 mg/day, alpha-tocopherol (vitamin E) 50 mg/day, both, or placebo, for 5–8 years (median 6.1 years)
cards.result: Beta-carotene: lung cancer incidence +18% (95% CI 3 to 36%) and total mortality +8% versus no beta-carotene. Alpha-tocopherol: no effect on lung cancer incidence (−2%; 95% CI −14 to +12%)
cards.watchOut: The harm is high-dose beta-carotene in people who smoke — not carotenoids in food. ATBC (1994) came first; CARET (Card 1, 1996) confirmed the harm in a second high-risk population, and the field stopped testing beta-carotene for lung-cancer prevention.
cards.source: The Alpha-Tocopherol, Beta Carotene Cancer Prevention Study Group. The effect of vitamin E and beta carotene on the incidence of lung cancer and other cancers in male smokers. N Engl J Med 1994;330(15):1029–1035. DOI 10.1056/NEJM199404143301501. PMID 8127329.
cards.search: atbc 1994 alpha tocopherol beta carotene cancer prevention study group finland male smokers lung cancer vitamin e randomized trial factorial harm new england journal medicine pmid 8127329 doi 10.1056/nejm199404143301501

shelves.title: Vitamin D and respiratory infection in children
shelves.question: Does high-dose vitamin D prevent upper respiratory infection in children?
shelves.balance: The two child RCTs split — Urashima positive for influenza A specifically ( RR 0.58 ), Aglipay null for all viral upper respiratory infections when extra dose is added on top of standard intake in replete toddlers; the 2017 IPD child stratum was strongly positive ( OR 0.60 ) while the pooled children-only meta-analysis (Carboo) is null and imprecise. The signal may be real for influenza and for deficient children; it is not a general “vitamin D prevents colds in kids” result.

cards.headline: In children, high-dose vitamin D’s effect on upper respiratory infection is not significant — and rests on just two trials
cards.summary: URTI OR 0.83 (0.62–1.10) , not significant — 5,748 children across the review; the URTI estimate pools only two trials.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs, Nutr Rev 2024
cards.people: 5,748 children across the review; the upper-respiratory-infection estimate pools only two trials
cards.result: URTI OR 0.83 (0.62–1.10) , not significant
cards.watchOut: The URTI result rests on just two trials, so it is imprecise
cards.source: Carboo JA, Dolman-Macleod RC, Malan L, et al. Nutr Rev 2024;82(5):579–599. DOI 10.1093/nutrit/nuad082. PMID 37428896
cards.search: carboo 2024 high-dose vitamin d upper respiratory infection children urti meta-analysis nutrition reviews pmid 37428896 two trials

cards.headline: Urashima 2010: vitamin D3 cut influenza A in Japanese schoolchildren
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 334 schoolchildren, vitamin D3 1,200 IU/day vs placebo, Dec 2008–Mar 2009 — influenza A 10.8% vs 18.6% ; RR 0.58 (0.34–0.99) , P = 0.04. No effect on influenza B.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, Am J Clin Nutr 2010
cards.people: 334 Japanese schoolchildren (167 vitamin D3, 167 placebo), Dec 2008–Mar 2009
cards.result: Influenza A: 18/167 (10.8%) vs 31/167 (18.6%) ; RR 0.58 (95% CI 0.34–0.99) , P = 0.04. No effect on influenza B. Secondary outcome — asthma attacks in children with prior asthma: 2 vs 12 ; RR 0.17 (0.04–0.73), P = 0.006
cards.watchOut: One winter season in one country; the asthma finding is a secondary outcome in a small subgroup
cards.source: Urashima M et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2010;91(5):1255–1260. DOI 10.3945/ajcn.2009.29094
cards.search: urashima 2010 vitamin d3 influenza a schoolchildren japan randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial asthma attacks american journal clinical nutrition doi 10.3945/ajcn.2009.29094

cards.headline: Aglipay 2017 (DO IT): extra vitamin D did not prevent winter colds in young children
cards.summary: Randomized trial, Toronto, 703 children aged 1–5 — 2,000 vs 400 IU/day for at least 4 winter months: laboratory-confirmed viral upper respiratory infections IRR 0.97 (0.80–1.16) , no difference.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (DO IT trial, Toronto), JAMA 2017
cards.people: 703 children aged 1–5 years: 349 assigned vitamin D 2,000 IU/day, 354 assigned 400 IU/day, for at least 4 winter months
cards.result: Laboratory-confirmed viral upper respiratory infections: incidence rate ratio 0.97 (95% CI 0.80–1.16) — no difference. Parent-reported infections 625 vs 600 , IRR 1.01 (0.88–1.16). End-of-study 25(OH)D 48.7 vs 36.8 ng/mL . The authors conclude routine high-dose vitamin D is not supported for preventing winter colds in young children
cards.watchOut: High-dose vs standard-dose — no placebo arm — in vitamin-D-replete toddlers; unlike Urashima’s placebo-controlled trial, it tests extra dose on top of standard intake
cards.search: aglipay 2017 do it trial vitamin d upper respiratory infection children toronto jama high dose standard dose winter colds doi 10.1001/jama.2017.8708

cards.headline: Martineau 2017: the child stratum of the IPD meta-analysis — the strongest protection of any age group
cards.summary: Child subgroup (ages 1–16) of a 25-RCT individual-participant-data meta-analysis — adjusted OR 0.60 (0.46–0.77) , P < 0.001; no significant protection under age 1. A mixed-age meta-analysis, not a children-only study.
cards.type: Individual-participant-data meta-analysis of 25 RCTs, all ages — this card reports the child stratum only, BMJ 2017
cards.people: 25 randomized trials overall (pooled adjusted OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.81–0.96); the child stratum covers ages 1–16 years
cards.result: In children aged 1–16 years, vitamin D was protective: adjusted OR 0.60 (95% CI 0.46–0.77) , P < 0.001 — the strongest effect of any age group. No significant protection in infants under 1 year
cards.watchOut: A subgroup of a mixed-age meta-analysis, not a children-only study; subgroup effects can overstate the benefit
cards.source: Martineau AR et al., BMJ 2017;356:i6583
cards.search: martineau 2017 vitamin d acute respiratory infection individual participant data meta-analysis bmj child subgroup ages 1 to 16 i6583

shelves.title: Vitamin D and bladder infection in adults
shelves.question: Does vitamin D help adults fight bladder infection — and does supplementation prevent urinary infection?
shelves.balance: In adults, low vitamin D tracks with more urinary infection — a 2019 meta-analysis puts the odds at 3.01 — but the link is observational, and the one trial that cut UTIs (Jorde, 18 vs 34 over five years) used self-reported outcomes as a secondary endpoint. The bladder mechanism is real in tissue (Hertting): vitamin D primes bladder cells to make cathelicidin on bacterial contact. Correcting deficiency is sensible care; preventing infection with vitamin D is still open.

cards.headline: Low vitamin D tracks with more urinary infection — in 1,921 people, insufficiency triples the odds
cards.summary: Vitamin D insufficiency associated with UTI, pooled OR 3.01 (2.31–3.91) — 9 studies, 1,921 participants, 580 with UTI.
cards.people: 9 studies, 1,921 participants, 580 with UTI
cards.result: Vitamin D insufficiency associated with UTI, pooled OR 3.01 (2.31–3.91) , I²=49.5%. Vitamin D level lower in the UTI group (SMD −1.65 , −2.69 to −0.60, I²=97.9%). Children subgroup OR 4.78 (3.08–7.44)
cards.watchOut: Association only — all observational; high heterogeneity on the level comparison
cards.source: Deng QF et al. Ann Clin Lab Sci 2019;49(1):134. PMID 30814089
cards.search: deng 2019 vitamin d insufficiency urinary tract infection uti meta-analysis pooled odds ratio 3.01 children subgroup annals clinical laboratory science pmid 30814089

cards.headline: Five years of weekly vitamin D cut reported UTIs by about half — 18 vs 34
cards.summary: UTI reported in 18 on vitamin D vs 34 on placebo ( p<0.02 ) — 511 adults with prediabetes, five years of weekly vitamin D3.
cards.people: 511 adults with prediabetes, vitamin D3 20,000 IU/week vs placebo for five years (256 vs 255; 116 vs 111 completed)
cards.result: UTI reported in 18 on vitamin D vs 34 on placebo (p<0.02). No significant difference for respiratory infection. Effect most pronounced in males; unrelated to baseline serum 25(OH)D (mean 60 nmol/L)
cards.watchOut: UTI by self-report questionnaire every 6 months; secondary outcome of a diabetes-prevention trial; only 227 of 511 completed five years
cards.search: jorde 2016 vitamin d supplementation urinary tract infection uti prediabetes randomised controlled trial 20000 iu weekly placebo five years pmid 27357103

cards.headline: Vitamin D switches on the bladder’s own antibiotic in tissue — but not in blood
cards.summary: Mechanistic study with a small human series — 8 postmenopausal women took 2,000 units of oral 25D3 daily for 12 weeks; serum 25D3 rose from 68.5 to 117 nmol/L and serum cathelicidin did NOT rise, but E. coli -infected bladder biopsies after supplementation produced more CAMP mRNA and cathelicidin protein (both P<0.05 ).
cards.type: Mechanistic study (bladder epithelial cells and biopsies) plus a small human supplementation series
cards.people: 22 postmenopausal + 6 premenopausal Swedish women analyzed for serum levels; 8 additional postmenopausal women (median age 62) supplemented
cards.result: 2,000 units oral 25D3 daily for 12 weeks raised serum 25D3 from median 68.5 to 104.5 nmol/L at 6 weeks (P<0.001) and 117 nmol/L at 12 weeks (P<0.01). Serum cathelicidin did NOT rise. But E. coli -infected bladder biopsies taken after supplementation expressed more CAMP mRNA ( P<0.05 ) and more cathelicidin protein ( P<0.05 ) than pre-supplementation biopsies
cards.watchOut: The human arm is 8 women, no control group; the effect is in tissue, not blood, and no infection outcome was measured
cards.source: Hertting O, Holm Å, Lüthje P, et al. PLoS One. 2010;5(12):e15580. PMID: 21179490. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0015580
cards.search: hertting 2010 vitamin d urinary bladder antibiotic cathelicidin camp ll-37 e coli infected biopsies postmenopausal women 25d3 supplementation plos one pmid 21179490 mechanistic

cards.headline: Women with UTI run about half the vitamin D of women without — 11 vs 24 ng/mL
cards.summary: Serum 25(OH)D 11.09 ± 7.571 ng/mL in women with UTI vs 24.08 ± 11.95 ng/mL in controls ( P<0.001 ) — 75 cases vs 35 controls.
cards.people: 75 women with UTI vs 35 healthy controls, ages 17–52, Rizgary Teaching Hospital, Erbil
cards.result: Serum 25(OH)D 11.09 ± 7.571 ng/mL in cases vs 24.08 ± 11.95 ng/mL in controls, P<0.001
cards.watchOut: Small, single-center, no adjusted odds ratio in the abstract
cards.search: ali 2020 vitamin d deficiency urinary tract infection women reproductive age case-control erbil rizgary serum 25ohd pmid 33100850

shelves.title: Vitamin D and bladder infection in children
shelves.question: Does vitamin D help children fight bladder infection — and does supplementation prevent urinary infection in children?
shelves.balance: In children, low vitamin D tracks with more urinary infection — a 2023 meta-analysis of 13 studies finds levels about 8 ng/mL lower in children with UTI, and below 20 ng/mL the odds rise fivefold — but every study is observational, and the one small trial of supplementation found nothing. Correcting deficiency is sensible; preventing UTI with vitamin D is unproven in children.

cards.headline: Children with UTI run about 8 ng/mL lower on vitamin D — and below 20 ng/mL the odds rise fivefold
cards.summary: Vitamin D lower in children with UTI (WMD −7.730 ng/mL , p<0.001); below 20 ng/mL, OR 5.49 — 839 children with UTI + 929 controls across 13 studies.
cards.people: 12 case-control studies + 1 cross-sectional, 839 children with UTI + 929 controls
cards.result: Vitamin D lower in children with UTI (WMD −7.730 ng/mL , −11.57 to −3.89, p<0.001). Low vitamin D associated with UTI (OR 2.80 , 1.55–5.05, p=0.001). Below 20 ng/mL the odds rise further (OR 5.49 , 1.12–27.04, p=0.036)
cards.watchOut: Case-control only; the below-20 estimate has a very wide confidence interval
cards.source: Gan Y et al. Nutrients 2023;15(12):2690. PMID 37375601
cards.search: gan yang 2023 vitamin d urinary tract infection children uti meta-analysis case-control below 20 ng ml odds ratio nutrients pmid 37375601

cards.headline: In children with recurrent UTI, 1,000 IU a day for six months changed nothing
cards.summary: UTI frequency NOT significantly different between groups ( P=0.72 ) — 68 children and adolescents with recurrent UTI, 1,000 IU/day for 6 months.
cards.people: 68 children and adolescents with recurrent UTI, vitamin D 1,000 IU/day vs placebo for 6 months (33 vs 32 completed)
cards.result: UTI frequency NOT significantly different between groups (P=0.72). Serum vitamin D rose in the intervention arm (15.80 to 20.56 ng/mL, P<0.001) and fell in placebo
cards.watchOut: Small, low dose, short follow-up; the authors suggest higher doses and longer follow-up
cards.source: Merrikhi A et al. Adv Biomed Res 2018
cards.search: merrikhi 2018 vitamin d supplementation recurrent urinary tract infection children uti randomised triple-masked placebo-controlled trial 1000 iu null advanced biomedical research

shelves.title: The vitamin D guideline: who should get vitamin D, and who shouldn’t be tested.
shelves.question: What does the 2024 Endocrine Society guideline say about who should get vitamin D — and who shouldn’t be tested for it?
shelves.balance: Thirteen years of guidance trace one arc — aim high and test (Endocrine 2011: target above 30 ng/mL , 1,500–2,000 IU/day); the nutrition establishment demurring the same year (IOM: 20 ng/mL suffices, bone outcomes only); prevention policy unable to judge screening (USPSTF 2021: I statement); and the specialty society finally landing on empiric supplementation for four defined groups with no routine testing and no definable target level (Endocrine 2024). The shelf is the record of a field correcting itself.

cards.headline: Vitamin D for everyone? No — for children, over-75s, pregnancy, and prediabetes. And stop testing everyone.
cards.summary: Empiric vitamin D suggested for ages 1–18 , adults ≥75 , pregnant people and high-risk prediabetes — against it in healthy adults under 75, and against routine 25(OH)D testing in everyone covered.
cards.type: Clinical practice guideline (GRADE methodology; 14 clinical questions; systematic reviews of randomized placebo-controlled trials in general populations without an established indication for vitamin D or testing).
cards.people: Guideline panel: 18 authors, including the developer (John A. Tayek, author 14 of 18; Harbor-UCLA Medical Center and Lundquist Institute). Populations considered: ages 1–18, adults ≥75, pregnant people, high-risk prediabetes, healthy adults <75, people with obesity or dark complexion.
cards.result: The panel suggests empiric vitamin D supplementation (intake above the Dietary Reference Intakes, without testing) for: children and adolescents aged 1–18 years (to prevent nutritional rickets and because of its potential to lower respiratory tract infections); adults aged 75 years and older (potential to lower mortality); pregnant people (potential to lower preeclampsia, intra-uterine mortality, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and neonatal mortality); and people with high-risk prediabetes (potential to reduce progression to diabetes). For nonpregnant people over 50 for whom vitamin D is indicated, daily administration is suggested over intermittent high doses. The panel suggests AGAINST empiric vitamin D above the current DRI to lower disease risk in healthy adults younger than 75 years, and AGAINST routine 25(OH)D testing in all populations considered — no trial evidence supports routine screening, including in obesity or dark complexion, and no optimal 25(OH)D target level for disease prevention could be defined.
cards.watchOut: All recommendations are conditional ("suggests"): the optimal doses for empiric supplementation remain unclear (trial doses varied considerably and many participants continued their own vitamin D supplements), and the optimal 25(OH)D level is undefined. The recommendations do not replace the current DRIs and do not apply to people with established indications for vitamin D treatment or 25(OH)D testing. Empiric supplementation was judged inexpensive, feasible, acceptable, and without negative effect on health equity.
cards.source: Demay MB, Pittas AG, Bikle DD, et al. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2024;109(8):1907–1947. PMID 38828931. DOI 10.1210/clinem/dgae290.
cards.search: demay 2024 endocrine society vitamin d guideline empiric supplementation 25(oh)d testing screening children adolescents pregnancy prediabetes elderly grade jcem pmid 38828931 doi 10.1210/clinem/dgae290 tayek founder

cards.headline: Holick 2011: the same society, 13 years earlier — aim above 30 ng/mL, and test the at-risk
cards.summary: Endocrine Society guideline 2011 — deficiency below 20 ng/mL , insufficiency 21–29 ng/mL , target above 30 ng/mL ; adults may need 1,500–2,000 IU/day to stay above 30; treatment 50,000 IU weekly for 8 weeks, then maintenance.
cards.type: Clinical practice guideline, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2011
cards.people: People at risk of vitamin D deficiency — 25(OH)D testing recommended for at-risk groups
cards.result: Vitamin D deficiency defined as 25(OH)D below 20 ng/mL , insufficiency 21–29 ng/mL , with a target above 30 ng/mL . Adults may need 1,500–2,000 IU/day to stay above 30. Deficient adults treated with 50,000 IU once weekly for 8 weeks (or about 6,000 IU/day), then maintenance 1,500–2,000 IU/day
cards.watchOut: The opposite posture to the 2024 guideline (Reference 1): test-and-target, where 2024 lands on empiric supplementation with no routine testing and no definable target
cards.source: Holick MF et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2011;96(7):1911–1930
cards.search: holick 2011 endocrine society vitamin d deficiency guideline evaluation treatment prevention jcem 25(oh)d target 30 ng/ml insufficiency 50000 iu

cards.headline: IOM 2011: 20 ng/mL is enough — RDA 600 IU/day, set on bone health alone
cards.summary: Dietary Reference Intakes 2011 — EAR 400 IU/day ; RDA 600 IU/day (ages 1–70) and 800 IU/day (71+), matching a serum 25(OH)D of 20 ng/mL for at least 97.5% of the population; tolerable upper level 4,000 IU/day .
cards.type: Dietary Reference Intakes report (Institute of Medicine, 2011), summarized by Ross et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2011
cards.people: The general population; the RDA is set to meet the needs of at least 97.5% of the population
cards.result: EAR 400 IU/day ; RDA 600 IU/day for ages 1–70 and 800 IU/day for 71+, corresponding to a serum 25(OH)D of 20 ng/mL . Tolerable upper intake level 4,000 IU/day . The committee based the numbers on bone health alone, finding the evidence for every non-skeletal outcome inconsistent or inconclusive, and noted U-shaped risk associations for some outcomes
cards.watchOut: Published the same year as the 2011 Endocrine Society guideline (Reference 2) with a target 10 ng/mL lower — the two 2011 documents disagreed from the start
cards.source: Institute of Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes for Calcium and Vitamin D. 2011; summary: Ross AC et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2011;96(1):53–58
cards.search: institute of medicine iom 2011 dietary reference intakes calcium vitamin d ross jcem ear rda 600 iu 800 upper level 4000 bone health 20 ng/ml

cards.headline: USPSTF 2021: screening for vitamin D deficiency — evidence insufficient (I statement)
cards.summary: USPSTF recommendation 2021 — I statement : evidence insufficient to assess screening for vitamin D deficiency in asymptomatic, community-dwelling, nonpregnant adults. The evidence review ( 46 studies , 16,205 participants) found no study that directly tested screening.
cards.type: Recommendation statement with systematic evidence review, JAMA 2021
cards.people: Asymptomatic, community-dwelling, nonpregnant adults; the evidence review covered 46 studies with 16,205 participants
cards.result: I statement : the evidence is insufficient to assess the benefits and harms of screening for vitamin D deficiency in this population. No study in the review directly tested screening, and treatment was not significantly linked to mortality, fractures, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, cancer, or depression
cards.watchOut: An I statement is not a recommendation against screening — it is a judgment that the evidence cannot support a recommendation either way
cards.source: US Preventive Services Task Force. JAMA 2021;325(14):1436–1442. DOI 10.1001/jama.2021.3069
cards.search: uspstf 2021 vitamin d deficiency screening asymptomatic adults i statement jama evidence review doi 10.1001/jama.2021.3069

shelves.title: Folic acid and neural tube defects
shelves.question: Does periconceptional folic acid prevent neural tube defects?
shelves.balance: Two randomized trials, two populations: 4 mg a day cut recurrence by 72% in women with a previous affected pregnancy, and 0.8 mg in a multivitamin eliminated first occurrences in the trial (0 vs 6). The 400–800 mcg a day recommendation is the public-health dose between them — lower than either trial dose, anchored by these two trials.

cards.headline: 4 mg folic acid a day cut neural-tube-defect recurrence by 72% — 6 vs 21 cases.
cards.summary: 27 neural tube defects in total: 6 in the folic-acid groups vs 21 in the no-folic-acid groups. Relative risk 0.28 (95% CI 0.12–0.71) — a 72% reduction. The effect was attributable to folic acid alone; the other-vitamins arm showed no effect.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, multicentre trial, 4 arms (folic acid 4 mg, other vitamins, folic acid + vitamins, no folic acid).
cards.people: 1,817 women with a previous neural-tube-defect pregnancy, recruited across 33 centres.
cards.result: 27 neural tube defects in total: 6 in the folic-acid groups vs 21 in the no-folic-acid groups. Relative risk 0.28 (95% CI 0.12–0.71) — a 72% reduction. The effect was attributable to folic acid alone; the other-vitamins arm showed no effect.
cards.watchOut: Recurrence population — women with a previous affected pregnancy, the highest-risk group; the 4 mg dose is ten times the usual 400 mcg recommendation; results do not by themselves establish the first-occurrence dose.
cards.source: MRC Vitamin Study Research Group. Lancet. 1991;338(8758):131–137. PMID 1677062. DOI 10.1016/0140-6736(91)90133-A.
cards.search: mrc vitamin study 1991 folic acid neural tube defects recurrence 4 mg lancet multicentre pmid 1677062 doi 10.1016/0140-6736(91)90133-a

cards.headline: A multivitamin with 0.8 mg folic acid: zero neural tube defects vs six in the control group.
cards.summary: No neural tube defects in the vitamin-supplement group vs 6 in the trace-element group ( P=0.029 ). Congenital malformations overall 13.3 vs 22.9 per 1,000 (P=0.02) . Cleft lip with or without cleft palate was not reduced.
cards.people: Pregnancy confirmed in 4,753 women planning a pregnancy (in most cases their first); outcome known in 2,104 women who received the vitamin supplement and 2,052 who received the trace-element supplement. One tablet daily from at least one month before conception until the second missed menstrual period or later.
cards.result: No neural tube defects in the vitamin-supplement group vs 6 in the trace-element group ( P=0.029 ). Congenital malformations overall 13.3 vs 22.9 per 1,000 (P=0.02) . Cleft lip with or without cleft palate was not reduced.
cards.watchOut: A multivitamin, not folic acid alone — the design cannot isolate folic acid from the other 11 vitamins, 4 minerals and 3 trace elements in the tablet; the control group received trace elements, not nothing.
cards.source: Czeizel AE, Dudás I. N Engl J Med. 1992;327(26):1832–1835. (PMID to confirm from the PubMed record before build.)

shelves.title: AREDS2 formulation and macular degeneration
shelves.question: Does the AREDS2 formulation slow progression to advanced age-related macular degeneration?
shelves.balance: The original AREDS formula's 25% reduction in progression stands; nothing added on top in AREDS2 helped further. AREDS2's real contribution is subtraction — beta-carotene out, because it raised lung cancer in former smokers, and lutein with zeaxanthin in.

cards.headline: Antioxidants plus zinc cut progression to advanced AMD by 25% at 5 years.
cards.summary: The formulation — vitamin C 500 mg, vitamin E 400 IU, beta-carotene 15 mg, zinc 80 mg, copper 2 mg — reduced progression to advanced AMD by 25% at 5 years in participants with intermediate AMD or advanced AMD in one eye (categories 3–4).
cards.people: 4,757 participants aged 55–80 with AMD categories 2–4 (early to advanced in one eye).
cards.result: The formulation — vitamin C 500 mg, vitamin E 400 IU, beta-carotene 15 mg, zinc 80 mg, copper 2 mg — reduced progression to advanced AMD by 25% at 5 years in participants with intermediate AMD or advanced AMD in one eye (categories 3–4).
cards.watchOut: Benefit only in intermediate/advanced disease (categories 3–4); no benefit in early AMD or no AMD; 25% is a relative reduction.
cards.source: Age-Related Eye Disease Study Research Group. Arch Ophthalmol. 2001;119(10):1417–1436. (PMID to confirm from the PubMed record before build.)
cards.search: areds 2001 age-related eye disease study antioxidants zinc vitamin c vitamin e beta-carotene macular degeneration amd progression archives ophthalmology

cards.headline: Adding lutein, zeaxanthin, or omega-3 added nothing — but swapping beta-carotene out for lutein/zeaxanthin cut progression ~18% and removed a lung-cancer signal.
cards.summary: No statistically significant further reduction in progression to advanced AMD from adding lutein 10 mg + zeaxanthin 2 mg, DHA 350 mg + EPA 650 mg, or both. Five-year probabilities of progression: placebo 31% , lutein + zeaxanthin 29% , DHA + EPA 31% , both 30% ( HR 0.90, 98.7% CI 0.76–1.07 ). Eliminating beta-carotene or lowering zinc to 25 mg did not change progression. More lung cancers occurred with beta-carotene than without ( 23 [2%] vs 11 [0.9%] ), mostly in former smokers. Secondary analysis: lutein + zeaxanthin without beta-carotene gave ~18% lower progression than the beta-carotene version, and 26% lower in participants with low dietary lutein/zeaxanthin intake.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, 2006–2012.
cards.people: 4,203 participants aged 50–85 at risk for progression to advanced AMD (bilateral large drusen, or large drusen in one eye and advanced AMD in the fellow eye); median follow-up 4.9 years. All participants took the original AREDS formulation or a secondary randomization to four variations (beta-carotene eliminated, lower zinc, or both).
cards.result: No statistically significant further reduction in progression to advanced AMD from adding lutein 10 mg + zeaxanthin 2 mg, DHA 350 mg + EPA 650 mg, or both. Five-year probabilities of progression: placebo 31% , lutein + zeaxanthin 29% , DHA + EPA 31% , both 30% ( HR 0.90, 98.7% CI 0.76–1.07 ). Eliminating beta-carotene or lowering zinc to 25 mg did not change progression. More lung cancers occurred with beta-carotene than without ( 23 [2%] vs 11 [0.9%] ), mostly in former smokers. Secondary analysis: lutein + zeaxanthin without beta-carotene gave ~18% lower progression than the beta-carotene version, and 26% lower in participants with low dietary lutein/zeaxanthin intake.
cards.watchOut: The primary result is a null for the additions; the 18% and 26% figures are secondary/subgroup analyses, not the primary outcome; current smokers were excluded from beta-carotene arms from the start, so the lung-cancer signal is mostly in former smokers.
cards.source: Age-Related Eye Disease Study 2 Research Group (Chew EY et al.). JAMA. 2013;309(19):2005–2015. (PMID to confirm from the PubMed record before build.)
cards.search: areds2 2013 lutein zeaxanthin omega-3 dha epa beta-carotene lung cancer jama chew age-related eye disease study macular degeneration amd

shelves.title: Routine calcium plus vitamin D (fracture prevention)
shelves.question: Does routine calcium plus vitamin D prevent fractures in healthy adults?
shelves.balance: The biggest trial says no significant hip-fracture benefit and more kidney stones; the 69-trial pool says little to no clinically meaningful fracture effect. Routine calcium plus D for fracture prevention in healthy adults is a near-null with a real stone risk.

cards.headline: 69 trials, 154,000 adults: calcium, vitamin D, or both — little to no clinically meaningful fracture effect.
cards.summary: Any-fracture risk ratios: calcium alone 0.91 , vitamin D alone 1.00 , combined calcium + vitamin D 0.91 — little to no clinically meaningful effect.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials.
cards.people: 69 RCTs, 153,902 adults.
cards.result: Any-fracture risk ratios: calcium alone 0.91 , vitamin D alone 1.00 , combined calcium + vitamin D 0.91 — little to no clinically meaningful effect.
cards.watchOut: Pooled across doses, durations, and populations; the 0.91s are small relative reductions that do not clear a clinical threshold; the authors' read is "little to no clinically meaningful effect," not "no effect at all."
cards.source: Massé et al. BMJ. 2026;393:e088050.
cards.search: masse 2026 calcium vitamin d fractures falls systematic review meta-analysis 69 trials bmj e088050

cards.headline: 36,282 women, 7 years: hip fracture HR 0.88, not significant — kidney stones HR 1.17.
cards.summary: Hip fracture HR 0.88 (not significant). Kidney stones HR 1.17 (95% CI 1.02–1.34) . Hip bone mineral density +1.06% vs placebo.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Women's Health Initiative).
cards.people: 36,282 postmenopausal women; calcium carbonate 1,000 mg + vitamin D3 400 IU daily vs placebo, 7 years.
cards.result: Hip fracture HR 0.88 (not significant). Kidney stones HR 1.17 (95% CI 1.02–1.34) . Hip bone mineral density +1.06% vs placebo.
cards.watchOut: Adherence was low (~59% took ≥80% of pills); per-protocol analyses look better, but the intention-to-treat result is the headline; the kidney-stone signal is the harm to weigh against a non-significant fracture benefit.
cards.source: Jackson RD et al. N Engl J Med. 2006;354(7):669–683.
cards.search: jackson 2006 women health initiative whi calcium vitamin d hip fracture kidney stones new england journal medicine

shelves.title: High-dose zinc (copper depletion)
shelves.question: What happens when zinc is taken far above the recommended intake?
shelves.balance: The guidance threshold is real and the clinical harm is documented — NIH puts the upper limit at 40 mg/day and warns that 50 mg/day or more for weeks blocks copper absorption; the denture-cream case series (Nations 2008; Hedera 2009) show the neurologic syndrome at extreme exposure, with improvement only mild after the zinc stops; and routine prescribing itself often crosses the line without monitoring ( 62% of audited prescriptions at copper-depleting doses, copper checked in 2 of 70 — Duncan 2015). High-dose zinc’s main verifiable effect is copper deficiency, preventable and partly irreversible.

cards.headline: Above 40 mg a day, zinc starts stealing your copper.
cards.summary: Intakes of 50 mg/day or more for weeks inhibit copper absorption, risking copper deficiency — anemia, neutropenia, and neurologic symptoms. Acute high doses cause nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite.
cards.type: Reference/guidance (NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Health Professional fact sheet).
cards.people: Adults; tolerable upper intake level 40 mg/day (total intake, food plus supplements).
cards.result: Intakes of 50 mg/day or more for weeks inhibit copper absorption, risking copper deficiency — anemia, neutropenia, and neurologic symptoms. Acute high doses cause nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite.
cards.watchOut: The upper level counts total intake, not the supplement alone; the copper effect takes weeks at ≥50 mg/day — it is a chronic-excess problem, not a single-dose problem; zinc lozenges and "immune" formulas routinely exceed 40 mg/day.
cards.source: National Institutes of Health, Office of Dietary Supplements. Zinc — Fact Sheet for Health Professionals.
cards.search: nih office dietary supplements zinc fact sheet copper deficiency upper intake level 40 mg anemia neutropenia guidance

cards.headline: Nations 2008: denture-cream zinc caused copper-deficiency neurologic disease in four patients — and stopping it barely reversed the harm
cards.summary: Case series, 4 patients — copper deficiency (hypocupremia with high or normal zinc) and progressive neurologic disease, all users of zinc-containing denture cream ( 17,000–34,000 µg of zinc per gram). After stopping the cream and starting IV or oral copper, neurologic improvement was only mild.
cards.people: 4 patients with copper deficiency (hypocupremia with high or normal zinc) and progressive neurologic disease, all users of zinc-containing denture cream
cards.result: The creams contained 17,000–34,000 µg of zinc per gram. After stopping the cream and starting IV or oral copper, neurologic improvement was only mild — the harm did not fully reverse
cards.watchOut: A case series cannot give incidence — but it establishes the syndrome and its partial irreversibility at extreme exposure
cards.search: nations 2008 copper deficiency denture cream zinc neurology myelopathy hypocupremia hyperzincemia doi 10.1212/01.wnl.0000324713.22011.b3

cards.headline: Hedera 2009: eleven cases of copper-deficiency myeloneuropathy — denture cream was the source in all eleven
cards.summary: Case series, 11 patients with copper-deficiency myeloneuropathy — marked hyperzincemia from excessive denture-cream use was the source in all 11; zinc levels normalized after cessation.
cards.people: 11 patients with copper-deficiency myeloneuropathy
cards.result: Marked hyperzincemia from excessive denture-cream use was the source in all 11 patients; zinc levels normalized after cessation. The authors conclude that excessive use of zinc-containing denture cream should be considered in an otherwise unexplained myeloneuropathy associated with copper deficiency
cards.watchOut: Case series — no denominator and no incidence; the strength is the uniform exposure history across all 11 cases
cards.source: Hedera P et al., Neurotoxicology 2009
cards.search: hedera 2009 copper deficiency myeloneuropathy denture cream hyperzincemia neurotoxicology case series zinc

cards.headline: Duncan 2015: 62% of audited zinc prescriptions could deplete copper — and copper was checked in 2 of 70 patients
cards.summary: Prescribing audit, 70 patients across three Glasgow hospitals in 2013 — 62% were prescribed doses with the potential to cause copper deficiency; copper levels checked in only 2 patients, risk documented in only 1 chart; unexplained anaemia in 9% (6/70) and neurological symptoms in 7% (5/70).
cards.people: 70 patients prescribed zinc across three Glasgow hospitals in 2013
cards.result: 62% were prescribed doses with the potential to cause copper deficiency; copper levels were nevertheless checked in only 2 patients and the risk documented in only 1 chart; consequences included unexplained anaemia in 9% (6/70) and neurological symptoms in 7% (5/70)
cards.watchOut: A single-city audit of prescribing practice, not an incidence study — it shows the monitoring gap, not how often harm follows
cards.source: Duncan A et al., J Clin Pathol 2015 (published online May 2015). PMID 26085547
cards.search: duncan 2015 zinc prescribing audit copper deficiency glasgow journal of clinical pathology pmid 26085547 monitoring anaemia neurological symptoms

cards.headline: Six years of prescribed zinc: copper 12 µg/dL (Japanese Nobelzin case, 2022)
cards.summary: Serum zinc 135 µg/dL , serum copper 12 µg/dL — pancytopenia after six years of prescribed zinc acetate (Nobelzin®); stopping the zinc and supplementing copper restored copper and improved the leukopenia within about two months.

cards.headline: Myelopathy from oysters: dietary zinc excess (Motooka & Yamamoto 2016)
cards.summary: Copper-deficiency myelopathy — progressive spasticity, sensory disturbance, gait failure, dorsal-column T2 signal — traced to 15–20 oysters every day for more than five years ; serum copper and ceruloplasmin low.
cards.search: motooka yamamoto 2016 copper deficiency myelopathy oysters dietary zinc excess rinsho shinkeigaku clinical neurology dorsal column doi 10.5692/clinicalneurol.cn-000926

cards.headline: A zinc ceiling from dialysis data: keep serum zinc under ~78 µg/dL (Nishime 2020)
cards.summary: 65 hemodialysis patients vs 67 controls — serum zinc above 109.7 µg/dL corresponded to copper below 41.0 µg/dL ; proposed safety ranges: zinc 41.3–78.3 µg/dL , copper 66.5–96.5 µg/dL .
cards.search: nishime 2020 zinc burden copper deficiency hypoalbuminemic hemodialysis patients nutrients serum zinc ceiling safety range pmid 32102170

shelves.title: High-dose biotin (false laboratory results)
shelves.question: Can high-dose biotin falsify laboratory results?
shelves.balance: The FDA warning is not theoretical: a controlled human experiment shows a standard 10 mg/day supplement dose corrupts 39% of biotin-based assays within a week (TSH driven below range on one platform), and about 1 in 13 outpatients and emergency patients carry biotin at or above interference levels. The failure mode is a falsified result in a patient who never mentions the supplement.

cards.headline: High-dose biotin can fake a normal troponin — one death is on the record.
cards.summary: Biotin interferes with laboratory tests that use streptavidin-biotin technology, including troponin — producing falsely low results. The FDA reported one death in a patient whose troponin was falsely low after high-dose biotin use. Other affected assays include thyroid and hormone tests, which can read falsely high or low depending on the assay design.
cards.type: Regulatory safety communications (U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2017; updated 2019).
cards.people: Patients taking high-dose biotin supplements (doses far above the dietary requirement, as sold for hair, skin, and nails).
cards.result: Biotin interferes with laboratory tests that use streptavidin-biotin technology, including troponin — producing falsely low results. The FDA reported one death in a patient whose troponin was falsely low after high-dose biotin use. Other affected assays include thyroid and hormone tests, which can read falsely high or low depending on the assay design.
cards.watchOut: The risk is a missed diagnosis, not a toxic effect of biotin itself; the interference clears when biotin is stopped, but the test taken while on it is the one that misleads; patients must tell the lab, and labs must ask.
cards.source: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Safety Communications: biotin interference with laboratory tests (2017; updated 2019).
cards.search: fda biotin interference laboratory tests troponin falsely low safety communication hair skin nails immunoassay

cards.headline: A standard supplement dose corrupts 39% of biotin-based lab assays within a week.
cards.summary: Nonrandomized crossover experiment, 6 healthy adults on biotin 10 mg/day for 7 days — interference in 9 of 23 (39%) biotinylated assays vs 0 of 14 non-biotinylated assays (P = .007). TSH fell 94% on the Vitros platform (below the reference range) and 37% on Roche.
cards.people: 6 healthy adults taking biotin 10 mg/day — a common "hair, skin and nails" supplement dose — for 7 days.
cards.result: Interference in 9 of 23 (39%) biotinylated assays vs 0 of 14 non-biotinylated assays (P = .007). Competitive assays read falsely high ( 5 of 8, 63% ); sandwich assays read falsely low ( 4 of 15, 27% ). TSH fell 94% on the Vitros platform (below the reference range) and 37% on Roche. Serum biotin rose from ~774 to >3,600 pg/mL and normalized by day 14.
cards.watchOut: Troponin was not among the 11 analytes tested in this experiment — the troponin claim stays with the FDA card (Reference 1); this card proves the mechanism and magnitude in humans at ordinary supplement doses. Small study (n = 6), but the effect is an assay-chemistry measurement, not a clinical outcome.
cards.source: Li D, Radulescu A, Shrestha RT, et al. Association of biotin ingestion with performance of hormone and nonhormone assays in healthy adults. JAMA 2017;318(13):1150–1160. DOI 10.1001/jama.2017.13705. PMID 28973622.
cards.search: li 2017 biotin ingestion assay interference healthy adults jama tsh vitros roche crossover pmid 28973622

cards.headline: About 1 in 13 outpatients and ED patients already carry interfering biotin levels.
cards.summary: Prevalence study (Mayo Clinic) — 7.7% of 1,944 outpatients reported taking biotin supplements; 7.4% of 1,442 emergency-department plasma samples carried biotin ≥10 ng/mL, the lowest known interference threshold for Roche immunoassays at the time.
cards.type: Prevalence study — outpatient survey plus emergency-department plasma measurements (Mayo Clinic).
cards.people: 1,944 outpatients surveyed; 1,442 emergency-department plasma samples.
cards.result: 7.7% (95% CI 6.6–8.9) of outpatients reported taking biotin supplements; 7.4% (6.2–8.9) of ED plasma samples had biotin ≥10 ng/mL — the lowest known interference threshold for Roche immunoassays at the time.
cards.watchOut: Self-reported use in the survey arm; the ED arm measured plasma directly. The exposure is common in exactly the population getting troponins and thyroid panels — and patients rarely volunteer supplement use.
cards.source: Katzman BM, et al. Prevalence of biotin supplement usage in outpatients and plasma biotin concentrations in patients presenting to the emergency department. Clinical Biochemistry 2018.
cards.search: katzman 2018 biotin prevalence outpatients emergency department plasma mayo clinic clinical biochemistry interference threshold

shelves.title: Selenium and prostate cancer (SELECT)
shelves.question: Does selenium prevent prostate cancer?
shelves.balance: Selenium doesn't prevent prostate cancer — and in men who already have enough, supplementing raises high-grade disease by about 90%. The supplement helps no one in SELECT and harms the replete. The vitamin E harm from the same trial lives on Shelf #29 (Klein 2011, HR 1.17).

cards.headline: 35,533 men: selenium 200 µg a day did not prevent prostate cancer — HR 1.04.
cards.summary: Prostate cancer hazard ratios (99% CI): selenium 1.04 (0.87–1.24; n=432) , vitamin E 1.13 (0.95–1.35; n=473) , selenium + vitamin E 1.05 (0.88–1.25; n=437) vs placebo (n=416). No significant differences in any prespecified cancer endpoint. Type 2 diabetes risk in the selenium group: relative risk 1.07 (99% CI 0.94–1.22; P=0.16) — not significant. The trial was stopped early for futility.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Selenium and Vitamin E Cancer Prevention Trial, SELECT), 4 arms.
cards.people: 35,533 men from 427 sites in the United States, Canada, and Puerto Rico; age ≥55 (≥50 if African American); PSA ≤4 ng/mL; normal digital rectal examination. Selenium 200 µg/day from L-selenomethionine vs vitamin E 400 IU/day vs both vs placebo; median follow-up 5.46 years.
cards.result: Prostate cancer hazard ratios (99% CI): selenium 1.04 (0.87–1.24; n=432) , vitamin E 1.13 (0.95–1.35; n=473) , selenium + vitamin E 1.05 (0.88–1.25; n=437) vs placebo (n=416). No significant differences in any prespecified cancer endpoint. Type 2 diabetes risk in the selenium group: relative risk 1.07 (99% CI 0.94–1.22; P=0.16) — not significant. The trial was stopped early for futility.
cards.watchOut: The diabetes signal was non-significant at first report; the trial's planned 7–12 year follow-up was cut short, but the futility call was unanimous.
cards.source: Lippman SM et al. JAMA. 2009;301(1):39–51. PMID 19066370.
cards.search: lippman 2009 select selenium prostate cancer prevention vitamin e jama pmid 19066370

cards.headline: In men who already had enough selenium, supplementing raised high-grade prostate cancer by 91%.
cards.summary: Selenium supplementation increased high-grade prostate cancer risk by 91% (P=0.007) in men with higher baseline selenium; no effect in men with low baseline selenium.
cards.people: 1,739 prostate cancer cases (489 high-grade) and 3,117 subcohort members from SELECT, with baseline toenail selenium measured.
cards.result: Selenium supplementation increased high-grade prostate cancer risk by 91% (P=0.007) in men with higher baseline selenium; no effect in men with low baseline selenium.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup-by-baseline interaction, not the main effect — the finding is about who is harmed, not about an average benefit; toenail selenium is the baseline measure, not blood level.
cards.source: Kristal AR et al. J Natl Cancer Inst. 2014;106(3):djt456. PMID 24563519.
cards.search: kristal 2014 select baseline selenium high-grade prostate cancer toenail case-cohort jnci pmid 24563519

shelves.title: High-dose vitamin B6 (neuropathy)
shelves.question: Can high-dose vitamin B6 cause neuropathy?
shelves.balance: The story runs from gram-dose abuse in 1983 to a European limit of 12 mg a day in 2023. Dose and duration decide: grams injure in months, a few hundred milligrams over a year or two, and case reports reach toward 50 mg — and the mechanism is a paradox, the supplement form blocking the active form. No safe dose below 50 mg a day has been established by trial.

cards.headline: The first description: grams of pyridoxine a day produced a severe sensory neuropathy.
cards.summary: Severe sensory neuropathy in all seven — progressive paresthesia of hands and feet, marked sensory ataxia, absent tendon reflexes; four could not walk. Symptoms improved after pyridoxine was stopped.
cards.people: 7 patients (5 women, 2 men) taking pyridoxine 2,000–6,000 mg/day for 2–40 months.
cards.result: Severe sensory neuropathy in all seven — progressive paresthesia of hands and feet, marked sensory ataxia, absent tendon reflexes; four could not walk. Symptoms improved after pyridoxine was stopped.
cards.watchOut: Gram-level megadoses, far above any supplement recommendation; a case series defines the syndrome, not the risk at ordinary doses.
cards.source: Schaumburg H et al. N Engl J Med. 1983;309(8):445–448. PMID 6308447.
cards.search: schaumburg 1983 vitamin b6 pyridoxine sensory neuropathy megadose case series new england journal pmid 6308447

cards.headline: Lower doses, longer fuses: time to neuropathy stretched as the dose fell.
cards.summary: A consistent pure sensory central-peripheral distal axonopathy; time to symptoms was inversely proportional to daily dose (about 23 months on average at ≤500 mg/day; about 3 months at 5 g/day); biopsies showed axonal degeneration; all patients with adequate follow-up improved after stopping.
cards.people: 16 patients with neuropathy on pyridoxine 0.2–5 g/day (200–5,000 mg/day); 7 electrophysiologically confirmed, 2 sural nerve biopsies.
cards.result: A consistent pure sensory central-peripheral distal axonopathy; time to symptoms was inversely proportional to daily dose (about 23 months on average at ≤500 mg/day; about 3 months at 5 g/day); biopsies showed axonal degeneration; all patients with adequate follow-up improved after stopping.
cards.watchOut: Even the low end (200 mg/day) is well above supplement norms; exact intakes uncertain — other supplements were not fully accounted for.
cards.source: Parry GJ, Bredesen DE. Neurology. 1985;35(10):1466–1468. PMID 2993949.
cards.search: parry bredesen 1985 vitamin b6 pyridoxine neuropathy dose duration case series neurology pmid 2993949

cards.headline: The B6 paradox: the supplement form blocks the active form.
cards.summary: Pyridoxine — and only pyridoxine among the vitamers — killed neuronal cells concentration-dependently, raised Bax and caspase-8, and inhibited both pyridoxal-5′-phosphate-dependent enzymes tested: the inactive form competitively inhibits the active form, so excess produces deficiency-like symptoms.
cards.type: In vitro mechanistic study (SH-SY5Y neuronal and CaCo-2 cells).
cards.people: Cell lines exposed to the B6 vitamers for 24 hours; no human participants.
cards.result: Pyridoxine — and only pyridoxine among the vitamers — killed neuronal cells concentration-dependently, raised Bax and caspase-8, and inhibited both pyridoxal-5′-phosphate-dependent enzymes tested: the inactive form competitively inhibits the active form, so excess produces deficiency-like symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Cell culture, not patients; in vitro concentrations may not match human tissue levels. This card explains the syndrome; it does not measure its risk.
cards.source: Vrolijk MF et al. Toxicol In Vitro. 2017;44:206–212. PMID 28716455.
cards.search: vrolijk 2017 vitamin b6 pyridoxine mechanism paradox pyridoxal phosphate in vitro toxicology pmid 28716455

cards.headline: 90 neuropathy reports on vitamin B6 — and doses under 50 mg a day can't be ruled out.
cards.summary: Causality assessed as plausible for vitamin B6-associated neuropathy. Doses below 50 mg/day could not be excluded as a cause.
cards.type: Pharmacovigilance case-series analysis (Netherlands Pharmacovigilance Centre Lareb).
cards.people: 90 reports of B6-associated neuropathy; doses 1.4–100 mg per tablet; serum B6 measured in 36 cases (mean 907 nmol/L).
cards.result: Causality assessed as plausible for vitamin B6-associated neuropathy. Doses below 50 mg/day could not be excluded as a cause.
cards.watchOut: Case reports, not a trial — no denominator, no controlled comparison; the signal is sensory neuropathy (tingling, numbness); causality is plausible, not proven; the under-50 mg point matters because many B-complex and "energy" tablets sit in that range.
cards.source: van Hunsel F et al. Drug Saf. 2018;41(9):859–869.
cards.search: van hunsel 2018 vitamin b6 pyridoxine neuropathy pharmacovigilance lareb case series drug safety

cards.headline: Europe's limit: 12 mg a day, set on the neuropathy evidence.
cards.summary: Tolerable upper intake level 12 mg/day . Peripheral neuropathy is the critical effect; the panel took a reference point of 50 mg/day from a case-control study, supported by case reports and vigilance data, and applied an uncertainty factor of 4; a dog study independently gave 11.7 mg/day.
cards.people: Adult population assessment, including pregnant and lactating women.
cards.result: Tolerable upper intake level 12 mg/day . Peripheral neuropathy is the critical effect; the panel took a reference point of 50 mg/day from a case-control study, supported by case reports and vigilance data, and applied an uncertainty factor of 4; a dog study independently gave 11.7 mg/day.
cards.watchOut: A safety limit with an uncertainty factor built in — not a measured toxicity threshold. The US upper limit remains 100 mg/day, set on older reasoning.
cards.source: EFSA Panel on Nutrition, Novel Foods and Food Allergens. EFSA Journal. 2023;21(5):e08006. PMID 37207271.
