shelves.title: Vitamin B6 deficiency neuropathy
shelves.question: Can too little vitamin B6 damage peripheral nerves?
shelves.balance: Yes — and the proof is a drug: isoniazid switches B6 off, nerves fail, and pyridoxine switches it back on. On high-dose isoniazid without B6 protection about a third of patients developed neuropathy, and giving B6 reversed it; in dialysis patients today, isoniazid prevention still produces neuropathy in about 1 in 6, and raising the pyridoxine dose resolves most cases. The deficiency state is measurable and reversible — the failure mode is not checking the level.

cards.headline: The controlled proof: block B6 and nerves fail; give it back and they recover.
cards.summary: Prevention: neuropathy developed in 6 of 18 patients on placebo and 5 of 18 on a pyridoxine-free B-vitamin preparation — B vitamins without B6 did not protect (glutamic acid: 2 of 19, not significant). Treatment: the preparation containing pyridoxine (6 mg/day) improved 8 of 9 patients with established neuropathy, while the B6-free preparation let 5 of 7 progress. Slow inactivators of isoniazid were affected significantly more often.
cards.people: Tuberculosis patients on high-dose isoniazid (12.5–15.2 mg/kg); prevention arms of 18–19 patients; 16 patients in the treatment comparison.
cards.result: Prevention: neuropathy developed in 6 of 18 patients on placebo and 5 of 18 on a pyridoxine-free B-vitamin preparation — B vitamins without B6 did not protect (glutamic acid: 2 of 19, not significant). Treatment: the preparation containing pyridoxine (6 mg/day) improved 8 of 9 patients with established neuropathy, while the B6-free preparation let 5 of 7 progress. Slow inactivators of isoniazid were affected significantly more often.
cards.watchOut: Isoniazid doses far above modern regimens — the one-in-three frequency is a high-dose figure. What carries to modern practice is the direction: B6 prevents and treats, and modern prophylaxis (10–25 mg/day for at-risk patients) exists because of this work.
cards.source: Tuberculosis Chemotherapy Centre, Madras. Bull World Health Organ. 1960. PMCID PMC2554736.

cards.headline: Dialysis, 2025: isoniazid prevention caused neuropathy in 1 in 6 — and more B6 cured most of it.

shelves.title: Selenium and type 2 diabetes — an unresolved signal
shelves.question: Does selenium supplementation cause type 2 diabetes?
shelves.balance: Two randomized trials disagree. In the NPC trial’s secondary analysis, selenium raised new diabetes (HR 1.55), and the risk climbed with baseline selenium — highest tertile HR 2.70. In SELECT, nearly thirty times larger, the same 200 µg/day dose showed no significant increase (RR 1.07; extended follow-up 1.04). If the harm is real, it likely sits in people already selenium-replete — but the biggest trial, run in exactly such men, is null. This shelf records a disagreement, not a verdict.

cards.headline: Selenium raised new diabetes 55% — and the higher the starting selenium, the higher the risk.
cards.summary: NPC trial secondary analysis — new type 2 diabetes in 58 selenium vs 39 placebo recipients, incidence 12.6 vs 8.4 per 1,000 person-years, HR 1.55 (95% CI 1.03–2.33) ; the risk rose across baseline plasma selenium tertiles to HR 2.70 (1.30–5.61) in the highest tertile.
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (the Nutritional Prevention of Cancer trial)
cards.people: 1,202 people without diabetes at baseline (600 selenium / 602 placebo), dermatology patients in low-selenium areas of the eastern United States; selenium 200 µg/day (selenized yeast) for a mean of 7.7 years
cards.result: New type 2 diabetes in 58 selenium vs 39 placebo recipients — incidence 12.6 vs 8.4 per 1,000 person-years, HR 1.55 (95% CI 1.03–2.33) . The risk rose across baseline plasma selenium tertiles, reaching HR 2.70 (1.30–5.61) in the highest tertile (>121.6 µg/L)
cards.watchOut: Diabetes was a secondary outcome of a skin-cancer trial, and diagnoses were self-reported (validated in most participants); the sample was older and mostly white. A secondary-endpoint signal is hypothesis-grade until a second trial confirms it — and the second trial (Reference 2) did not
cards.source: Stranges S, Marshall JR, Natarajan R, et al. Effects of long-term selenium supplementation on the incidence of type 2 diabetes: a randomized trial. Ann Intern Med 2007;147(4):217–223. PMID 17620655.

cards.headline: The much larger trial found no significant diabetes increase on the same dose.

cards.type: Prespecified secondary endpoint of a large randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, with extended follow-up
cards.people: 35,533 healthy men in the US, Canada and Puerto Rico; selenium 200 µg/day (L-selenomethionine), vitamin E, both, or placebo
cards.result: Diabetes risk on selenium vs placebo: RR 1.07 (99% CI 0.94–1.22; P = .16) in the primary report — not significant — and RR 1.04 (0.91–1.18) in the extended follow-up. The point estimates sit near 1 in the largest selenium trial ever run

shelves.title: Vitamin A toxicity: birth defects and fragile bone
shelves.question: Can too much preformed vitamin A (retinol) — from supplements and fortified food — cause birth defects, fractures, or liver damage?
shelves.balance: Four exhibits — three large cohorts (97,407 participants) and one biopsy series; no trials — this harm can never be randomized. The pregnancy signal is the strong one: vitamin A supplements above about 10,000 IU a day carried about 4.8 times the prevalence of cranial-neural-crest birth defects, with an apparent threshold near that dose, the risk concentrated in exposure before the seventh week — the finding the 3,000 µg/day upper limit for preformed vitamin A rests on. The bone signal is real but uneven against the developer's floor: hip fracture at the highest blood levels (2.47×) and the top 1% of blood levels (~7× any fracture) clear the 2.0 line, while the broad dietary estimates (1.5–1.9×) sit inside the band the developer calls not solid. Every signal names retinol — beta-carotene showed no association in any cohort. The liver story is the same shape: never measured in trials, but biopsy-proven and dose-graded at sustained intakes from 25,000 IU/day (Reference 4) — a poison's signature, not a population risk estimate. Posted as a possible: the birth-defect evidence is strong for observational data; the fracture evidence is moderate.

A smoothed curve suggested a threshold near 10,000 IU/day of supplemental vitamin A; the excess was concentrated in exposure before the seventh week of gestation. The authors estimated about 1 infant in 57 exposed above 10,000 IU/day had a malformation attributable to the supplement.

cards.headline: The biopsy series: cirrhosis in 17 of 41 vitamin A–poisoned livers, graded by cumulative dose
cards.summary: Cirrhosis in 17, mild chronic hepatitis in 10, noncirrhotic portal hypertension in 5, storage changes only in 9; 6 patients died of liver-related causes over a mean follow-up of 4.6 years.
cards.type: Case series with liver histology (no control group)
cards.people: 41 consecutive patients with vitamin A hepatotoxicity at a Belgian referral centre; intake precisely reconstructed in 29
cards.result: Cirrhosis in 17, mild chronic hepatitis in 10, noncirrhotic portal hypertension in 5, storage changes only in 9; 6 patients died of liver-related causes over a mean follow-up of 4.6 years. Cumulative intake was highest in the cirrhosis group (423 ± 103 million IU vs 88.5 ± 41 million IU in noncirrhotic disease, P<0.02). The smallest continuous intake that produced cirrhosis was 25,000 IU/day for 6 years; ≥100,000 IU/day produced the same lesions in 2½ years.
cards.watchOut: A case series proves a poison can do this, not how often it does — no denominator, no odds ratio. The one case-control study reporting huge ratios (OR 33.6 in teetotalers; 45.0 in light drinkers) rests on dietary recall with confidence intervals running to nearly 1,000. And blood retinol falls as liver disease advances, so serum-based population studies point the other way (low retinol tracks fibrosis in NHANES III) — reverse causation, not exoneration of high-dose intake.

shelves.title: Vitamin C and the common cold
shelves.question: Does vitamin C prevent the common cold, shorten it, or treat it once it starts?
shelves.balance: Seventy years of argument, and the pooled answer is narrow. Vitamin C taken every day does not stop ordinary people catching colds — across 29 trial comparisons and 11,306 participants the risk was essentially unchanged (RR 0.97), far inside the developer's not-solid band. What regular use does do, consistently, is shorten colds a little: about 8% in adults and 14% in children — roughly half a day on a week's cold. Starting vitamin C only after symptoms begin has no consistent effect. The one large effect is real but narrow: in five trials of 598 marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers under brief extreme physical stress, regular vitamin C halved cold incidence (RR 0.48) — the clearest exhibit is the Comrades ultramarathon trial, 33% vs 68%. And the shelf carries its own warning label: the famous 1975 NIH trial, whose apparent benefit dissolved once participants guessed their capsules by taste — the reason this literature is read with suspicion, though the reanalysis disputes how clean that lesson is. Routine prevention: no. A modest duration effect, and a genuine niche under extreme exertion: yes.

cards.headline: The pooled answer: no prevention for ordinary people, slightly shorter colds, half the colds under extreme exertion
cards.summary: Daily vitamin C did not reduce cold incidence in the general community: pooled RR 0.97 (0.94–1.00). In the five exertion trials incidence was halved: RR 0.48 (0.35–0.64). Regular use shortened colds by 8% in adults and 14% in children.
cards.type: Pooled analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials (Cochrane systematic review) — counts as one exhibit
cards.people: 29 trial comparisons, 11,306 participants for incidence (doses ≥0.2 g/day); 31 comparisons, 9,745 cold episodes for duration; five exertion trials, 598 participants
cards.result: Daily vitamin C did not reduce cold incidence in the general community: pooled RR 0.97 (0.94–1.00) across 10,708 participants. In the five exertion trials (marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers on subarctic exercises) incidence was halved: RR 0.48 (0.35–0.64). Regular use shortened colds by 8% (3–12) in adults and 14% (7–21) in children; in children, 1–2 g/day shortened colds by 18%. Started only after symptoms began (7 comparisons, 3,249 episodes), vitamin C had no consistent effect on duration or severity.
cards.watchOut: A pooled analysis counts as one exhibit in this library, however many trials it pools. The two landmark trials below are inside this pool — shown separately because each teaches something the average hides.

cards.headline: The trial that taught the field about broken blinding: the benefit lived in the participants who had guessed their capsules
cards.summary: On the surface, a small dose-dependent shortening of colds — the highest-dose group (6 g/day) ran about 17% shorter (P=0.046). But when the authors split participants by whether they had guessed correctly, the benefit sat in the unblinded group.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (prophylactic and therapeutic) — blinding failed
cards.people: 311 NIH employees; 1 g ascorbic acid or lactose placebo three times daily for nine months, plus an extra 3 g/day at cold onset; 190 completed the study
cards.result: On the surface, a small dose-dependent shortening of colds — the highest-dose group (6 g/day) ran about 17% shorter (P=0.046). But the placebo was sweet lactose and the vitamin tart: many participants tasted their way to their assignment, dropout ran 44% on placebo vs 34% on vitamin C, and when the authors split participants by whether they had guessed correctly, the benefit sat in the unblinded group. Their conclusion: ascorbic acid had 'at best only a minor influence on the duration and severity of colds, and that the effects demonstrated might be explained equally well by a break in the double blind.'
cards.watchOut: Hemilä's 1996 reanalysis disputes the famous split — 42% of cold episodes were missing from the blinded-versus-unblinded comparison, so the 'pure placebo effect' reading is itself contested. The durable lesson is narrower: check whether the blind held, and match your placebo's taste.

shelves.title: Vitamin B12 replacement: pills or injections?
shelves.question: For vitamin B12 deficiency, does high-dose oral B12 work as well as intramuscular injections?
shelves.balance: Three randomized trials, 391 patients, one pooled review — and the needle mostly loses. High-dose oral B12 (1–2 mg a day) corrected deficiency as reliably as injections in every trial: blood counts and neurologic findings recovered the same (Bolaman), and in the most careful small trial the pill finished ahead on chemistry (B12 1,005 vs 325 pg/mL; methylmalonic acid 169 vs 265 nmol/L at four months) — because roughly 1% of a large oral dose crosses the gut by passive diffusion even when intrinsic factor is absent, pernicious anemia included. The 2018 Cochrane review of the small trials (3 trials, 153 patients) called the evidence low quality but found no difference in normalization, and lower cost by mouth. The caution comes from the largest and most pragmatic trial: in 283 primary-care patients over 65, oral matched injections at 8 weeks, but once-weekly oral maintenance had slipped behind monthly injections by week 52 (74% vs 80% still normal; non-inferiority not established) — even as 83% of patients preferred the pill. So: pills replace shots to correct deficiency, and for maintenance when the dose stays substantial or the level is rechecked; a token weekly tablet is where the route fails. Developer's verdict: POSSIBLE — consistent direction across three randomized trials, but small, open-label, and largely biochemical outcomes.

cards.headline: The careful small trial: 2 mg by mouth daily matched the shots — and finished with higher B12 and lower methylmalonic acid.

At 4 months the oral group stood higher on B12 (1,005 vs 325 pg/mL, P<.0005) and lower on methylmalonic acid (169 vs 265 nmol/L, P<.05); homocysteine 10.6 vs 12.2 µmol/L. The authors' conclusion: oral was as effective as IM ‘and may be superior.’

cards.headline: Megaloblastic anemia: same blood recovery, same neurologic gains, cheaper by mouth.
cards.summary: Reticulocytosis in every patient; hemoglobin rose, MCV fell, white cells and platelets recovered — significantly and similarly in both groups. Serum B12 rose from ~73 to 214 pg/mL orally vs ~70 to 226 pg/mL injected by day 90.
cards.people: 70 randomized, 60 completed (26 oral, 34 IM), age ≥16, single center in Türkiye; 1,000 µg daily for 10 days by either route, then weekly for 4 weeks, then monthly
cards.result: Reticulocytosis in every patient. Hemoglobin rose, MCV fell, white cells and platelets recovered — significantly and similarly in both groups. Serum B12 rose from ~73 to 214 pg/mL orally vs ~70 to 226 pg/mL injected by day 90. Neurologic improvement at day 30: 7 of 9 (78%) oral vs 9 of 12 (75%) IM. Oral was better tolerated and less expensive.

shelves.title: Vitamin A supplementation in deficient children: does it save lives?
shelves.question: In populations where vitamin A deficiency is common, does giving preschool children periodic vitamin A reduce deaths?
shelves.balance: Four positive trials and one enormous null — and the shelf's grade turns on how you weigh them. In the high-deficiency, high-mortality settings of the 1980s and early 1990s, vitamin A supplementation cut preschool deaths by 34% (Aceh, open), 54% (Tamil Nadu, masked, weekly small dose), 30% (Nepal, double-masked, placebo-controlled), and 19% (Ghana, double-blind) — four randomized designs, one direction, and the reason WHO built programs on it. Then DEVTA randomized about a million Indian children and found nothing: mortality ratio 0.96. DEVTA's authors, pooling their null with the eight earlier trials, put the overall effect at 11%; the Cochrane pool lands at 12% (RR 0.88). The reconciling read: the benefit is real where deficiency is severe and child mortality is high — the early trials' worlds — and shrinks toward zero as deficiency and mortality fall, which is the direction the world has moved. Developer's verdict: POSSIBLE — a mortality benefit in deficient populations, unproven in replete ones.

shelves.title: Vitamin K and fractures
shelves.question: Does vitamin K — K1, or high-dose K2 (MK-4) — prevent fractures in postmenopausal women?
shelves.balance: The most dramatic vitamin-K numbers in the library — and the least trustworthy address they live at. The fracture claim rests on Japanese trials of high-dose MK-4 (45 mg a day, a drug dose, not a supplement dose): pooled in 2006, they showed odds ratios of 0.40 for vertebral, 0.23 for hip, and 0.19 for nonvertebral fractures — far past the developer's 0.5 benefit line. But every one of those seven trials was small and most were open-label, and when the same York group updated the pool in 2019 — after the integrity of some earlier trials had been questioned — the vertebral-fracture effect vanished entirely (OR 0.98) and the remaining clinical-fracture signal (OR 0.74) lost significance when restricted to low-risk-of-bias trials (0.76; 0.58 to 1.01). The one large double-blind trial, ECKO, found no effect on bone density at all; its fewer fractures (9 vs 20) were a secondary endpoint in a trial not powered for them. Developer's verdict: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a claim whose size shrinks every time the methods improve.

cards.headline: MK-4 45 mg/day: fewer fractures, bone density merely held — in an open-label trial with no placebo.
cards.summary: New clinical fractures occurred significantly more often in the untreated group (P=0.027) — reviews report roughly 15% of treated patients vs 35% of controls fracturing, mostly vertebral. Lumbar BMD at 24 months: −0.5% vs −3.3% (P=0.034) — sustained, not increased.
cards.people: 241 patients with osteoporosis in Japan: 120 assigned vitamin K2 45 mg/day orally, 121 assigned no treatment
cards.result: New clinical fractures occurred significantly more often in the untreated group (P=0.027); reviews of the trial report roughly 15% of treated patients vs 35% of controls sustaining fractures, mostly vertebral (relative risk ≈0.45). Lumbar bone density at 24 months: −0.5% treated vs −3.3% control (P=0.034) — density was sustained, not increased. γ-Carboxylation of osteocalcin rose, confirming the drug performed its known biochemistry.
cards.watchOut: Open label with an untreated control — everyone knew who was treated, and clinical (symptom-driven) fracture ascertainment is exactly the endpoint that knowledge can move. No placebo, one country, 241 patients: the trial anchoring the claim is the kind of trial the claim needs to escape. (The 15%/35% proportions come from reviews citing the trial; the abstract itself reports the significance test and the BMD figures.)

shelves.title: Zinc lozenges for the common cold
shelves.question: Do zinc lozenges started at cold onset shorten how long a cold lasts?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Common Cold/drug therapy · Cough/drug therapy · Fever/drug therapy · Gluconates/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Headache/drug therapy · Hoarseness/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: properly composed zinc lozenges at more than 75 mg/day of elemental zinc, started within 24 hours, shortened colds in the placebo-controlled trials — median resolution 4.4 vs 7.6 days in Mossad 1996, a recovery rate ratio of 3.1 in an individual-patient-data meta-analysis of three zinc acetate trials (199 patients), and a 33% relative reduction in mean duration across seven trials (575 participants). The ceiling is POSSIBLE, not higher: the trials are small, lozenge taste threatens blinding (bad-taste reactions 80% vs 30% in Mossad), formulations vary, and side effects are common (90% vs 62% in Mossad).

cards.headline: Mossad 1996: zinc gluconate lozenges cut median cold duration from 7.6 to 4.4 days
cards.summary: Mossad 1996: zinc gluconate lozenges cut median cold duration from 7.6 to 4.4 days (P<0.001), one lozenge every 2 hours while awake.
cards.people: 100 employees of the Cleveland Clinic who developed common-cold symptoms within 24 hours before enrolment (50 zinc, 50 placebo); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Time to complete resolution of symptoms was significantly shorter with zinc gluconate lozenges (13.3 mg zinc, one every 2 hours while awake) than with placebo (median 4.4 days compared with 7.6 days; P<0.001), with significantly fewer days of coughing, headache, hoarseness, nasal congestion, nasal drainage and sore throat. Side effects were more frequent with zinc (90% compared with 62%; P<0.001), including nausea (20% compared with 4%; P=0.02) and bad-taste reactions (80% compared with 30%; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The very high bad-taste rate in the zinc group (80%) threatens blinding in a trial whose outcomes are subjective symptom scores.

cards.headline: Across seven trials, colds were a relative 33% shorter on zinc — acetate and gluconate looked similar
cards.summary: Across seven trials, colds were a relative 33% shorter [21% to 45%] on zinc at doses above ~75 mg/day.
cards.people: 7 randomised trials with 575 participants with naturally acquired common colds, all using zinc doses above 75 mg/day; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean common-cold duration was a relative 33% shorter (95% CI 21% to 45%) in the zinc groups. Colds were shortened by 40% in the three zinc acetate trials and by 28% in the four zinc gluconate trials, a non-significant difference of 12 percentage points (95% CI -12 to +36). Trials using 80-92 mg/day found a 33% relative reduction and trials using 192-207 mg/day a 35% relative reduction, a non-significant difference of 2 percentage points (-29 to +32), so there is no evidence that doses over 100 mg/day work better.
cards.watchOut: Percentages are relative reductions in mean duration pooled from small trials with differing lozenge compositions; the analysis cannot identify the optimal formulation or dosing scheme.
cards.source: Hemilä H. Zinc lozenges and the common cold: a meta-analysis comparing zinc acetate and zinc gluconate, and the role of zinc dosage. JRSM Open. 2017;8(5):2054270417694291. PMID: 28515951. Registry ID: none in the record's databank — meta-analysis, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: zinc lozenges probably shorten colds when started early at adequate dose — with frequent taste side effects
cards.summary: Zinc lozenges probably shorten colds when started early at adequate dose — with frequent taste side effects; POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Mossad 1996 (100 patients), the zinc acetate individual-patient-data meta-analysis (3 trials, 199 patients) and the dosage meta-analysis (7 trials, 575 participants).
cards.result: The direction is consistent across the small trial programme: median resolution 4.4 vs 7.6 days (Mossad), recovery rate ratio 3.1 (2.1-4.7) for zinc acetate, and a relative 33% (21% to 45%) shortening of mean duration across seven trials at doses above 75 mg/day, with no added benefit above 100 mg/day. This shelf is stamped POSSIBLE: the trials are small, formulations differ, taste side effects are very common (90% vs 62% in Mossad, including bad taste in 80%), and blinding is fragile — so the size of the benefit is less certain than its direction.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is about treating a cold that has started, within 24 hours, with properly composed lozenges; it says nothing about zinc for prevention, wound healing (Shelf #10), childhood diarrhoea (Shelf #207) or high-dose zinc harm (Shelf #57).

shelves.title: Magnesium for nocturnal leg cramps
shelves.question: Does oral magnesium prevent night-time leg cramps, in older adults or in pregnancy?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Cross-Over Studies · Magnesium/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Muscle Cramp/drug therapy/etiology · Muscle, Skeletal · Placebos/therapeutic use · Pregnancy
shelves.balance: Split stamp. LIKELY the null in older adults: the Cochrane review (Garrison 2020) found, for idiopathic cramps in older adults (trial mean ages 61.6 to 69.3 years), differences versus placebo that were small, non-significant and homogeneous — cramps per week MD -0.18 (-0.84 to 0.49) and a ≥25% cramp-reduction responder rate ratio of 1.04 (0.84 to 1.29) on high-certainty evidence — and concludes clinically meaningful prophylaxis is unlikely. MAYBE (weak evidence) in pregnancy: the same review could not pool the five pregnancy trials (408 participants) because their results conflict, and the two primary trials carded here disagree — Dahle 1995 positive, Nygaard 2008 null — all judged at high risk of bias.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2020: magnesium did not prevent idiopathic cramps in older adults; pregnancy trials conflicted
cards.summary: Cochrane 2020, older adults: cramps per week difference −0.18 [−0.84 to 0.49] — a tight null for idiopathic cramps.
cards.people: 11 trials enrolling 735 individuals (118 cross-over participants additionally served as their own controls): five trials in pregnancy-associated leg cramps (408 participants), five in idiopathic cramps (271 participants) and one in liver cirrhosis (29 people). In the idiopathic-cramp trials, largely older adults, mean ages were 61.6 to 69.3 years; the abstract does not state the overall sex mix.
cards.result: For idiopathic cramps at four weeks, magnesium versus placebo showed a percentage change in cramps per week of MD -9.59% (95% CI -23.14% to 3.97%; 3 studies, 177 participants; moderate-certainty evidence), a difference in cramps per week of MD -0.18 (-0.84 to 0.49; 5 studies, 307 participants; moderate-certainty), and no difference in the proportion achieving a ≥25% reduction in cramp rate (RR 1.04; 0.84 to 1.29; 3 studies, 177 participants; high-certainty evidence); cramp intensity and duration also did not differ significantly. For pregnancy-associated cramps, meta-analysis was not possible: of three placebo-controlled trials, one found no benefit, one found benefit on frequency and intensity, and one reported inconsistent frequency results. Major adverse events (2 of 72 magnesium vs 3 of 68 placebo) and withdrawals did not differ significantly; minor adverse events were more frequent with magnesium (RR 1.51; 0.98 to 2.33), mostly gastrointestinal (e.g. diarrhoea) in 11% to 37% of participants versus 10% to 14% of controls. The authors conclude it is unlikely magnesium provides clinically meaningful cramp prophylaxis to older adults, while the pregnancy literature is conflicting and needs further research.
cards.watchOut: All five pregnancy trials and the cirrhosis trial were judged at high risk of bias; only one of the five idiopathic-cramp trials was. No randomised trials evaluated magnesium for exercise-associated or disease-state cramps.
cards.source: Garrison SR et al. Magnesium for skeletal muscle cramps. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2020;9(9):CD009402. PMID: 32956536. Registry ID: the record's databank lists ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03082625 — a trial registration associated with the review record, not a registration of the review itself.

cards.headline: Dahle 1995: oral magnesium reduced leg-cramp distress in pregnancy
cards.summary: Dahle 1995 (pregnancy): oral magnesium reduced leg-cramp distress vs placebo (p<0.05).
cards.people: 73 women with pregnancy-related leg cramps, treated for 3 weeks; serum magnesium and diurnal magnesium excretion were measured in 50% of patients. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Oral magnesium decreased leg-cramp distress compared with placebo (p<0.05) and compared with initial complaints (p<0.001), without significantly increasing serum magnesium levels; urinary magnesium excretion increased (p<0.002). Baseline serum magnesium levels were at or below the lower reference limit, as is also often the case in healthy pregnant patients. The authors conclude oral magnesium seems to be a valuable therapeutic tool for pregnancy-related leg cramps.
cards.watchOut: A small, short trial judged at high risk of bias in the Cochrane review, using a distress interview rather than counted cramps; its result conflicts with the later Nygaard trial.
cards.source: Dahle LO et al. The effect of oral magnesium substitution on pregnancy-induced leg cramps. Am J Obstet Gynecol. 1995;173(1):175-80. PMID: 7631676. Registry ID: no registry ID appears in the record's databank.

cards.headline: Nygaard 2008: 360 mg magnesium did not reduce pregnancy leg cramps
cards.summary: Nygaard 2008 (pregnancy): 360 mg magnesium — cramps 9.5 vs 7.7 and intensity 13.2 vs 11.4, not significant and numerically worse.
cards.people: 45 healthy pregnant women between 18 and 36 weeks of pregnancy with painful leg cramps at least twice a week were enrolled and 38 completed 2 weeks of magnesium 360 mg daily or placebo; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: There were no significant differences between groups in cramp frequency or intensity: mean number and intensity of cramps were 9.5 (SD 5.1) and 13.2 (SD 6.5) in the magnesium group compared with 7.7 (SD 4.7) and 11.4 (SD 8.5) in the placebo group. Serum magnesium and calcium did not differ between or within groups, although magnesium excretion increased significantly in the magnesium group (p<0.01). The study was powered to detect a 50% reduction in leg cramps, and none was found.
cards.watchOut: Small and short (2 weeks, 38 completers), and also among the pregnancy trials the Cochrane review judged at high risk of bias — it refutes a large effect, not a small one.
cards.source: Nygaard IH et al. Does oral magnesium substitution relieve pregnancy-induced leg cramps? Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol. 2008;141(1):23-6. PMID: 18768245. Registry ID: no registry ID appears in the record's databank.

cards.headline: Synthesis: older adults — LIKELY no meaningful benefit; pregnancy — MAYBE (weak evidence), trials disagree
cards.summary: Older adults: LIKELY no meaningful benefit. Pregnancy: the two trials disagree — MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the Cochrane review (11 trials, 735 individuals), Dahle 1995 (73 pregnant women) and Nygaard 2008 (38 pregnant completers).
cards.result: For idiopathic nocturnal cramps in older adults the pooled estimates are tightly null (cramps per week MD -0.18, -0.84 to 0.49; responder RR 1.04, 0.84 to 1.29, high-certainty), supporting LIKELY the null. For pregnancy, the evidence cannot be pooled and the primary trials conflict — distress reduced in Dahle (p<0.05 vs placebo) and no frequency or intensity effect in Nygaard — supporting only MAYBE (weak evidence). Minor, mostly gastrointestinal adverse events are more common on magnesium.
cards.watchOut: Do not carry the older-adult null into pregnancy, or the pregnancy uncertainty into older adults; they are different populations with different evidence, which is why this shelf carries a split stamp.

shelves.title: Vitamin D for preventing asthma exacerbations
shelves.question: Does vitamin D supplementation reduce asthma exacerbations in people with asthma?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Administration, Oral · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/administration & dosage · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/administration & dosage · Asthma/complications/drug therapy/physiopathology · Cholecalciferol/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug
shelves.balance: Split stamp. LIKELY the null overall: both large primary trials were null on their primary outcomes — VIDA (n=408; treatment failure 28% vs 29%, adjusted HR 0.9, 0.6-1.3) and ViDiAs (n=250; time to first severe exacerbation adjusted HR 1.02, 0.69-1.53) — and the 2023 Cochrane update (20 studies) found no effect on the proportion having an exacerbation treated with systemic corticosteroids (OR 1.04, 0.81-1.34; high-quality evidence). MAYBE (weak evidence) for profound deficiency: a 2017 individual-patient-data meta-analysis found a lower exacerbation rate overall (adjusted incidence rate ratio 0.74, 0.56-0.97), with the largest point estimate in participants below 25 nmol/L — but that subgroup held only 92 participants, the interaction test was not significant (p=0.25), and the Cochrane update found no effect modification by baseline vitamin D status, with profound deficiency poorly represented.

cards.headline: VIDA: vitamin D3 did not reduce treatment failure or exacerbation in adults with asthma and low vitamin D
cards.summary: VIDA: first treatment failure 28% vs 29% (adjusted hazard ratio 0.9 ) — vitamin D3 did not reduce failure or exacerbation.
cards.people: 408 adults with symptomatic asthma and serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 30 ng/mL randomised across 9 US academic centres (201 to vitamin D3, 207 to placebo), all on inhaled ciclesonide; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Vitamin D3 (100,000 IU once, then 4,000 IU/day for 28 weeks) did not alter the rate of first treatment failure (28% [95% CI 21%-34%] with vitamin D3 vs 29% [23%-35%] with placebo; adjusted hazard ratio 0.9 [0.6-1.3]). Of nine analysed prespecified secondary outcomes, including asthma exacerbation, the only statistically significant one was a small difference in the overall ciclesonide dose required to maintain control (111.3 vs 126.2 µg/day; difference 14.9 µg/day [2.1-27.7]). The authors conclude the findings do not support therapeutic vitamin D3 supplementation in symptomatic asthma.
cards.watchOut: Enrolment required vitamin D below 30 ng/mL, so this null already applies to a vitamin-D-insufficient population — though not specifically to profound deficiency below 25 nmol/L.
cards.source: Castro M et al. Effect of vitamin D3 on asthma treatment failures in adults with symptomatic asthma and lower vitamin D levels: the VIDA randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2014;311(20):2083-91. PMID: 24838406. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01248065, from the record's databank.

cards.headline: ViDiAs: bolus vitamin D3 did not delay severe exacerbation or upper respiratory infection
cards.summary: ViDiAs: time to first severe exacerbation, hazard ratio 1.02 — null again.
cards.people: 250 adults with asthma in London, UK (125 to vitamin D3, 125 to placebo); 82% (206 of 250) were vitamin D insufficient at baseline. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Six 2-monthly oral doses of 3 mg vitamin D3 over 1 year did not influence time to first severe exacerbation (adjusted HR 1.02; 95% CI 0.69 to 1.53; p=0.91) or time to first upper respiratory infection (adjusted HR 0.87; 0.64 to 1.16; p=0.34), and no clinically important effect was seen on asthma control, quality-of-life scores, exhaled nitric oxide or sputum inflammatory markers. Effects were not modified by baseline vitamin D status or by genotype for 34 vitamin D pathway polymorphisms.
cards.watchOut: A bolus regimen rather than daily dosing; the daily-dosing question is covered by VIDA and by the syntheses carded below.

cards.headline: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis 2017: exacerbation rate fell, driven by the rate — not the proportion — outcome
cards.summary: The 2017 individual-patient analysis: exacerbation rate ratio 0.74 [0.56 to 0.97] — but no significant difference in the proportion exacerbating.
cards.type: Individual participant data meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: Eight eligible randomised trials totalling 1,078 participants with asthma; individual participant data were obtained for seven studies (955 participants). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Vitamin D supplementation reduced the rate of asthma exacerbations requiring treatment with systemic corticosteroids (adjusted incidence rate ratio 0.74; 95% CI 0.56-0.97; p=0.03; 955 participants in seven studies; rated high-quality evidence by the authors), but there were no significant differences in the proportion of participants with at least one exacerbation or in time to first exacerbation. In subgroup analysis the point estimate was larger at baseline 25(OH)D below 25 nmol/L (aIRR 0.33; 0.11-0.98; 92 participants in three studies) than at higher levels (aIRR 0.77; 0.58-1.03; 764 participants in six studies), but the interaction test was not significant (p=0.25), so the authors did not show the effect is stronger in any subgroup.
cards.watchOut: A rate-ratio result without a corresponding difference in the proportion affected, resting on few events in the low-vitamin-D subgroup; the later Cochrane update, carded next, includes more trials and does not reproduce the overall effect.
cards.source: Jolliffe DA et al. Vitamin D supplementation to prevent asthma exacerbations: a systematic review and meta-analysis of individual participant data. Lancet Respir Med. 2017;5(11):881-890. PMID: 28986128. Registry ID: none in the record's databank — meta-analysis, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2023 update: no effect on exacerbations across 20 studies, and no subgroup modification
cards.summary: Cochrane 2023 (20 studies): proportion exacerbating, odds ratio 1.04 [0.81 to 1.34] — no effect, no subgroup modification.
cards.people: 20 studies included; 15 trials with 1,155 children and 5 trials with 1,070 adults contributed data to analyses. Participant ages ranged from 1 to 84 years; across the trials 1,245 participants were male and 1,229 female, with two studies not reporting sex distribution. Most participants had mild to moderate asthma, and profound vitamin D deficiency (25(OH)D below 25 nmol/L) at baseline was rare.
cards.result: Vitamin D or its hydroxylated metabolites did not reduce or increase the proportion of participants experiencing one or more exacerbations treated with systemic corticosteroids (OR 1.04; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.34; 14 studies, 1,778 participants; high-quality evidence), equating to an absolute risk of 226 per 1,000 on vitamin D versus a baseline risk of 219 per 1,000 on placebo. The exacerbation rate ratio was 0.86 (0.62 to 1.19) and the hazard ratio for time to first exacerbation 0.82 (0.59 to 1.15), both non-significant, and subgroup analysis found no effect modification by baseline vitamin D status, dose, dosing frequency or age. Serious adverse events did not differ (OR 0.89; 0.56 to 1.41). The authors conclude this updated review does not find evidence to support a role for vitamin D supplementation to reduce exacerbation risk or improve asthma control, while noting severe asthma and profound deficiency were poorly represented.
cards.watchOut: This update supersedes the same programme's earlier, more favourable conclusions — the contrast with the 2017 individual-patient-data analysis is the shelf's central tension, and it is resolved here in favour of the larger, later synthesis for the overall question.
cards.source: Williamson A et al. Vitamin D for the management of asthma. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2023;2:CD011511. PMID: 36744416. Registry ID: none in the record's databank — systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.summary: Overall LIKELY no benefit in established asthma; benefit confined to profound deficiency remains MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: VIDA (408 adults), ViDiAs (250 adults), the 2017 individual-patient-data meta-analysis (955 participants with data) and the 2023 Cochrane update (20 studies).
cards.result: Two large primary trials are null on their primary outcomes (adjusted HRs 0.9 and 1.02), and the most complete synthesis finds no effect on exacerbations (OR 1.04, 0.81-1.34, with absolute risks 226 vs 219 per 1,000). The one positive synthesis (rate ratio 0.74 in 2017) was not reproduced when more trials were added, and its low-vitamin-D subgroup signal (92 participants; interaction p=0.25) is hypothesis-grade only. This shelf therefore carries a split stamp: LIKELY the null overall; MAYBE (weak evidence) for benefit in profound vitamin D deficiency, where trial representation is poor.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is about exacerbations in established asthma, not vitamin D for respiratory infection (Shelf #4), falls, or guideline testing questions (Shelf #46) — do not carry conclusions between them.

shelves.title: Alternate-day oral iron absorption (Stoffel programme)
shelves.question: In iron-depleted and iron-deficiency-anaemic women, is fractional iron absorption from oral supplements higher when doses are given on alternate days as single morning doses than on consecutive days or split twice daily (Stoffel's randomised absorption trials)?
shelves.mesh: Absorption, Physicochemical/drug effects · Administration, Oral · Drug Administration Schedule · Hepcidins/blood · Iron/administration & dosage,metabolism,pharmacology · Iron Deficiencies · Anemia, Iron-Deficiency/drug therapy,etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The absorption physiology is consistent across the programme, but every endpoint on this shelf is absorption, not a clinical outcome. In iron-depleted women (Stoffel 2017, two trials in one report), cumulative fractional absorption was 21.8% on alternate-day dosing versus 16.3% on consecutive-day dosing (p=0.0013), with total absorbed iron 175.3 versus 131.0 mg (p=0.0010); splitting the daily dose in two did not help (fractional absorption 11.8% once daily versus 13.1% twice daily; p=0.33). In women with iron-deficiency anaemia (Stoffel 2020, crossover), fractional absorption on the alternate-spaced day was 40–50% higher than on the second consecutive day (P<0.001) for both 100 and 200 mg doses. Dosing raises hepcidin for about 24 hours, and the next day's dose pays for it. Whether the absorption gain converts into faster anaemia correction in routine care is not tested here — hence POSSIBLE, on absorption endpoints alone. Intravenous iron shelves (#122, #294, #369, #673) are different questions and are not re-carded.

cards.headline: Stoffel 2017: alternate-day dosing raised cumulative fractional absorption to 21.8% vs 16.3% on consecutive days; split dosing gained nothing
cards.summary: Stoffel 2017: alternate-day dosing raised cumulative fractional absorption to 21.8% vs 16.3% on consecutive days; split dosing gained nothing.
cards.type: Two prospective, open-label, randomised controlled absorption trials using stable-isotope-labelled ferrous sulfate
cards.people: Study 1: 40 iron-depleted women (serum ferritin ≤25 µg/L) aged 18–40 years, recruited in Zurich, assigned to 60 mg iron each morning on consecutive days for 14 days (21) or on alternate days for 28 days (19). Study 2: 20 women assigned to 120 mg iron once each morning or split as 60 mg twice daily for three consecutive days, then crossed over after 14 days. All participants were women; mean age is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Study 1: at the end of treatment, geometric mean cumulative fractional iron absorption was 16.3% (consecutive days) versus 21.8% (alternate days) (p=0.0013), and cumulative total iron absorption 131.0 mg versus 175.3 mg (p=0.0010); serum hepcidin during the first 14 days was higher with consecutive-day dosing (p=0.0031). Study 2: no significant difference in fractional absorption between once-daily and twice-daily split dosing (day 1–3 geometric mean 11.8% versus 13.1%; p=0.33) or total absorption (44.3 versus 49.4 mg; p=0.33), although twice-daily dosing produced higher serum hepcidin (p=0.013). No grade 3 or 4 adverse events were reported in either study.
cards.watchOut: Open-label absorption studies in young, iron-depleted but non-anaemic Swiss women, using isotope incorporation as the endpoint: they establish how iron is absorbed, not which schedule corrects anaemia fastest or is easiest to adhere to in clinic populations.
cards.source: Stoffel NU et al. Iron absorption from oral iron supplements given on consecutive versus alternate days and as single morning doses versus twice-daily split dosing in iron-depleted women: two open-label, randomised controlled trials. Lancet Haematol. 2017;4(11):e524-e533. PMID: 29032957. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02175888 (study 1) and NCT02177851 (study 2), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Stoffel 2020: in iron-deficiency anaemia, absorption on an alternate-spaced day was 40–50% higher than on the second consecutive day
cards.summary: Stoffel 2020: in iron-deficiency anaemia, absorption on an alternate-spaced day was 40–50% higher than on the second consecutive day.
cards.type: Randomised crossover iron-absorption study using stable iron isotopes
cards.people: 19 women with iron-deficiency anaemia who received 100 or 200 mg iron as ferrous sulfate at 8 AM on days 2, 3 and 5 of each period, crossing to the other dose after a 16-day incorporation period; absorption on consecutive days (days 2 and 3) was compared with the alternate-spaced day (day 5). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: For both doses, serum hepcidin was higher on day 3 than on day 2 (P<0.001) or day 5 (P<0.01), with no significant difference between days 2 and 5; fractional iron absorption on days 2 and 5 was 40–50% higher than on day 3 (P<0.001), with no significant difference between days 2 and 5. Total iron absorption from a single 200 mg dose on alternate days was approximately twice that from 100 mg given on consecutive days (P<0.001). There was no significant difference in gastrointestinal side effects between the two doses (P=0.105).
cards.watchOut: Nineteen women, absorption endpoints, and the comparison is within a dosing sequence rather than between two long-term regimens: it supports the alternate-day logic in anaemia but does not measure haemoglobin recovery. (The record's abstract prints the cohort's haemoglobin and ferritin with implausible units; those two values are not reproduced on this card.)

cards.headline: Synthesis: spacing doses a day apart absorbs more iron per dose — POSSIBLE, on absorption evidence
cards.summary: Spacing doses a day apart absorbs more iron per dose — POSSIBLE, on absorption evidence; the stamp is capped because no endpoint is anaemia correction.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Stoffel 2017 (40 and 20 women, two trials) and Stoffel 2020 (19 anaemic women, crossover).
cards.result: The mechanism and the measurements line up in both populations: a dose raises hepcidin for ~24 hours, a next-day dose is absorbed 40–50% less well in fractional terms, and alternate-day schedules recover the difference (cumulative fractional absorption 21.8% versus 16.3%). Splitting one day's dose in two gains nothing. The stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because the shelf's outcomes stop at absorption — no trial here randomised patients to schedules and measured anaemia correction, symptoms or adherence.
cards.watchOut: Do not translate 'more absorption per dose' into 'prescribe alternate-day iron to everyone': total absorbed iron also depends on the total dose given and on whether patients actually take a less frequent schedule.

shelves.title: Early high-dose vitamin D in critically ill vitamin-D-deficient patients (VIOLET, VITdAL-ICU)
shelves.question: In critically ill patients with vitamin D deficiency, does a single early high dose of vitamin D3 (540,000 IU) reduce mortality versus placebo (VIOLET, stopped for futility) — and what did the earlier VITdAL-ICU trial show?
shelves.mesh: Cholecalciferol/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Critical Illness/mortality,therapy · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Length of Stay · Organ Dysfunction Scores · Treatment Failure · Vitamin D/analogs & derivatives,blood
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C; 90-day mortality was VIOLET's primary outcome): VIOLET (1,078 patients in the primary analysis) found 90-day mortality of 23.5% on a single 540,000 IU dose of vitamin D3 versus 20.6% on placebo (difference 2.9 percentage points, 95% CI −2.1 to 7.9; P=0.26) despite day-3 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels of 46.9 versus 11.4 ng/mL — the drug corrected the number and did not change the outcome; the trial was stopped for futility. VITdAL-ICU (475 patients analysed) likewise found no significant difference in its primary outcome (hospital stay) or in hospital mortality (28.3% versus 35.3%; HR 0.81, 0.58 to 1.11) or 6-month mortality (HR 0.78, 0.58 to 1.04); its lower hospital mortality in the severe-deficiency subgroup (28.6% versus 46.1%; HR 0.56) was labelled hypothesis-generating by its own authors and is not a benefit claim. No albumin claim is made on this shelf: where albumin appears in critical-illness nutrition at all, it is read as an inflammation/injury marker, never as a diet effect, per standing rule.

cards.headline: VIOLET 2019: early 540,000 IU vitamin D3 did not reduce 90-day mortality — 23.5% vs 20.6% (P=0.26); trial stopped for futility
cards.summary: VIOLET 2019: early 540,000 IU vitamin D3 did not reduce 90-day mortality — 23.5% vs 20.6% (P=0.26); the trial stopped for futility.
cards.people: 1,360 critically ill, vitamin-D-deficient patients at high risk for death underwent randomisation within 12 hours of the ICU admission decision; 1,078 with confirmed baseline deficiency (25-hydroxyvitamin D below 20 ng/mL) formed the primary analysis population (531 vitamin D, 528 placebo with outcome data), receiving a single enteral dose of 540,000 IU vitamin D3 or matched placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The mean day-3 25-hydroxyvitamin D level was 46.9 ± 23.2 ng/mL in the vitamin D group versus 11.4 ± 5.6 ng/mL on placebo (difference 35.5 ng/mL, 95% CI 31.5 to 39.6). Ninety-day mortality (the primary endpoint) was 23.5% (125 of 531) on vitamin D versus 20.6% (109 of 528) on placebo (difference 2.9 percentage points, 95% CI −2.1 to 7.9; P=0.26). There were no clinically important differences in secondary clinical, physiological or safety endpoints, and the severity of baseline deficiency did not modify the (null) association with mortality.
cards.watchOut: The point estimate favours placebo, not vitamin D — this is not a near-miss. VIOLET tested one very early single dose in confirmed deficiency; it does not address prolonged repletion, but as a test of the acute-rescue hypothesis it is definitive enough to have been stopped for futility.

cards.headline: VITdAL-ICU 2014: high-dose vitamin D3 changed neither hospital stay nor mortality overall; a severe-deficiency subgroup signal was hypothesis-generating only
cards.summary: VITdAL-ICU 2014: high-dose vitamin D3 changed neither hospital stay nor overall mortality; its severe-deficiency subgroup signal (HR 0.56) is carried labelled hypothesis-generating.
cards.people: 492 critically ill adult patients with vitamin D deficiency (≤20 ng/mL) at 5 ICUs, assigned to vitamin D3 (249) or placebo (243) — a single 540,000 IU dose followed by monthly 90,000 IU maintenance for 5 months; 475 patients were included in the final analysis (237 vitamin D3, 238 placebo). The abstract does not state mean age; the enrolled population is described as white patients.
cards.result: Median hospital length of stay (the primary outcome) was 20.1 days (IQR 11.1–33.3) on vitamin D3 versus 19.3 days (11.1–34.9) on placebo (P=.98). Hospital mortality was 28.3% versus 35.3% (hazard ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.11; P=.18 — relative, not significant) and 6-month mortality 35.0% versus 42.9% (HR 0.78, 0.58 to 1.04; P=.09). In the predefined severe-deficiency subgroup (≤12 ng/mL; n=200), hospital mortality was lower on vitamin D3 (28 of 98, 28.6%, versus 47 of 102, 46.1%; HR 0.56, 0.35 to 0.90; P for interaction = .04) but 6-month mortality was not significantly different by the interaction test (HR 0.60, 0.39 to 0.93; P for interaction = .12); the authors state this finding should be considered hypothesis generating and requires further study.
cards.watchOut: The subgroup signal is exactly the kind of finding VIOLET then tested at scale — including by baseline severity — and did not reproduce. It stays on this card labelled as its authors labelled it, and it does not soften the shelf's null.

shelves.title: Monthly vitamin D and mortality in older adults: the D-Health trial, with ViDA
shelves.question: Does monthly high-dose vitamin D reduce all-cause mortality in older adults, most of whom are not vitamin-D-deficient?
shelves.mesh: Australia/epidemiology · Cardiovascular Diseases/drug therapy,prevention & control · Cholecalciferol/therapeutic use · Dietary Supplements · Vitamin D · Vitamins/therapeutic use · Angina Pectoris/epidemiology,prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, because all-cause mortality was the primary outcome): D-Health (21,315 Australians aged 60+, monthly 60,000 IU vitamin D3 for 5 years) found all-cause mortality of 5.3% versus 5.1% (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.18), cardiovascular mortality hazard ratio 0.96 and cancer mortality 1.15, with an exploratory signal toward higher cancer mortality after the first 2 years. The companion monthly-dosing trial, ViDA (5,108 New Zealand adults), found cardiovascular events in 11.8% versus 11.5% (adjusted hazard ratio 1.02) — printed with its mortality-inclusive primary outcome as reported. Two very large monthly-dosing trials, both null on their primaries, carry LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for monthly dosing in largely replete older adults. The VITAL trial is an anchor in an earlier drafted wave and is fenced against its home, not re-carded here. Fracture, falls and respiratory-infection vitamin D questions live on Shelves #56, #30, #4 and #37.

cards.headline: D-Health (Neale 2022): all-cause mortality 5.3% versus 5.1% (relative hazard ratio 1.04, CI 0.93 to 1.18) — monthly vitamin D did not reduce deaths
cards.summary: D-Health (2022): all-cause mortality 5.3% vs 5.1% (HR 1.04 relative, CI 0.93 to 1.18) — monthly vitamin D did not reduce deaths.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Australia-wide recruitment via the electoral roll; 5-year intervention)
cards.people: 21,315 Australians aged 60 years or older, randomised to monthly oral vitamin D3 60,000 IU (10,662) or placebo (10,653) for 5 years; median follow-up 5.7 years; in sampled participants, mean serum 25-hydroxy-vitamin D during follow-up was 115 (SD 30) nmol/L on vitamin D versus 77 (SD 25) on placebo. Sex mix is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: There were 1,100 deaths: 562 (5.3%) on vitamin D versus 538 (5.1%) on placebo. Hazard ratios: all-cause mortality 1.04 (95% CI 0.93 to 1.18; p=0.47); cardiovascular mortality 0.96 (0.72 to 1.28); cancer mortality 1.15 (0.96 to 1.39); other-cause mortality 0.83 (0.65 to 1.07) — relative figures, with the absolute death rates beside the primary. The per-protocol odds ratio was 1.18 (1.00 to 1.40). In exploratory analyses excluding the first 2 years, cancer mortality was numerically higher on vitamin D (hazard ratio 1.24, 1.01 to 1.54; p=0.05), and the authors suggest this dosing regimen might not be appropriate in vitamin-D-replete people. Mortality is the headline here and is paired with the cardiovascular figures on this card, as the library requires. Registry ID: ACTRN12613000743763, stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.
cards.watchOut: Unscreened, largely vitamin-D-replete older Australians on a monthly bolus regimen — the null governs monthly dosing in replete populations, not daily dosing, and not treatment of measured deficiency. The cancer-mortality signal is exploratory and hypothesis-generating only. Tier C proposed.
cards.source: Neale RE et al. The D-Health Trial: a randomised controlled trial of the effect of vitamin D on mortality. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2022;10(2):120-128. PMID: 35026158. shelves.title: Selenium for sepsis: the 1,089-patient trial found mortality a touch higher on selenite (28.3% vs 25.5%) — the antioxidant hypothesis, properly tested, did not survive
shelves.question: In adults with severe sepsis or septic shock, does high-dose intravenous selenium (sodium selenite), with procalcitonin-guided antibiotic therapy, reduce mortality compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Algorithms · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Antioxidants/therapeutic use · Biomarkers/blood · Calcitonin/blood · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Monitoring/methods · Female · Germany/epidemiology · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Intensive Care Units · Male · Middle Aged · Sepsis/drug therapy, mortality · Severity of Illness Index · Shock, Septic/drug therapy, mortality · Sodium Selenite/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the largest and best trial is null, and the pooled literature cannot agree with itself. In SISPCT (Bloos F et al., PMID: 27428731), 1,089 patients with severe sepsis or septic shock received a 1,000 µg selenite loading dose then 1,000 µg daily: 28-day mortality was 28.3% versus 25.5% on placebo (p=0.30) — the point estimate favours placebo — and the trial's procalcitonin-guidance factor was likewise null (25.6% vs 28.2%, p=0.34) while reducing antimicrobial exposure by 4.5%. A later meta-analysis of just 5 trials (Kong L et al., PMID: 34394308) reports no 28-day mortality effect (risk ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.73–1.19) yet a significant all-cause mortality effect (risk ratio 0.78, 0.63–0.98) — an internal inconsistency that signals small-study and timepoint selection rather than a real benefit hiding from the big trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): high-dose intravenous selenium should not be given for sepsis outside a trial; the honest summary is 'tested properly once, did not work, and the meta-analytic residue is noise-prone'.

cards.headline: Bloos 2016 (SISPCT): high-dose selenite in 1,089 patients with severe sepsis — 28-day mortality 28.3% vs 25.5% on placebo (p=0.30); procalcitonin guidance also null

cards.people: 1,089 patients with severe sepsis or septic shock in 33 intensive care units in Germany, in a multicentre 2×2 factorial randomised trial (2009–2013, 90-day follow-up): sodium selenite 1,000 µg intravenous loading dose then 1,000 µg/day continuous infusion until ICU discharge (maximum 21 days) versus placebo, crossed with procalcitonin-guided versus non-guided anti-infective therapy.
cards.result: 28-day mortality was 28.3% (95% CI 24.5%–32.3%) in the selenite group (543 patients) and 25.5% (21.8%–29.4%) in the placebo group (546 patients) (p=0.30). Procalcitonin guidance likewise did not reduce 28-day mortality (25.6% vs 28.2%, p=0.34), did not change diagnostic or therapeutic procedures, but reduced antimicrobial exposure by 4.5%. The authors conclude neither intervention improved outcome and the findings do not support high-dose sodium selenite in severe sepsis.
cards.watchOut: The factorial design means the selenium estimate averages across the procalcitonin factor (no interaction was reported as changing the conclusion), and the population is severe sepsis under older definitions in German ICUs. The confidence interval around the 28-day rates does not exclude a small benefit — but with the point estimate on placebo's side, 'unproven' here leans toward 'probably not'.
cards.source: Bloos F et al. Effect of Sodium Selenite Administration and Procalcitonin-Guided Therapy on Mortality in Patients With Severe Sepsis or Septic Shock: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2016. PMID: 27428731. Registry ID: NCT00832039. cards.headline: Kong 2021 (meta-analysis): 5 trials, 1,482 patients — 28-day mortality null (risk ratio 0.93) yet all-cause mortality positive (risk ratio 0.78): a pooling that contradicts itself
cards.summary: Kong 2021 (meta-analysis): 5 trials, 1,482 patients — 28-day mortality null (risk ratio 0.93) yet all-cause mortality positive (risk ratio 0.78): a pooling that contradicts itself
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 randomised trials (1,482 patients) of selenium administration in severe sepsis or septic shock, searched to May 2020; SISPCT supplies most of the patients.
cards.result: Selenium was not associated with reduced 28-day mortality (risk ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.73–1.19, p=0.58), but was associated with lower all-cause mortality (risk ratio 0.78, 0.63–0.98, p=0.03) and shorter hospital stay (mean difference −3.09 days, −5.68 to −0.50, p=0.02). There were no substantial effects on ICU stay, vasopressor duration, acute renal failure, adverse events, or serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: When a meta-analysis finds benefit on 'all-cause mortality' but not on the prespecified 28-day mortality in substantially the same patients, the likeliest explanation is which small trials reported which timepoint — not biology. With five trials and the largest one null with a placebo-leaning point estimate, the pooled positive should not outweigh SISPCT.
cards.source: Kong L et al. The impact of selenium administration on severe sepsis or septic shock: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. African Health Sciences. 2021. PMID: 34394308. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large null trial outweighs a self-contradictory meta-analysis — high-dose selenium for sepsis is a tested and failed antioxidant idea
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large null trial outweighs a self-contradictory meta-analysis — high-dose selenium for sepsis is a tested and failed antioxidant idea
cards.people: One large factorial RCT (SISPCT, 1,089 patients) and a 5-trial meta-analysis (1,482 patients) of high-dose intravenous selenium (sodium selenite) in severe sepsis or septic shock.
cards.result: 28-day mortality: 28.3% vs 25.5% (p=0.30) in SISPCT; pooled risk ratio 0.93 (95% CI 0.73–1.19). All-cause mortality: pooled risk ratio 0.78 (0.63–0.98) — inconsistent with the 28-day result and with the dominant trial. Hospital stay: pooled −3.09 days. Renal failure, vasopressor duration, adverse events: no differences. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: This shelf is about pharmacologic high-dose intravenous selenite in sepsis — it says nothing about dietary selenium or correcting deficiency, and the other selenium shelves (prostate #59, diabetes #67, thyroid and eye shelves) ask unrelated questions. Tier C is set because, SISPCT apart, the literature is a handful of small trials whose pooled signals flip with the timepoint chosen.

shelves.title: Too thin on paper, fine in person: vitamin K brought the INR down twice as fast and prevented no bleeding whatsoever (15.8% vs 16.3%)
shelves.question: In adults on warfarin with excessive anticoagulation (INR 4.5–10) and no bleeding, does low-dose oral vitamin K correct the INR faster without increasing thrombosis or later warfarin resistance, compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anticoagulants/adverse effects · Antifibrinolytic Agents/administration & dosage · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced, drug therapy, prevention & control · Humans · International Normalized Ratio · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Thromboembolism/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome · Vitamin K/administration & dosage · Warfarin/adverse effects
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — vitamin K does exactly what the blood test asks and nothing the patient can feel. In the one large trial (Crowther MA et al., PMID: 19258557), 712 non-bleeding warfarin patients with INR 4.5–10.0 received 1.25 mg oral vitamin K or placebo: the INR fell faster (mean fall 2.8 vs 1.4 by the next day, p<0.001), but over 90 days bleeding occurred in 15.8% versus 16.3% (absolute difference −0.5 percentage points, 95% CI −6.1 to 5.1), major bleeding was numerically more frequent with vitamin K (2.5% vs 1.1%; difference 1.5 points, −0.8 to 3.7), and thromboembolism was similar (1.1% vs 0.8%). No systematic review answers this acute-correction question — the Cochrane vitamin K review addresses chronic low-dose supplementation for unstable control, a different intervention — so the shelf rests on the single trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): holding warfarin and watching is a defensible default for the non-bleeding patient in this INR range; low-dose oral vitamin K is a reasonable option where a faster fall is wanted, but no one should promise it prevents bleeding, because the trial that looked found none prevented.

cards.headline: Crowther 2009: 1.25 mg oral vitamin K halved the time the INR spent falling (drop 2.8 vs 1.4 in a day) — and bleeding over 90 days was 15.8% vs 16.3%, no benefit at all
cards.summary: Crowther 2009: 1.25 mg oral vitamin K halved the time the INR spent falling (drop 2.8 vs 1.4 in a day) — and bleeding over 90 days was 15.8% vs 16.3%, no benefit at all
cards.people: 712 analysed non-bleeding patients (724 randomised) with INR values of 4.5 to 10.0 on warfarin, recruited at 14 anticoagulant clinics in Canada, the United States, and Italy, in a multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial of oral vitamin K 1.25 mg (347 analysed) versus matching placebo (365 analysed), followed for 90 days.
cards.result: At least one bleeding complication occurred in 56 patients (15.8%) in the vitamin K group and 60 (16.3%) in the placebo group (absolute difference −0.5 percentage points, 95% CI −6.1 to 5.1). Major bleeding occurred in 9 patients (2.5%) versus 4 (1.1%) (absolute difference 1.5 percentage points, −0.8 to 3.7). Thromboembolism occurred in 4 (1.1%) versus 3 (0.8%) (difference 0.3 points, −1.4 to 2.0). The day after treatment, the INR had decreased by a mean of 1.4 in the placebo group and 2.8 in the vitamin K group (p<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Patients who were actively bleeding were excluded, and warfarin dosing after enrolment was neither mandated nor followed — the trial answers 'give vitamin K or not, alongside usual care', not a full management protocol. The bleeding confidence interval (−6.1 to +5.1 points) is wide enough to hide a modest benefit or harm, and the numerically higher major-bleeding count on vitamin K, while compatible with chance, forbids any safety claim in the other direction.
cards.source: Crowther MA et al. Oral vitamin K versus placebo to correct excessive anticoagulation in patients receiving warfarin: a randomized trial. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2009. PMID: 19258557. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: faster INR correction, unchanged bleeding — a laboratory benefit in search of a clinical one
cards.summary: Synthesis: faster INR correction, unchanged bleeding — a laboratory benefit in search of a clinical one
cards.people: One multicentre RCT (712 analysed patients) is the entire randomised record on low-dose oral vitamin K versus placebo for non-bleeding warfarin patients with INR 4.5–10.0; no systematic review of this acute-correction question was found (the Cochrane vitamin K review covers chronic supplementation for unstable INR control, a different question, and is not carded).
cards.result: INR fall by day 1: 2.8 vs 1.4 (p<0.001). Any bleeding at 90 days: 15.8% vs 16.3% (difference −0.5 points, 95% CI −6.1 to 5.1). Major bleeding: 2.5% vs 1.1%. Thromboembolism: 1.1% vs 0.8%. Later warfarin resistance: not assessed in the trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Do not generalise beyond the trial's frame: INRs above 10, any bleeding, and urgent surgery were outside it, and intravenous vitamin K or prothrombin complex concentrate are different interventions for different situations. The result also presumes warfarin is simply held — the comparison is vitamin K plus holding versus holding alone. Tier C is set because a single trial, however well run, carries the whole shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Crowther MA et al. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2009 (PMID: 19258557).

shelves.title: Iron instead of blood in the ICU: 39 fewer units transfused on iron — in a 140-patient trial too small to call that a finding rather than a hint
shelves.question: In critically ill adults with anaemia, does intravenous iron reduce red-cell transfusion and improve haemoglobin recovery compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Adult · Aged · Allografts · Anemia/blood, drug therapy · Confidence Intervals · Critical Illness · Double-Blind Method · Erythrocyte Transfusion/statistics & numerical data · Female · Ferric Compounds/administration & dosage · Hemoglobins/analysis · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Maltose/administration & dosage, analogs & derivatives · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small trial, a blood-count win and a transfusion trend that never reached significance. In IRONMAN (Litton E et al., PMID: 27686346), 140 anaemic ICU patients received intravenous iron or placebo: transfusion use was 97 versus 136 red-cell units (incidence rate ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.43–1.18, p=0.19) — a point estimate suggesting fewer units, with a confidence interval spanning meaningful benefit and none — while haemoglobin at hospital discharge was significantly higher on iron (median 107 vs 100 g/L, p=0.02), and no safety outcome differed. No systematic review specific to intravenous iron in critically ill patients was found to strengthen the shelf (the available syntheses address surgical patients and exclude critical illness), so the claim must stay at the size of its evidence. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): intravenous iron in ICU anaemia plausibly reduces transfusion and speeds haemoglobin recovery, but with 140 patients the trial proves only the haemoglobin part; a transfusion-sparing claim awaits a trial powered for it.

cards.headline: Litton 2016 (IRONMAN): IV iron in 140 anaemic ICU patients — transfusions 97 vs 136 units (rate ratio 0.71, p=0.19, not significant), discharge haemoglobin higher (107 vs 100 g/L, p=0.02), no safety differences
cards.summary: Litton 2016 (IRONMAN): IV iron in 140 anaemic ICU patients — transfusions 97 vs 136 units (rate ratio 0.71, p=0.19, not significant), discharge haemoglobin higher (107 vs 100 g/L, p=0.02), no safety differences
cards.people: 140 anaemic critically ill patients admitted to intensive care, in a multicentre randomised placebo-controlled blinded trial of early intravenous iron (ferric carboxymaltose, per the record's ferric compounds/maltose indexing) versus placebo, 70 patients per group; primary outcomes were allogeneic red-cell transfusion during hospital stay and haemoglobin at hospital discharge.
cards.result: The iron group received 97 red blood cell units versus 136 in the placebo group (incidence rate ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.43–1.18, p=0.19) — not a significant reduction. Median haemoglobin at hospital discharge was significantly higher with iron (107 g/L, IQR 97–115) than placebo (100 g/L, IQR 89–111, p=0.02). There was no significant difference between groups in any safety outcome.
cards.watchOut: With 140 patients the trial was powered for neither transfusion nor safety: the rate ratio's interval (0.43–1.18) is compatible with a large transfusion saving and with none, and rare harms of intravenous iron (infection signals, hypophosphataemia) cannot be excluded by a sample this size. Haemoglobin at discharge is a surrogate — patients do not feel a 7 g/L difference the way they feel a avoided transfusion or a complication.
cards.source: Litton E et al. Intravenous iron or placebo for anaemia in intensive care: the IRONMAN multicentre randomized blinded trial: A randomized trial of IV iron in critical illness. Intensive Care Medicine. 2016. PMID: 27686346. Registry ID: ACTRN12612001249842. cards.headline: Synthesis: a promising point estimate trapped inside a small trial — iron raises the discharge haemoglobin; whether it spares blood is still an open question
cards.summary: Synthesis: a promising point estimate trapped inside a small trial — iron raises the discharge haemoglobin; whether it spares blood is still an open question
cards.people: One multicentre RCT (IRONMAN, 140 patients) is the randomised record for intravenous iron versus placebo in anaemic critically ill adults; no ICU-specific systematic review was found (surgical-population syntheses explicitly exclude critical illness and are not carded).
cards.result: Transfusion: 97 vs 136 units (incidence rate ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.43–1.18, p=0.19). Discharge haemoglobin: median 107 vs 100 g/L (p=0.02). Safety: no significant differences, on very small numbers. Mortality and functional outcomes: not shown to differ. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: This shelf complements, and does not replace, the transfusion-threshold shelves (#124): iron is proposed as a way to need fewer units under any threshold, and IRONMAN cannot yet carry that claim. Iron in heart failure, kidney disease, and pregnancy (shelves #122, #294, #673) involves different patients and much larger trials — do not borrow their certainty for the ICU. Tier C is set because the whole shelf is one 140-patient trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Litton E et al. Intensive Care Medicine. 2016 (PMID: 27686346).

shelves.title: Vitamin B6 for PMS: double the odds of feeling better across nine small trials — every one of them too weak to fully trust
shelves.question: In women with premenstrual syndrome, does vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) reduce premenstrual symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Premenstrual Syndrome/drug therapy · Pyridoxine/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a positive pooled result standing on low-quality legs. The BMJ systematic review (Wyatt KM et al., PMID: 10334745) pooled nine published randomised placebo-controlled trials in 940 women with premenstrual syndrome: the odds of overall symptom improvement were about double on vitamin B6 (odds ratio 2.32, 95% CI 1.95–2.54), and for premenstrual depressive symptoms the odds ratio was 1.69 (1.39–2.06) across four trials and 541 patients, at doses up to 100 mg/day. But the reviewers state plainly that conclusions are limited by the low quality of most included trials — small, old, and variably reported — and no large modern trial has since settled the question. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): vitamin B6 at up to 100 mg/day may ease premenstrual symptoms and is cheap and familiar, but the evidence would not survive the standards applied elsewhere in this library, and the dose ceiling matters — chronic high-dose B6 is itself a cause of neuropathy (shelf #60).

cards.headline: Wyatt 1999 (BMJ systematic review): nine trials, 940 women — odds of overall PMS improvement 2.32 on vitamin B6 versus placebo, with the reviewers' own warning that most trials were low quality
cards.summary: Wyatt 1999 (BMJ systematic review): nine trials, 940 women — odds of overall PMS improvement 2.32 on vitamin B6 versus placebo, with the reviewers' own warning that most trials were low quality
cards.people: Systematic review of nine published randomised placebo-controlled trials (940 women with premenstrual syndrome) of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) for premenstrual symptoms; a secondary analysis covered premenstrual depressive symptoms in four trials (541 patients). Doses in the underlying trials were up to 100 mg/day.
cards.result: The odds ratio relative to placebo for improvement in overall premenstrual symptoms was 2.32 (95% CI 1.95–2.54). For premenstrual depressive symptoms, the odds ratio was 1.69 (1.39–2.06). The reviewers conclude that conclusions are limited by the low quality of most of the trials included, and that doses of vitamin B6 up to 100 mg/day are likely to be of benefit in treating premenstrual symptoms and premenstrual depression.
cards.watchOut: An odds ratio of 2.32 from small, low-quality trials is exactly the profile that shrinks toward null when a large rigorous trial is done — none has been. The review is from 1999, symptom outcomes are subjective and PMS definitions varied across trials, and unpublished trials were sought but the published set is what carries the estimate. Benefit, if real, is on symptom scores, not on any hard outcome.

shelves.title: Oral magnesium lowers blood pressure a little — about 2 mmHg systolic at 300 mg a day or more, in two concordant meta-analyses of placebo-controlled trials
shelves.question: In adults with hypertension, does oral magnesium supplementation lower blood pressure in a dose-dependent way versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antihypertensive Agents/pharmacology · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Blood Pressure Determination · Dietary Supplements · Humans · Hypertension/blood/diagnosis/drug therapy · Magnesium/blood/pharmacology · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small, real, dose-related effect. Zhang X et al. (PMID: 27402922), pooling 34 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials (2,028 participants), found oral magnesium at a median dose of 368 mg/day for a median of 3 months lowered systolic blood pressure by 2.00 mmHg (95% CI 0.43–3.58) and diastolic by 1.78 mmHg (95% CI 0.73–2.82), with a dose–response analysis suggesting 300 mg/day for 1 month is enough to raise serum magnesium and lower blood pressure. Kass L et al. (PMID: 22318649), pooling 22 trials (1,173 participants, mean dose 410 mg/day), found a similar 3–4 mmHg systolic and 2–3 mmHg diastolic fall, larger at intakes above 370 mg/day. Neither meta-analysis reports clinical events, and individual trials were mostly small and short — this is a blood-pressure effect of a few mmHg, not a substitute for antihypertensive drugs. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): oral magnesium lowers blood pressure modestly and dose-dependently, on the pooled evidence of two concordant meta-analyses of placebo-controlled trials.

cards.headline: Zhang 2016: magnesium lowered systolic BP by 2.00 mmHg and diastolic by 1.78 mmHg across 34 placebo-controlled trials — with a dose–response signal at ≥300 mg/day
cards.summary: Zhang 2016: magnesium lowered systolic BP by 2.00 mmHg and diastolic by 1.78 mmHg across 34 placebo-controlled trials — with a dose–response signal at ≥300 mg/day
cards.people: 34 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials involving 2,028 normotensive and hypertensive adults; magnesium supplementation at a median dose of 368 mg/day for a median duration of 3 months, versus placebo.
cards.result: Systolic blood pressure fell by 2.00 mmHg (95% CI 0.43–3.58) and diastolic by 1.78 mmHg (95% CI 0.73–2.82) with magnesium versus placebo, accompanied by a 0.05 mmol/L (95% CI 0.03–0.07) rise in serum magnesium. A restricted cubic spline dose–response analysis suggested a dose of 300 mg/day or a duration of 1 month is sufficient to elevate serum magnesium and reduce blood pressure; serum magnesium was negatively associated with diastolic but not systolic blood pressure.
cards.watchOut: The pooled effect is small, trials were short (median 3 months), and residual heterogeneity persisted after subgroup analyses; greater reductions appeared in higher-quality, low-dropout trials, which cuts both ways. No trial measured strokes, heart attacks, or death.
cards.source: Zhang X et al. Effects of Magnesium Supplementation on Blood Pressure: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled Trials. Hypertension. 2016. PMID: 27402922.
