cards.headline: Kass 2012: 22 trials show a 3–4 mmHg systolic and 2–3 mmHg diastolic fall, larger above 370 mg/day and in crossover trials
cards.summary: Kass 2012: 22 trials show a 3–4 mmHg systolic and 2–3 mmHg diastolic fall, larger above 370 mg/day and in crossover trials
cards.people: 22 trials (23 data sets, 1,173 participants) of oral magnesium supplementation, doses 120–973 mg elemental magnesium (mean 410 mg/day), with 3 to 24 weeks of follow-up, versus placebo or control.
cards.result: Combining all trials showed a decrease in systolic blood pressure of 3–4 mmHg and diastolic of 2–3 mmHg (standardised effect sizes 0.32 for systolic, 95% CI 0.23–0.41, and 0.36 for diastolic, 95% CI 0.27–0.44), with larger effects in crossover trials and at intakes above 370 mg/day, although not all individual trials showed a significant reduction.
cards.watchOut: Effect sizes are standardised (Hedges g), so the mmHg figures are the authors' translation, not a direct pooled mmHg estimate; doses and formulations varied widely across small trials, and publication bias was not excluded.
cards.source: Kass L et al. Effect of magnesium supplementation on blood pressure: a meta-analysis. European Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2012. PMID: 22318649. cards.headline: Synthesis: two independent meta-analyses, one small consistent answer — a few mmHg, dose-related, no outcome data
cards.summary: Synthesis: two independent meta-analyses, one small consistent answer — a few mmHg, dose-related, no outcome data
cards.people: Two meta-analyses of randomised placebo-controlled trials of oral magnesium in adults (Zhang 2016: 34 trials, 2,028 participants; Kass 2012: 22 trials, 1,173 participants), overlapping trial sets published four years apart.
cards.result: Systolic blood pressure falls of 2.00 mmHg (Zhang) and 3–4 mmHg (Kass), diastolic falls of 1.78 mmHg and 2–3 mmHg, with both analyses finding larger effects at higher doses (≥300 mg/day in Zhang; >370 mg/day in Kass). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the direction is consistent and dose-related, the size is small, and no cardiovascular outcome has been tested.
cards.watchOut: The two meta-analyses share many of the same small underlying trials, so they are not fully independent confirmations; the honest claim is a modest surrogate effect, and anyone with hypertension still needs proven drug therapy. Tier C is not set: the base is pooled randomised-trial evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Zhang X et al. Hypertension. 2016 (PMID: 27402922); Kass L et al. European Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2012 (PMID: 22318649).

shelves.title: Nutritional rickets heals best with calcium in the regimen: calcium beat vitamin D alone in Nigeria, and daily vitamin D matched weekly high-dose vitamin D in India
shelves.question: In children with nutritional rickets, what vitamin D and calcium treatment regimens heal rickets — daily dosing versus single large (stoss) doses?
shelves.mesh: Alkaline Phosphatase/blood · Calcium/administration & dosage/blood/therapeutic use · Calcium, Dietary/administration & dosage · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Nigeria · Rickets/blood/drug therapy · Vitamin D/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for calcium-containing regimens, and for daily vitamin D over no treatment; the daily-versus-bolus question itself is a draw. In the Nigerian randomised trial (Thacher TD et al., PMID: 10451461), 123 children with rickets treated for 24 weeks reached the combined healing endpoint (alkaline phosphatase ≤350 U/L plus near-complete radiographic healing) in 61% on calcium alone and 58% on calcium plus vitamin D, versus only 19% on vitamin D alone (600,000 U intramuscularly, a stoss-style regimen) (P<0.001) — in a population whose dietary calcium intake was very low (median 203 mg/day). In India, Dabas A et al. (PMID: 35550679) randomised 132 children to daily vitamin D3 2,000 IU for 12 weeks or weekly 60,000 IU for 3 or 6 weeks: complete radiological healing at 12 weeks was 75% with daily dosing versus 60.5% and 61.9% with the weekly regimens, a non-significant difference (P=0.15). No trial here tested a single one-off oral stoss dose against daily dosing head-to-head. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): where dietary calcium is low, calcium (with or without vitamin D) heals rickets far better than vitamin D alone; daily and weekly high-dose vitamin D regimens heal at similar rates.

cards.headline: Thacher 1999: healing in 61% on calcium and 58% on calcium plus vitamin D versus 19% on vitamin D alone (P<0.001)
cards.summary: Thacher 1999: healing in 61% on calcium and 58% on calcium plus vitamin D versus 19% on vitamin D alone (P<0.001)
cards.people: 123 Nigerian children with nutritional rickets (median age 46 months), randomised to 24 weeks of vitamin D (600,000 U intramuscularly at enrolment and at 12 weeks), calcium 1,000 mg daily, or both; baseline dietary calcium intake was low (median 203 mg/day in children with rickets, 196 mg/day in matched controls).
cards.result: The combined endpoint of alkaline phosphatase ≤350 U/L plus radiographic evidence of nearly complete healing was reached by 61% of the calcium group and 58% of the combination group versus 19% of the vitamin D group (P<0.001). Mean serum calcium rose from 7.5±0.8 to 9.0±0.6 mg/dL on calcium and from 7.7±1.0 to 9.1±0.6 mg/dL on combination therapy, versus 7.8±0.8 to 8.3±0.7 mg/dL on vitamin D alone (P<0.001 for both comparisons).
cards.watchOut: This was calcium-deficiency rickets in Nigerian children with very low dietary calcium; in populations where vitamin D deficiency dominates and calcium intake is adequate, vitamin D alone may perform better. The vitamin D regimen was intramuscular and given twice, not a single oral stoss dose.
cards.source: Thacher TD et al. A comparison of calcium, vitamin D, or both for nutritional rickets in Nigerian children. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1999. PMID: 10451461. cards.headline: Dabas 2023: complete radiological healing in 75% on daily vitamin D versus 60.5% and 61.9% on weekly regimens — no significant difference (P=0.15)
cards.summary: Dabas 2023: complete radiological healing in 75% on daily vitamin D versus 60.5% and 61.9% on weekly regimens — no significant difference (P=0.15)
cards.people: 132 Indian children aged 6 months to 12 years with nutritional rickets, randomised to vitamin D3 2,000 IU daily for 12 weeks (group A), 60,000 IU weekly for 3 weeks (group B), or 60,000 IU weekly for 6 weeks (group C); 90.2% had baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D ≤20 ng/mL and 72.7% were hypocalcaemic; 120 children completed the study.
cards.result: Complete radiological healing at 12 weeks occurred in 30 children (75%) in group A, 23 (60.5%) in group B, and 26 (61.9%) in group C (P=0.15), with comparable endline X-ray scores (P=0.31). The median change in X-ray score was larger with daily dosing (7, IQR 4–9) than with weekly dosing for 3 weeks (5, IQR 2.25–6) or 6 weeks (6, IQR 4–7) (P=0.019); endline 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels were 50.0, 42.1, and 53.5 ng/mL respectively (P=0.045).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-centre, and the weekly regimens are repeated high doses rather than a single stoss dose; the trial was not powered to prove equivalence, so 'no significant difference' is not proof the regimens are identical. The record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.source: Dabas A et al. Daily v. weekly oral vitamin D(3) therapy for nutritional rickets in Indian children: a randomised controlled open-label trial. The British Journal of Nutrition. 2023. PMID: 35550679. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: give calcium where the diet lacks it; the dosing schedule of vitamin D matters less than giving enough of it
cards.summary: Synthesis: give calcium where the diet lacks it; the dosing schedule of vitamin D matters less than giving enough of it
cards.people: Two randomised trials in children with nutritional rickets: Thacher 1999 (Nigeria, n=123; calcium vs vitamin D vs both) and Dabas 2023 (India, n=132; daily vs weekly vitamin D3).

shelves.title: High-dose multivitamins at the start of HIV treatment made no difference to progression or death — and raised liver enzymes; the pre-treatment-era mortality signal did not survive the ART era
shelves.question: In adults starting antiretroviral therapy for HIV, does high-dose multivitamin supplementation reduce disease progression or death versus standard-dose multivitamins?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antiretroviral Therapy, Highly Active · Ascorbic Acid/administration & dosage · Body Mass Index · CD4 Lymphocyte Count · Dietary Supplements · Disease Progression · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · HIV Infections/drug therapy/mortality · Humans · Male · Nutritional Status · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome · Viral Load · Vitamin B Complex/administration & dosage · Vitamin E/administration & dosage · Vitamins/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the question as asked, in the treatment era. Isanaka S et al. (PMID: 23073950) randomised 3,418 adults initiating HAART in Tanzania to high-dose versus standard-dose multivitamins (B complex, C, and E) for 24 months: the absolute risk of HIV progression or death was 72% in both groups (risk ratio 1.00; 95% CI 0.96–1.04), with no effect on CD4 count, viral load, BMI, or haemoglobin — and the trial was stopped early because high-dose supplementation increased alanine transaminase elevations (risk ratio 1.44; 95% CI 1.11–1.87). The older, pre-HAART-era trial by Jiamton S et al. (PMID: 14600517) in Bangkok (481 patients, 48 weeks) found a lower death rate on multiple micronutrients that was not significant overall (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.22–1.25; P=0.1), with significant subgroup signals only at CD4 counts below 200 and below 100. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): at ART initiation, high-dose multivitamins do not reduce progression or death compared with standard-dose, and they carry a liver-enzyme price.

cards.headline: Isanaka 2012: progression or death in 72% on high-dose and 72% on standard-dose multivitamins (RR 1.00) — trial stopped early for ALT elevations (RR 1.44)
cards.summary: Isanaka 2012: progression or death in 72% on high-dose and 72% on standard-dose multivitamins (RR 1.00) — trial stopped early for ALT elevations (RR 1.44)
cards.people: 3,418 adults with HIV initiating HAART at 7 clinics in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania (enrolled November 2006–November 2008), randomised to daily vitamin B complex, C, and E at high dose or at standard recommended-dietary-allowance dose for 24 months; median follow-up 15 months when the trial was stopped early.
cards.result: There were 2,374 HIV disease progression events and 453 deaths (2,460 combined events). The absolute risk of HIV progression or death was 72% in the high-dose group versus 72% in the standard-dose group (risk ratio 1.00; 95% CI 0.96–1.04). High-dose supplementation had no effect on CD4 count, plasma viral load, body mass index, or haemoglobin, but increased ALT elevations (1,239 events per 1,215 person-years versus 879 per 1,236 person-years; risk ratio 1.44; 95% CI 1.11–1.87); the trial was stopped early in March 2009 for this safety signal.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was a standard-dose multivitamin, not placebo — so this trial cannot say whether standard-dose supplementation itself helps or harms. Early stopping for the ALT signal truncated the planned 24-month follow-up (median 15 months).
cards.source: Isanaka S et al. Effect of high-dose vs standard-dose multivitamin supplementation at the initiation of HAART on HIV disease progression and mortality in Tanzania: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2012. PMID: 23073950. Registry ID: NCT00383669. cards.headline: Jiamton 2003 (pre-HAART era): mortality hazard ratio 0.53 overall — not significant (P=0.1); significant only in the lowest-CD4 subgroups
cards.summary: Jiamton 2003 (pre-HAART era): mortality hazard ratio 0.53 overall — not significant (P=0.1); significant only in the lowest-CD4 subgroups
cards.people: 481 HIV-infected men and women in Bangkok, Thailand, with CD4 counts 50–550 × 10(6)/L, randomised to multiple micronutrients or placebo for 48 weeks, in an era and setting with poor access to antiretroviral therapy; 79 participants (16%) were lost to follow-up and 23 (5%) died.
cards.result: The mortality hazard ratio on micronutrients was 0.53 (95% CI 0.22–1.25; P=0.1) overall, 0.37 (95% CI 0.13–1.06; P=0.052) among those with CD4 counts below 200 × 10(6)/L, and 0.26 (95% CI 0.07–0.97; P=0.03) among those below 100 × 10(6)/L. There was no impact on CD4 cell count or plasma viral load.
cards.watchOut: Only 23 deaths, 16% lost to follow-up, and the significant results are subgroup findings — the classic profile of a signal that needs replication. It also answers a different question (supplements versus placebo, without HAART) from the shelf's question (high dose versus standard dose, with HAART).
cards.source: Jiamton S et al. A randomized trial of the impact of multiple micronutrient supplementation on mortality among HIV-infected individuals living in Bangkok. AIDS. 2003. PMID: 14600517. cards.headline: Synthesis: in the ART era the high-dose question is answered — no benefit, a liver price; the older mortality signal belongs to a world without treatment access
cards.summary: Synthesis: in the ART era the high-dose question is answered — no benefit, a liver price; the older mortality signal belongs to a world without treatment access
cards.people: One large double-blind trial at HAART initiation (Isanaka 2012, n=3,418, Tanzania) and one small pre-HAART placebo-controlled trial (Jiamton 2003, n=481, Thailand).
cards.result: Progression or death: 72% versus 72% (RR 1.00; 95% CI 0.96–1.04) for high-dose versus standard-dose in Isanaka; mortality hazard ratio 0.53 (95% CI 0.22–1.25) for micronutrients versus placebo in Jiamton. Harm: ALT elevations RR 1.44 (95% CI 1.11–1.87) with high doses in Isanaka. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), with the ALT harm on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Tier C is set: the headline question rests on a single ART-era trial and the outcome includes mortality, so the developer reviews this shelf personally. Nothing here addresses standard-dose supplementation versus none in patients already stable on ART.
cards.source: Synthesis of Isanaka S et al. JAMA. 2012 (PMID: 23073950); Jiamton S et al. AIDS. 2003 (PMID: 14600517).

shelves.title: Vitamin A for extremely-low-birth-weight infants: death or chronic lung disease in 55% versus 62% — one extra survivor without lung disease for every 14–15 treated
shelves.question: In extremely-low-birth-weight infants, does vitamin A supplementation reduce chronic lung disease (bronchopulmonary dysplasia) and death versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Chronic Disease · Cross Infection/prevention & control · Humans · Infant Mortality · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Very Low Birth Weight/blood · Injections, Intramuscular · Lung Diseases/prevention & control · Sepsis/prevention & control · Single-Blind Method · Vitamin A/blood/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a slight but real reduction in the composite of death or chronic lung disease. In the NICHD Neonatal Research Network trial (Tyson JE et al., PMID: 10379020), 807 extremely-low-birth-weight infants needing respiratory support received intramuscular vitamin A 5,000 IU three times a week for four weeks or sham treatment: death or chronic lung disease at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age occurred in 55% versus 62% (relative risk 0.89; 95% CI 0.80–0.99) — one additional infant survived without chronic lung disease for every 14 to 15 treated — while death alone was 15% versus 14%, essentially unchanged. The Cochrane review by Darlow BA et al. (PMID: 21975731; 9 trials) found the same pattern: oxygen requirement at 36 weeks reduced (risk ratio 0.87; 95% CI 0.77–0.98; number needed to treat 13) and death or oxygen requirement at one month reduced (risk ratio 0.93; 95% CI 0.88–0.99), with no difference in neurodevelopment at 18–22 months in the largest trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): vitamin A slightly reduces chronic lung disease in extremely-low-birth-weight infants; it does not reduce death on its own.

cards.headline: Tyson 1999 (NICHD): death or chronic lung disease in 55% on vitamin A versus 62% on sham (RR 0.89) — death alone 15% versus 14%
cards.summary: Tyson 1999 (NICHD): death or chronic lung disease in 55% on vitamin A versus 62% on sham (RR 0.89) — death alone 15% versus 14%
cards.people: 807 extremely-low-birth-weight infants (mean birth weight 770 g vitamin A group, 769 g control; gestational age 26.8 and 26.7 weeks) who needed respiratory support 24 hours after birth, randomised to intramuscular vitamin A 5,000 IU three times weekly for 4 weeks or sham treatment.
cards.result: The primary outcome — death or chronic lung disease at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age — occurred in 55% of the vitamin A group versus 62% of controls (relative risk 0.89; 95% CI 0.80–0.99); one additional infant survived without chronic lung disease for every 14 to 15 infants treated. Death by 36 weeks occurred in 59 of 405 infants (15%) on vitamin A and 55 of 402 (14%) on sham. Serum retinol below 20 µg/dL was less common on vitamin A (25% versus 54%, P<0.001), and signs of potential vitamin A toxicity were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is carried by the lung component of the composite, not by survival; the regimen means repeated intramuscular injections in fragile infants, and the trial predates modern surfactant, caffeine, and ventilation practice, which may shrink the absolute benefit today.
cards.source: Tyson JE et al. Vitamin A supplementation for extremely-low-birth-weight infants. National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Neonatal Research Network. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1999. PMID: 10379020. cards.headline: Darlow 2011 Cochrane: oxygen requirement at 36 weeks RR 0.87 (NNT 13); death or oxygen at one month RR 0.93; no neurodevelopmental difference
cards.summary: Darlow 2011 Cochrane: oxygen requirement at 36 weeks RR 0.87 (NNT 13); death or oxygen at one month RR 0.93; no neurodevelopmental difference
cards.people: 9 randomised trials in very-low-birth-weight infants (birth weight ≤1,500 g or <32 weeks' gestation); 8 trials (1,291 infants) compared vitamin A supplementation with control, and 1 trial (120 infants) compared dosage regimens.
cards.result: Vitamin A reduced death or oxygen requirement at one month of age (risk ratio 0.93; 95% CI 0.88–0.99; risk difference −0.05; number needed to treat to benefit 20; 1,165 infants) and oxygen requirement at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age (risk ratio 0.87; 95% CI 0.77–0.98; risk difference −0.08; NNT 13; 824 infants), with a trend for death or oxygen requirement at 36 weeks (risk ratio 0.91; 95% CI 0.82–1.00; 1,001 infants). Neurodevelopmental assessment of 88% of survivors in the largest trial showed no differences at 18–22 months corrected age.
cards.watchOut: The pooled benefit is modest and dominated by the single large Tyson trial, so the review and the trial are not independent confirmations; the reviewers themselves note the decision hinges on local chronic-lung-disease incidence and the acceptability of repeated injections.
cards.source: Darlow BA et al. Vitamin A supplementation to prevent mortality and short- and long-term morbidity in very low birthweight infants. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2011. PMID: 21975731. cards.headline: Synthesis: a small lung benefit, bought with injections, with survival unchanged
cards.summary: Synthesis: a small lung benefit, bought with injections, with survival unchanged
cards.people: The NICHD trial (Tyson 1999, n=807) and the Cochrane review of 9 trials in very-low-birth-weight infants (Darlow 2011).
cards.result: Death or chronic lung disease at 36 weeks: 55% versus 62% (RR 0.89) in Tyson; oxygen requirement at 36 weeks RR 0.87 and death-or-oxygen at one month RR 0.93 in the Cochrane pooling. Death alone: 15% versus 14% in Tyson. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): real, slight, and confined to the lung outcome.
cards.watchOut: Effect sizes are small enough that changes in neonatal practice since 1999 matter; units with low baseline chronic-lung-disease rates will see less absolute gain. Tier C is not set: a large randomised trial plus a concordant Cochrane review carry the shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tyson JE et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1999 (PMID: 10379020); Darlow BA et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2011 (PMID: 21975731).

shelves.title: Ferric maltol in IBD iron-deficiency anaemia: haemoglobin up 2.25 g/dL more than placebo at 12 weeks, normalised in two-thirds — one trial programme, in patients who had already failed ordinary oral iron
shelves.question: In adults with inflammatory bowel disease and iron-deficiency anaemia who do not tolerate standard oral iron, does ferric maltol correct anaemia versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Anemia, Iron-Deficiency/drug therapy/etiology · Colitis, Ulcerative/complications/pathology · Crohn Disease/complications/pathology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Ferric Compounds/therapeutic use · Hemoglobins/analysis · Humans · Male · Maximum Tolerated Dose · Prognosis · Pyrones/therapeutic use · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a clear haemoglobin effect in a single phase 3 programme. Gasche C et al. (PMID: 25545376) randomised 128 patients with quiescent or mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease and mild-to-moderate iron-deficiency anaemia, all with documented failure on previous oral ferrous products, to ferric maltol 30 mg twice daily or placebo for 12 weeks: haemoglobin rose by a mean of 2.25 g/dL (SE 0.19) more than placebo at week 12 (P<0.0001), with significant separation already at week 4 (1.04 g/dL), and haemoglobin normalised in two-thirds of patients by week 12; the safety profile was comparable to placebo with no impact on IBD severity. In the open-label extension (Schmidt C et al., PMID: 27237709), haemoglobin gains were maintained to week 64 (rise of 3.07 g/dL from baseline in those continued on ferric maltol), with normal haemoglobin in 89% of continued and 83% of switched patients — but with no placebo comparator after week 12. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ferric maltol corrects iron-deficiency anaemia in IBD patients who failed ferrous iron, on one randomised trial plus its extension.

cards.headline: Gasche 2015 (AEGIS): haemoglobin +2.25 g/dL versus placebo at week 12 (P<0.0001); normalised in two-thirds
cards.summary: Gasche 2015 (AEGIS): haemoglobin +2.25 g/dL versus placebo at week 12 (P<0.0001); normalised in two-thirds
cards.type: Randomised double-blind phase 3 trial (Gasche 2015, AEGIS programme)
cards.people: 128 adults with quiescent or mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease and mild-to-moderate iron-deficiency anaemia (haemoglobin 9.5–12.0 g/dL in women, 9.5–13.0 g/dL in men) and documented failure on previous oral ferrous products, randomised to ferric maltol 30 mg twice daily or identical placebo for 12 weeks; 86% (ferric maltol) and 83% (placebo) completed.
cards.result: Haemoglobin improved significantly more with ferric maltol than placebo at weeks 4, 8, and 12: mean (SE) differences of 1.04 (0.11), 1.76 (0.15), and 2.25 (0.19) g/dL respectively (P<0.0001 at all time points). Haemoglobin was normalised in two-thirds of ferric-maltol patients by week 12. The safety profile was comparable with placebo, with no impact on inflammatory bowel disease severity.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week haemoglobin endpoint in patients with quiescent or mild-to-moderate disease; the trial says nothing about severe anaemia, active flares, transfusion avoidance, or how ferric maltol compares with intravenous iron, which is the real-world alternative for many of these patients.
cards.source: Gasche C et al. Ferric maltol is effective in correcting iron deficiency anemia in patients with inflammatory bowel disease: results from a phase-3 clinical trial program. Inflammatory Bowel Diseases. 2015. PMID: 25545376. cards.headline: Schmidt 2016 extension: haemoglobin up 3.07 g/dL by week 64 in continued patients; normal haemoglobin in 89% (continued) and 83% (switched) — no comparator
cards.summary: Schmidt 2016 extension: haemoglobin up 3.07 g/dL by week 64 in continued patients; normal haemoglobin in 89% (continued) and 83% (switched) — no comparator
cards.people: 97 of the 111 patients who completed the randomised phase entered a 52-week open-label extension on ferric maltol 30 mg twice daily (50 'continued' from ferric maltol, 47 'switch' from placebo).
cards.result: Mean haemoglobin increased by 3.07±1.46 g/dL from baseline to week 64 in continued patients and by 2.19±1.61 g/dL in switch patients; normal haemoglobin was achieved in 89% and 83% respectively at week 64. Serum ferritin rose from 8.9 µg/L at baseline to 26.0 µg/L at week 12 on ferric maltol and 57.4 µg/L among all patients at week 64. Overall 80% of patients reported at least one adverse event by week 64; adverse events considered related to ferric maltol occurred in 27 of 111 patients (24%), and 8 of 18 discontinuations for adverse events were treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and uncontrolled after week 12, in the subset who tolerated and completed the randomised phase — durability and long-term tolerability in all-comers will look worse than in this selected group. One patient was withdrawn for increased ulcerative colitis activity.
cards.source: Schmidt C et al. Ferric maltol therapy for iron deficiency anaemia in patients with inflammatory bowel disease: long-term extension data from a Phase 3 study. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2016. PMID: 27237709. shelves.title: Low-dose iron after blood donation: haemoglobin recovery in about a month instead of five — and low-haemoglobin deferral cut to a third in the pooled trials
shelves.question: In regular blood donors, does low-dose iron supplementation prevent iron deficiency and donor deferral versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Blood Cell Count · Blood Donors · Dietary Supplements · Female · Ferritins/blood · Ferrous Compounds/therapeutic use · Hemoglobins/analysis · Humans · Iron · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for recovery of haemoglobin and iron stores after donation, with more minor side effects as the price. In the STRIDE randomised trial (Kiss JE et al., PMID: 25668261), 215 donors took ferrous gluconate (37.5 mg elemental iron) daily or no iron for 24 weeks after donating a unit of whole blood: time to recover 80% of the haemoglobin lost was a mean of 32 days versus 158 days in low-ferritin donors (≤26 ng/mL) and 31 versus 78 days in higher-ferritin donors, and without iron 67% of participants had not recovered their iron stores by 168 days. The Cochrane review by Smith GA et al. (PMID: 24990381; 30 trials, 4,704 participants) found iron supplementation cut deferral for low haemoglobin to a risk ratio of 0.34 (95% CI 0.21–0.55) at the first donation after starting iron and 0.25 (95% CI 0.15–0.41) at subsequent donations, with higher haemoglobin (mean difference 2.36 g/L) and ferritin (mean difference 13.98 ng/mL) — and more adverse effects (risk ratio 1.60; 95% CI 1.23–2.07). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): low-dose iron after donation speeds haemoglobin and iron-store recovery and prevents deferral.

cards.headline: Kiss 2015 (STRIDE): 80% haemoglobin recovery in 32 versus 158 days (low ferritin) and 31 versus 78 days (higher ferritin) with daily low-dose iron
cards.summary: Kiss 2015 (STRIDE): 80% haemoglobin recovery in 32 versus 158 days (low ferritin) and 31 versus 78 days (higher ferritin) with daily low-dose iron
cards.people: 215 blood donors aged 18–79 at 4 US regional blood centres who had not donated whole blood or red cells within 4 months, stratified by ferritin (≤26 versus >26 ng/mL), sex, and age, randomised to ferrous gluconate (37.5 mg elemental iron) daily or no iron for 24 weeks after donating 500 mL of whole blood; the trial was not blinded.
cards.result: Compared with no iron, supplementation shortened time to 80% recovery of the post-donation haemoglobin decrease in both the low-ferritin group (mean 32 days, IQR 30–34, versus 158 days, IQR 126 to >168) and the higher-ferritin group (31 days, IQR 29–33, versus 78 days, IQR 66–95). Median recovery of iron stores took 76 days (IQR 20–126) with iron versus longer than 168 days without (P<0.001); without supplements, 67% of participants did not recover iron stores by 168 days.
cards.watchOut: Non-blinded, and the endpoints are recovery times for haemoglobin and ferritin — laboratory recovery, not symptoms; whether donors feel better, or donate more often over years, was not shown. Gastrointestinal side effects of daily iron are the usual practical limit.
cards.source: Kiss JE et al. Oral iron supplementation after blood donation: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2015. PMID: 25668261. Registry ID: NCT01555060. cards.headline: Smith 2014 Cochrane: deferral for low haemoglobin RR 0.34 at the first donation and 0.25 subsequently; adverse effects RR 1.60
cards.summary: Smith 2014 Cochrane: deferral for low haemoglobin RR 0.34 at the first donation and 0.25 subsequently; adverse effects RR 1.60
cards.people: 30 randomised trials with 4,704 blood donors, including 19 comparisons of iron supplementation versus placebo or control; the reviewers rated the evidence moderate quality, with many trials at low or uncertain methodological quality.
cards.result: Iron supplementation reduced deferral due to low haemoglobin at the first donation visit after starting iron (risk ratio 0.34; 95% CI 0.21–0.55; 4 studies, 1,194 participants) and at subsequent donations (risk ratio 0.25; 95% CI 0.15–0.41; 3 studies, 793 participants). Haemoglobin was higher by a mean difference of 2.36 g/L (95% CI 0.06–4.66) and ferritin by 13.98 ng/mL (95% CI 8.92–19.03) before further donation. Adverse effects were more frequent with iron (risk ratio 1.60; 95% CI 1.23–2.07).
cards.watchOut: Preparations, doses, and durations varied across the 30 trials, and many were small or at uncertain risk of bias; the deferral benefit is consistent, but the best dose and duration remain unsettled, and the adverse-effect excess is real.
cards.source: Smith GA et al. Oral or parenteral iron supplementation to reduce deferral, iron deficiency and/or anaemia in blood donors. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014. PMID: 24990381. cards.headline: Synthesis: iron after donation works on every measured outcome — recovery time, stores, and deferral
cards.summary: Synthesis: iron after donation works on every measured outcome — recovery time, stores, and deferral
cards.people: One randomised trial of 215 US donors (Kiss 2015) and a Cochrane review of 30 trials (4,704 donors; Smith 2014).
cards.result: 80% haemoglobin recovery in about one month with iron versus up to five months without (low-ferritin donors); deferral risk ratio 0.34 falling to 0.25 at later donations; adverse effects risk ratio 1.60. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): the effect is large, mechanistically direct, and consistent across designs.
cards.watchOut: LIKELY rather than higher because the underlying trials are mostly small and the flagship trial was unblinded; the claim is about laboratory recovery and deferral, not about donor symptoms or long-term donation careers. Tier C is not set.

shelves.title: Folinic acid for language impairment in autism: verbal communication improved by 5.7 standardised points in one small trial — strongest in children with folate-receptor autoantibodies
shelves.question: In children with autism spectrum disorder and language impairment, does folinic acid (leucovorin) improve verbal communication versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Autism Spectrum Disorder/drug therapy · Autistic Disorder/drug therapy · Child · Child Development Disorders, Pervasive/drug therapy · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Female · Folate Receptor 1/metabolism · Humans · Language Development Disorders/drug therapy · Language Disorders/drug therapy · Leucovorin/metabolism/pharmacology · Male · Placebo Effect · Receptors, Peptide/metabolism · Treatment Outcome · Verbal Behavior/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from a single small trial, with a plausible responder subgroup. Frye RE et al. (PMID: 27752075) randomised 48 children with non-syndromic autism and language impairment to high-dose folinic acid (2 mg/kg/day, maximum 50 mg/day) or placebo for 12 weeks: verbal communication improved by 5.7 standardised points more on folinic acid (95% CI 1.0–10.4; Cohen's d=0.70), and by 7.3 points (95% CI 1.4–13.2; d=0.91) in children positive for folate receptor-α autoantibodies, with no significant difference in adverse effects. The systematic review by Rossignol DA et al. (PMID: 34834493) found 21 leucovorin studies in autism — only four of them placebo-controlled — reporting improvements in communication with medium-to-large effect sizes, alongside mostly mild adverse effects (agitation or excitement 11.7%, aggression 9.5%, insomnia 8.5%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): promising, FRAA-guided, and still resting on one small randomised trial.

cards.headline: Frye 2018: verbal communication +5.7 standardised points versus placebo (d=0.70); +7.3 points (d=0.91) in FRAA-positive children
cards.summary: Frye 2018: verbal communication +5.7 standardised points versus placebo (d=0.70); +7.3 points (d=0.91) in FRAA-positive children
cards.people: 48 children with non-syndromic autism spectrum disorder and language impairment (mean age 7 years 4 months; 82% male), randomised to high-dose folinic acid 2 mg/kg/day (maximum 50 mg/day; n=23) or placebo (n=25) for 12 weeks, subtyped by folate receptor-α autoantibody (FRAA) status.
cards.result: Improvement in verbal communication was significantly greater on folinic acid than placebo: an effect of 5.7 standardised points (95% CI 1.0–10.4) with a medium-to-large effect size (Cohen's d=0.70). In FRAA-positive participants the effect was 7.3 points (95% CI 1.4–13.2; d=0.91). Improvements on the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scale, Aberrant Behavior Checklist, Autism Symptom Questionnaire, and Behavioral Assessment System for Children subscales were also significantly greater on folinic acid, and there was no significant difference in adverse effects between groups.
cards.watchOut: Forty-eight children, one centre's programme, 12 weeks — a result this size in a sample this small is exactly the profile that shrinks on replication. The FRAA subgroup finding, though pre-specified by the trial's rationale, rests on still fewer children.
cards.source: Frye RE et al. Folinic acid improves verbal communication in children with autism and language impairment: a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial. Molecular Psychiatry. 2018. PMID: 27752075. Registry ID: NCT01602016. cards.headline: Rossignol 2021 review: 21 leucovorin studies in autism, only four placebo-controlled; communication improved with medium-to-large effects; agitation 11.7%, aggression 9.5%
cards.summary: Rossignol 2021 review: 21 leucovorin studies in autism, only four placebo-controlled; communication improved with medium-to-large effects; agitation 11.7%, aggression 9.5%
cards.people: 21 studies of d,l-leucovorin (folinic acid) treatment in autism spectrum disorder, including four placebo-controlled and three prospective controlled studies; the review also pooled folate-receptor autoantibody prevalence (71% in ASD) across studies.
cards.result: Leucovorin was found to significantly improve communication with medium-to-large effect sizes and to have positive effects on core autism symptoms and associated behaviours (attention, stereotypy) in individual studies. In cerebral folate deficiency with ASD, reported improvement rates included overall symptoms 67% and irritability 58%. Adverse effects were generally mild; the most common were excitement or agitation (11.7%), aggression (9.5%), insomnia (8.5%), increased tantrums (6.2%), and headache (4.9%).
cards.watchOut: Most included studies were uncontrolled, so the improvement percentages largely reflect open treatment and expectation; the review's two authors include the trialist of the anchor RCT, and the record carries no MeSH terms. This card supports plausibility, not confirmation.
cards.source: Rossignol DA et al. Cerebral Folate Deficiency, Folate Receptor Alpha Autoantibodies and Leucovorin (Folinic Acid) Treatment in Autism Spectrum Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Journal of Personalized Medicine. 2021. PMID: 34834493. MeSH: none in the record

cards.result: Verbal communication +5.7 standardised points versus placebo (d=0.70) overall and +7.3 points (d=0.91) in FRAA-positive children, with no excess adverse effects in the trial and mostly mild effects across the review. shelves.title: Doubling third-trimester choline sped up infants' information processing — in a controlled-feeding trial of 26 women; the attention benefit was still visible at age 7 in the 20 children followed
shelves.question: In healthy pregnant women, does higher-dose choline supplementation in the third trimester improve infant information-processing speed versus standard intake?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Child Development/drug effects · Choline/administration & dosage/pharmacology · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Male · Mental Processes/drug effects · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Trimester, Third · Visual Perception
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a genuine randomised signal from a very small, tightly controlled trial. Caudill MA et al. (PMID: 29217669) randomised 26 women entering the third trimester to 480 mg choline/day or 930 mg/day until delivery, with all food provided: infants of the 930 mg group had significantly faster mean reaction times (information-processing speed) averaged across testing at 4, 7, 10, and 13 months (24 infants tested), and within the 480 mg group, longer exposure predicted faster reaction times. In the 7-year follow-up (Bahnfleth CL et al., PMID: 34962672), 20 children from the same trial were tested on a sustained-attention task: the 930 mg group performed superiorly on the primary endpoint (P=0.02) and maintained correct detections across the session (P=0.02), while the 480 mg group showed a 22.9% decline in hits for the briefest signals versus a 1.5% increase in the 930 mg group (P=0.04). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): one small trial and its own follow-up point the same way, but 26 mothers is a narrow base for advice to all pregnant women.

cards.headline: Caudill 2018: infants of mothers on 930 mg choline/day had significantly faster reaction times across 4–13 months than infants on 480 mg/day
cards.summary: Caudill 2018: infants of mothers on 930 mg choline/day had significantly faster reaction times across 4–13 months than infants on 480 mg/day
cards.people: 26 healthy women entering the third trimester of pregnancy, randomised to consume 480 mg choline/day (n=13) or 930 mg choline/day (n=13) until delivery with intake of choline and other nutrients tightly controlled; infant information-processing speed and visuospatial memory were tested at 4, 7, 10, and 13 months (n=24 infants).
cards.result: Mean reaction time averaged across the four ages was significantly faster for infants born to mothers in the 930 mg/day group than the 480 mg/day group. Within the 480 mg/day group there was a significant linear effect of exposure duration — infants exposed longer showed faster reaction times — suggesting even modest increases in maternal choline intake may benefit offspring processing speed.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen women per arm, a single research group's feeding facility, and a laboratory reaction-time outcome — not school performance or diagnosed outcomes. The abstract reports significance without the absolute reaction-time values, so the size of the advantage in everyday terms is unknown.
cards.source: Caudill MA et al. Maternal choline supplementation during the third trimester of pregnancy improves infant information processing speed: a randomized, double-blind, controlled feeding study. The FASEB Journal. 2018. PMID: 29217669. cards.headline: Bahnfleth 2022 follow-up: at age 7, the 930 mg group kept detecting brief signals (hits −1.5% change vs −22.9% decline in the 480 mg group; P=0.04)
cards.summary: Bahnfleth 2022 follow-up: at age 7, the 930 mg group kept detecting brief signals (hits −1.5% change vs −22.9% decline in the 480 mg group; P=0.04)
cards.people: 20 children aged 7 years from the Caudill controlled-feeding trial (mothers randomised to 480 or 930 mg choline/day in the third trimester), assessed on a signal-detection sustained-attention task.
cards.result: Children in the 930 mg/day group showed superior performance on the primary endpoint (SAT score, P=0.02) and a superior ability to maintain correct signal detections (hits) across the 12-minute session (P=0.02). For the briefest (17 ms) signals, the 480 mg/day group showed a 22.9% decline in hits across the session compared with a 1.5% increase in the 930 mg/day group (P=0.04); groups did not differ in false alarms, omissions, or off-task behaviours.
cards.watchOut: Twenty children — six of the original 26 families were not followed — and one attention task at one age; attrition and multiple task parameters leave plenty of room for chance. This is the same single trial growing older, not an independent replication.
cards.source: Bahnfleth CL et al. Prenatal choline supplementation improves child sustained attention: A 7-year follow-up of a randomized controlled feeding trial. The FASEB Journal. 2022. PMID: 34962672. Registry ID: NCT01127022. cards.summary: Synthesis: one small feeding trial, followed faithfully for seven years, still pointing the same way
cards.people: A single randomised controlled-feeding trial programme: Caudill 2018 (26 women; infant testing to 13 months) and Bahnfleth 2022 (20 children at age 7).
cards.result: Faster infant information-processing speed with 930 versus 480 mg choline/day, and better sustained attention at age 7 (primary endpoint P=0.02; brief-signal hit decline 22.9% in the 480 mg group versus a 1.5% increase in the 930 mg group). shelves.title: Vitamin D repletion in type 2 diabetes: HbA1c lower by 0.30 percentage points across 24 controlled trials — a small average gain, with the deficiency-specific trial evidence still pilot-sized
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and documented vitamin D deficiency, does vitamin D repletion improve glycaemic control (HbA1c) versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/metabolism · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/complications/diet therapy/drug therapy · Dietary Supplements · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Vitamin D/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives/blood · Vitamin D Deficiency/blood/complications/diet therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small, and not yet proven to be a deficiency-only effect. Mirhosseini N et al. (PMID: 28957454) pooled 24 controlled trials (1,528 people with type 2 diabetes): vitamin D supplementation reduced HbA1c by a mean difference of 0.30 percentage points (95% CI −0.45 to −0.15; P<0.001), fasting glucose by 4.9 mg/dL (95% CI −8.1 to −1.6), and HOMA-IR by 0.66 (95% CI −1.06 to −0.26), while raising serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D by about 17 ng/mL; the authors note a minimum dose of 100 µg/day (4,000 IU/day) in the trials showing these effects. The deficiency-specific randomised pilot by Upreti V et al. (PMID: 29580871) — 60 patients with type 2 diabetes and hypovitaminosis D, 6 months — found within the supplemented group a fall in HbA1c from 7.29% to 7.02% (P=0.01) and in fasting glucose from 131.4 to 102.6 mg/dL (P=0.04), though the abstract reports within-group rather than between-group comparisons. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): repletion improves glycaemic measures modestly on average; whether deficient patients gain more is plausible but under-tested.

cards.headline: Mirhosseini 2017: HbA1c −0.30 points, fasting glucose −4.9 mg/dL, HOMA-IR −0.66 across 24 controlled trials in type 2 diabetes
cards.summary: Mirhosseini 2017: HbA1c −0.30 points, fasting glucose −4.9 mg/dL, HOMA-IR −0.66 across 24 controlled trials in type 2 diabetes
cards.people: 24 controlled trials including 1,528 individuals diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, evaluating vitamin D supplementation against control for HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose, and insulin resistance (search to January 2017).
cards.result: Vitamin D supplementation significantly reduced HbA1c (mean difference −0.30%; 95% CI −0.45 to −0.15; P<0.001), fasting plasma glucose (mean difference −4.9 mg/dL; 95% CI −8.1 to −1.6; P=0.003), and HOMA-IR (mean difference −0.66; 95% CI −1.06 to −0.26; P=0.001), and increased serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D by 17±2.4 ng/mL overall. The authors report that a minimum dose of 100 µg/day (4,000 IU/day) was associated with these effects.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials were not restricted to vitamin-D-deficient patients, doses and durations varied, and 'controlled trials' includes designs short of full randomisation — so the deficiency-specific question the shelf asks is only partly answered by this card. An average 0.30-point HbA1c shift is smaller than the effect of any standard glucose-lowering drug.
cards.source: Mirhosseini N et al. The Effect of Improved Serum 25-Hydroxyvitamin D Status on Glycemic Control in Diabetic Patients: A Meta-Analysis. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism. 2017. PMID: 28957454. cards.headline: Upreti 2018 pilot: in 60 deficient patients, HbA1c fell from 7.29% to 7.02% on vitamin D over 6 months (P=0.01) — reported within-group
cards.summary: Upreti 2018 pilot: in 60 deficient patients, HbA1c fell from 7.29% to 7.02% on vitamin D over 6 months (P=0.01) — reported within-group
cards.people: 60 patients with type 2 diabetes and coexisting hypovitaminosis D at an Indian tertiary-care hospital, randomised to oral vitamin D or microcrystalline-cellulose placebo for 6 months, with HbA1c and vitamin D levels at baseline and study end and monthly glucose monitoring.
cards.result: The supplemented group showed a significant decrease in mean HbA1c (7.29% to 7.02%; P=0.01), fasting plasma glucose (131.4 to 102.6 mg/dL; P=0.04), and postprandial glucose (196.2 to 135.0 mg/dL; P<0.001), with improvements also reported in blood pressure and total cholesterol. The two groups were comparable at baseline.
cards.watchOut: A 60-patient pilot whose abstract reports within-group changes rather than the decisive between-group differences; effects of this apparent size (fasting glucose −29 mg/dL) in a pilot usually shrink in definitive trials. Single-centre, and the dose regimen is not stated in the abstract.
cards.source: Upreti V et al. Effect of oral vitamin D supplementation on glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus with coexisting hypovitaminosis D: A parallel group placebo controlled randomized controlled pilot study. Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome. 2018. PMID: 29580871. cards.headline: Synthesis: a modest average glycaemic gain in the pooled trials; the deficient-patient trial is encouraging and tiny
cards.summary: Synthesis: a modest average glycaemic gain in the pooled trials; the deficient-patient trial is encouraging and tiny
cards.people: A meta-analysis of 24 controlled trials (1,528 patients; Mirhosseini 2017) and one deficiency-specific randomised pilot (60 patients; Upreti 2018).
cards.result: HbA1c −0.30 percentage points (95% CI −0.45 to −0.15) pooled; in the deficient pilot, HbA1c 7.29% to 7.02% and fasting glucose 131.4 to 102.6 mg/dL within the supplemented group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): worth correcting deficiency for its own sake, with a small glycaemic bonus likely — not a glucose-lowering treatment in its own right.
cards.watchOut: Correcting deficiency is standard care for bone indications regardless of this shelf; the open question is only the size of the glucose effect in truly deficient patients, which no large trial has yet isolated. Tier C is not set: a 24-trial meta-analysis carries the shelf.

shelves.title: Weekly vitamin A in pregnancy: maternal deaths cut by about 40% in Nepal — and no effect at all in Ghana's 207,000-woman trial; the answer splits by setting
shelves.question: In pregnant women in a vitamin-A-deficient population, does weekly low-dose vitamin A or beta-carotene supplementation reduce maternal mortality versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Cause of Death · Cluster Analysis · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Maternal Mortality · Nepal/epidemiology · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications/mortality/prevention & control · Rural Health/statistics & numerical data · Vitamin A/administration & dosage · beta Carotene/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two large trials flatly disagree. In Nepal (West KP Jr et al., PMID: 10037634; NNIPS-2), 44,646 women received weekly vitamin A (7,000 µg retinol equivalents), beta-carotene (42 mg), or placebo for over 3.5 years: pregnancy-related mortality was 704 per 100,000 pregnancies on placebo versus 426 on vitamin A (relative risk 0.60; 95% CI 0.37–0.97) and 361 on beta-carotene (relative risk 0.51; 95% CI 0.30–0.86) — reductions of 40% and 49%, with the maternal mortality ratio falling from 645 to 385 per 100,000 live births on combined supplementation. In Ghana (Kirkwood BR et al., PMID: 20435345; ObaapaVitA), 207,781 women received weekly vitamin A (25,000 IU) or placebo: pregnancy-related deaths were 348 versus 377 per 100,000 pregnancies (adjusted odds ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.73–1.17; P=0.51) and all-cause female mortality was identical (rate ratio 1.01; 95% CI 0.93–1.09). PROPOSED SPLIT: a large mortality benefit in the deficient Nepali population, none in Ghana — baseline deficiency, dose, and setting appear to decide the answer.

cards.headline: West 1999 (NNIPS-2, Nepal): pregnancy-related mortality 426 (vitamin A) and 361 (beta-carotene) versus 704 per 100,000 pregnancies on placebo
cards.summary: West 1999 (NNIPS-2, Nepal): pregnancy-related mortality 426 (vitamin A) and 361 (beta-carotene) versus 704 per 100,000 pregnancies on placebo
cards.people: 44,646 married women of reproductive age in rural Sarlahi district, Nepal, in 270 wards randomised to weekly placebo, vitamin A (7,000 µg retinol equivalents), or beta-carotene (42 mg) for over 3.5 years; 20,119 women became pregnant 22,189 times. The population was undernourished and vitamin-A-deficient.
cards.result: Mortality related to pregnancy was 704 (placebo), 426 (vitamin A), and 361 (beta-carotene) deaths per 100,000 pregnancies — relative risks 0.60 (95% CI 0.37–0.97) for vitamin A and 0.51 (95% CI 0.30–0.86) for beta-carotene, reductions of 40% (P<0.04) and 49% (P<0.01). Combined supplementation lowered mortality by 44% (relative risk 0.56; 95% CI 0.37–0.84) and reduced the maternal mortality ratio from 645 to 385 deaths per 100,000 live births (40%, P<0.02). Cause-of-death differences could not be reliably distinguished between groups.
cards.watchOut: Cluster-randomised with wide confidence intervals — the vitamin A interval (0.37–0.97) only just excludes no effect — and conducted in a severely deficient, undernourished population in the 1990s; neither the baseline risk nor the deficiency level transfers to better-nourished settings.
cards.source: West KP Jr et al. Double blind, cluster randomised trial of low dose supplementation with vitamin A or beta carotene on mortality related to pregnancy in Nepal. The NNIPS-2 Study Group. BMJ. 1999. PMID: 10037634. cards.headline: Kirkwood 2010 (ObaapaVitA, Ghana): pregnancy-related deaths 348 versus 377 per 100,000 (OR 0.92; P=0.51); all-cause mortality rate ratio 1.01
cards.summary: Kirkwood 2010 (ObaapaVitA, Ghana): pregnancy-related deaths 348 versus 377 per 100,000 (OR 0.92; P=0.51); all-cause mortality rate ratio 1.01
cards.people: 207,781 women of reproductive age (15–45 years) in seven districts of Brong Ahafo Region, Ghana, in 1,086 clusters randomised to weekly vitamin A (25,000 IU retinol equivalents) or placebo, distributed at 4-weekly home visits; 79,835 pregnancies were observed in the intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: Pregnancy-related deaths numbered 138 in the vitamin A group (348 per 100,000 pregnancies) versus 148 on placebo (377 per 100,000) — adjusted odds ratio 0.92 (95% CI 0.73–1.17; P=0.51). All-cause female mortality was 453 versus 449 deaths per 100,000 woman-years (adjusted rate ratio 1.01; 95% CI 0.93–1.09; P=0.85). The authors concluded the body of evidence does not support vitamin A supplementation for women in safe-motherhood strategies.
cards.watchOut: A null this size cannot be waved away — over 200,000 women — but Ghanaian women were less vitamin-A-deficient than the Nepali cohort, and weekly dosing at 25,000 IU in a better-nourished population may simply have had nothing to correct.
cards.source: Kirkwood BR et al. Effect of vitamin A supplementation in women of reproductive age on maternal survival in Ghana (ObaapaVitA): a cluster-randomised, placebo-controlled trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: same intervention, opposite answers — deficiency at baseline is the most plausible dividing line
cards.summary: Synthesis: same intervention, opposite answers — deficiency at baseline is the most plausible dividing line
cards.people: Two cluster-randomised trials of weekly low-dose vitamin A in women of reproductive age: Nepal (44,646 women; West 1999) and Ghana (207,781 women; Kirkwood 2010).
cards.result: Pregnancy-related mortality: relative risk 0.60 (vitamin A) and 0.51 (beta-carotene) versus placebo in Nepal; odds ratio 0.92 (95% CI 0.73–1.17) in Ghana. PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit where deficiency and undernutrition are severe, no benefit where they are not — a single global stamp would misstate one trial or the other.

shelves.title: Magnesium oxide for chronic constipation: overall improvement in 68.3% versus 11.7% on placebo at 28 days — matching senna (69.2%) in the only head-to-head placebo-controlled trial
shelves.question: In adults with chronic constipation, does magnesium oxide improve bowel movements and quality of life versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Chronic Disease · Constipation/drug therapy/physiopathology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Laxatives/therapeutic use · Magnesium Oxide/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Sennosides/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from one well-run 28-day trial. Morishita D et al. (PMID: 32969946) randomised 90 adults with chronic idiopathic constipation to senna 1.0 g, magnesium oxide 1.5 g, or placebo daily for 28 days: the response rate for overall improvement was 68.3% on magnesium oxide and 69.2% on senna versus 11.7% on placebo (P<0.0001); changes in spontaneous bowel movements and complete spontaneous bowel movements were significantly greater on both active treatments than placebo (P<0.001 and P<0.01), constipation quality-of-life scores improved significantly on magnesium oxide (P<0.001), and severe treatment-related adverse events were 0%. The systematic review by Kang SJ et al. (PMID: 34642269) of 23 randomised trials of laxatives in elderly patients likewise found magnesium-based osmotic laxatives among the agents more effective than placebo in the short term, with adverse-effect frequency and severity similar between arms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): magnesium oxide is an effective short-term osmotic laxative, on a single placebo-controlled trial supported by the elderly-laxative review literature.

cards.headline: Morishita 2021: overall improvement 68.3% on magnesium oxide and 69.2% on senna versus 11.7% on placebo (P<0.0001); no severe treatment-related adverse events
cards.summary: Morishita 2021: overall improvement 68.3% on magnesium oxide and 69.2% on senna versus 11.7% on placebo (P<0.0001); no severe treatment-related adverse events
cards.people: 90 adults with chronic idiopathic constipation (mean age 42 years; 93% women; mean symptom duration 9.9 years), randomised to senna 1.0 g, magnesium oxide 1.5 g, or placebo daily for 28 days; all 90 completed the study.
cards.result: The response rate for overall improvement was 11.7% on placebo, 69.2% on senna, and 68.3% on magnesium oxide (P<0.0001). Change in spontaneous bowel movements was significantly greater on senna and magnesium oxide than placebo (P<0.001), as was change in complete spontaneous bowel movements (P<0.01). Patient-assessed constipation quality-of-life scores improved significantly on senna (P<0.05) and magnesium oxide (P<0.001) versus placebo. The frequency of severe treatment-related adverse events was 0%.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-eight days, 90 patients, 93% women, one Japanese centre — nothing here speaks to long-term daily use, older or comorbid patients, or the hypermagnesaemia risk that matters in kidney impairment, which the trial's population would not reveal.
cards.source: Morishita D et al. Senna Versus Magnesium Oxide for the Treatment of Chronic Constipation: A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial. The American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2021. cards.headline: Kang 2021 review: across 23 elderly trials, magnesium hydroxide and other osmotic laxatives beat placebo short-term, with similar adverse effects between arms
cards.summary: Kang 2021 review: across 23 elderly trials, magnesium hydroxide and other osmotic laxatives beat placebo short-term, with similar adverse effects between arms
cards.people: 23 randomised controlled trials of laxatives for constipation in patients over 65 years, including 9 placebo-controlled studies; agents reviewed included psyllium, lactulose, polyethylene glycol, magnesium hydroxide, and stimulant laxatives.
cards.result: Bulk laxatives, osmotic laxatives (including magnesium hydroxide), stimulant laxatives with or without fibre, and newer agents were more effective than placebo in elderly constipation patients in the short term (within 3 months), and the frequency and severity of adverse effects were generally similar between study arms. Polyethylene glycol appeared safe and effective over about 6 months of use.
cards.watchOut: This review studied magnesium hydroxide rather than the oxide salt, in elderly patients, and the reviewers rate the underlying trial quality as not high with small samples — it supports the osmotic-magnesium class effect, not magnesium oxide specifically. The record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.source: Kang SJ et al. Medical Management of Constipation in Elderly Patients: Systematic Review. Journal of Neurogastroenterology and Motility. 2021. PMID: 34642269. MeSH: none in the record

shelves.title: Vitamin D for chronic musculoskeletal pain: pain scores fell a little more than placebo on change-score analysis (−0.57) but not on final scores (−0.06) — a small, analysis-dependent signal
shelves.question: In adults with chronic musculoskeletal pain, does vitamin D supplementation reduce pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Dietary Supplements · Humans · Pain/drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Vitamin D/therapeutic use · Vitamins/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the signal depends on how the trials are pooled. Wu Z et al. (PMID: 27676659), pooling 19 randomised trials (3,436 participants), found a significantly greater mean decrease in pain score with vitamin D than placebo (mean difference −0.57; 95% CI −1.00 to −0.15; P=0.007) in the 8 trials reporting change scores — but no difference in mean pain score at final follow-up (mean difference −0.06; 95% CI −0.44 to 0.33; P=0.78) across 14 studies, and a non-significant relative risk of 1.38 (95% CI 0.93–2.05) for reported pain improvement. Yong WC et al. (PMID: 28812209), pooling 4 trials (287 subjects) in chronic widespread pain and fibromyalgia, found lower visual analogue pain scores with vitamin D (mean difference 0.46; 95% CI 0.09–0.89, favouring treatment). In the small fibromyalgia trial by Wepner F et al. (PMID: 24438771), 30 women with low calcifediol randomised to cholecalciferol titrated to 32–48 ng/mL for 20 weeks showed a significant group effect on pain scores versus placebo. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): a small average pain reduction is possible, concentrated in patients with pre-existing pain, but the evidence is fragile to analysis choice.

cards.headline: Wu 2016: pain change scores favoured vitamin D (−0.57; P=0.007) but final pain scores did not (−0.06; P=0.78) across 19 trials
cards.summary: Wu 2016: pain change scores favoured vitamin D (−0.57; P=0.007) but final pain scores did not (−0.06; P=0.78) across 19 trials
cards.people: 19 randomised controlled trials of vitamin D supplementation versus placebo for pain, with 3,436 participants (1,780 on vitamin D, 1,656 on placebo), searched to October 2015.
cards.result: For the primary outcome (mean change in pain score), 8 trials (1,222 on vitamin D, 1,235 on placebo) showed a significantly greater decrease with vitamin D (mean difference −0.57; 95% CI −1.00 to −0.15; P=0.007), with a greater effect in patients recruited with pre-existing pain (interaction P=0.03). For mean pain score at final follow-up, 14 studies (1,548 versus 1,430) showed no statistical difference (mean difference −0.06; 95% CI −0.44 to 0.33; P=0.78). Reported pain improvement in 4 studies gave a relative risk of 1.38 (95% CI 0.93–2.05; P=0.11).
cards.watchOut: The headline depends on which of two legitimate analyses is chosen, and only a minority of trials reported change scores — a set vulnerable to reporting bias. The reviewers note they could not determine modifying effects of baseline vitamin D status or dose.
cards.source: Wu Z et al. Effect of Vitamin D Supplementation on Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Pain Physician. 2016. PMID: 27676659. MeSH: Dietary Supplements · Humans · Pain/drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Vitamin D/therapeutic use · Vitamins/therapeutic use

cards.headline: Yong 2017: in chronic widespread pain, vitamin D lowered VAS pain scores (mean difference 0.46; 95% CI 0.09–0.89) across 4 trials and 287 subjects
cards.summary: Yong 2017: in chronic widespread pain, vitamin D lowered VAS pain scores (mean difference 0.46; 95% CI 0.09–0.89) across 4 trials and 287 subjects
cards.people: 4 randomised trials involving 287 adults with chronic widespread pain or fibromyalgia syndrome (ACR criteria), comparing vitamin D treatment with placebo, searched to January 2017.
cards.result: Pooled results showed significantly lower visual analogue scale pain scores in patients who received vitamin D than in those on placebo (mean difference 0.46; 95% CI 0.09–0.89; I²=48%, reported as favouring the treatment group). Meta-regression found no significant relationship between the change in vitamin D level in the treatment group and the difference in mean VAS (coefficient 0.04; 95% CI −0.01 to 0.08; P=0.10).
cards.watchOut: Four small trials and 287 subjects, with moderate heterogeneity (I²=48%); the absence of a dose–response relationship between achieved vitamin D level and pain relief weakens the causal reading, and the mean difference is reported in the authors' sign convention.
cards.source: Yong WC et al. Effect of vitamin D supplementation in chronic widespread pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Rheumatology. 2017. PMID: 28812209. cards.headline: Wepner 2014: in 30 women with fibromyalgia and low calcifediol, titrating cholecalciferol to 32–48 ng/mL for 20 weeks produced a significant group effect on pain versus placebo
cards.summary: Wepner 2014: in 30 women with fibromyalgia and low calcifediol, titrating cholecalciferol to 32–48 ng/mL for 20 weeks produced a significant group effect on pain versus placebo
cards.people: 30 women with fibromyalgia syndrome (1990 and 2010 ACR criteria) and serum calcifediol below 32 ng/mL, randomised to oral cholecalciferol titrated to achieve calcifediol levels of 32–48 ng/mL for 20 weeks or placebo, with re-evaluation after a further 24 weeks without supplementation.
cards.result: A marked reduction in pain was noted over the treatment period in the treatment group: a 2×4 variance analysis showed a significant group effect in visual analogue scale scores, correlated with scores on the physical role functioning scale of the Short Form Health Survey 36. The authors describe the therapy as economical with a low side-effect profile.
cards.watchOut: Thirty participants and no absolute pain values in the abstract — the size of the benefit cannot be stated from the record, only its direction and significance. Fibromyalgia pain is also not interchangeable with all chronic musculoskeletal pain.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three lean-positive sources, one decisive caveat — the largest pooling is positive only on change scores
cards.summary: Synthesis: three lean-positive sources, one decisive caveat — the largest pooling is positive only on change scores
cards.people: Two meta-analyses (Wu 2016: 19 trials, 3,436 participants; Yong 2017: 4 trials, 287 subjects) and one small fibromyalgia RCT (Wepner 2014, n=30).
cards.result: Pain change-score difference −0.57 (95% CI −1.00 to −0.15) favouring vitamin D in Wu; final-score difference −0.06 (95% CI −0.44 to 0.33); widespread-pain VAS mean difference 0.46 (95% CI 0.09–0.89) favouring vitamin D in Yong. shelves.title: Vitamin C and iron absorption: a real dose-response at the meal — relative absorption up 1.65-fold at 25 mg and 9.57-fold at 1,000 mg — that shrinks to +30% relative for a supplement dose and to nothing for anaemia recovery
shelves.question: In people taking oral iron or eating iron-containing meals, does adding vitamin C (ascorbic acid) in different amounts increase iron absorption, and by how much?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anemia, Iron-Deficiency/drug therapy · Ascorbic Acid/administration & dosage · Ascorbic Acid/metabolism · Ascorbic Acid/pharmacology · Ascorbic Acid/therapeutic use · Diet · Dietary Supplements · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Ferrous Compounds/pharmacokinetics · Humans · Intestinal Absorption/drug effects · Iron/metabolism · Iron/pharmacokinetics · Iron, Dietary/pharmacokinetics · Male · Middle Aged · Phytic Acid/pharmacology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which claim is being made. For a single meal, the absorption effect is real and dose-graded: in the classic semisynthetic-meal experiments (Cook & Monsen 1977, PMID: 835510; 63 men), the relative ratio of iron absorption with versus without ascorbic acid rose from 1.65 at 25 mg to 9.57 at 1,000 mg, directly proportional to dose — and substantially less when the meal contained meat. Across real meals in 299 subjects (Hallberg 1986, PMID: 3700141), the enhancement was most pronounced in meals rich in inhibitors such as phytates and tannins, food vitamin C matched synthetic, and about 50 mg per main meal was judged enough for optimum effect; phytate itself inhibited absorption dose-dependently (by 18% relative at 2 mg and 82% relative at 250 mg) and ascorbic acid significantly counteracted it (Hallberg 1989, PMID: 2911999). With a modern supplement dose the gain is smaller and saturates early: 80 mg of ascorbic acid raised fractional absorption of a 100 mg ferrous fumarate dose by 30% relative, and 500 mg added nothing further (von Siebenthal 2023, PMID: 37357807). But the effect does not scale up to whole diets or to anaemia treatment: across complete diets at vitamin C intakes of 51–247 mg/day, absorption did not differ significantly (Cook & Reddy 2001, PMID: 11124756); and in 440 patients with iron-deficiency anaemia, iron plus 200 mg vitamin C three times daily was equivalent to iron alone for haemoglobin and ferritin recovery (Li 2020, PMID: 33136134), with a pooled advantage across trials of just 0.14 g/dL of haemoglobin (Deng 2024, PMID: 40765927). So the routine advice to pair vitamin C with iron rests on genuine meal-level physiology — and on the clinical question patients actually ask, the added vitamin C makes no measurable difference. PROPOSED SPLIT: vitamin C dose-dependently increases nonheme iron absorption from single meals and modestly from a supplement dose, but adding it to oral iron does not improve anaemia recovery (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: Cook & Monsen 1977: the absorption ratio rose from 1.65 at 25 mg of ascorbic acid to 9.57 at 1,000 mg — a graded, dose-proportional relative increase from a semisynthetic meal
cards.summary: Cook & Monsen 1977: the absorption ratio rose from 1.65 at 25 mg of ascorbic acid to 9.57 at 1,000 mg — a graded, dose-proportional relative increase from a semisynthetic meal
cards.type: Radioiron absorption study with graded ascorbic acid doses (Cook & Monsen 1977)
cards.people: 63 male subjects given multiple radioiron absorption tests with a semisynthetic meal, with ascorbic acid added in amounts from 25 to 1,000 mg; a telephone survey of 100 supplement users accompanied the absorption work.
cards.result: The increase in iron absorption was directly proportional to the amount of ascorbic acid added over the 25 to 1,000 mg range. The ratio of iron absorption with versus without ascorbic acid was 1.65 at 25 mg and 9.57 at 1,000 mg (both relative ratios). The relative increase was substantially less when the test meal contained meat, and a large dose of vitamin C taken with breakfast did not affect iron absorption from the noon or evening meal. At the surveyed average supplemental intake of 280 mg daily, the authors estimated a nearly 2-fold increase in the amount of iron absorbed daily if taken only with breakfast, and more than 3-fold if taken in divided doses with each meal.
cards.watchOut: A semisynthetic test meal in fasting volunteers is the most favourable possible stage for the effect, and absorption is expressed as a relative ratio against a low baseline — a 9.57 ratio is not a 9.57-fold rise in anyone's whole-day iron uptake, as the same group's complete-diet study (carded below) later showed. The ratios, not absolute absorption percentages, are what this paper reports.
cards.source: Cook JD, Monsen ER. Vitamin C, the common cold, and iron absorption. The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 1977. PMID: 835510. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era study). radioiron absorption study with graded ascorbic acid doses (cook & monsen 1977) 63 male subjects given multiple radioiron absorption tests with a semisynthetic meal, with ascorbic acid added in amounts from 25 to 1,000 mg; a telephone survey of 100 supplement users accompanied the absorption work. the increase in iron absorption was directly proportional to the amount of ascorbic acid added over the 25 to 1,000 mg range. the ratio of iron absorption with versus without ascorbic acid was 1.65 at 25 mg and 9.57 at 1,000 mg (both relative ratios). the relative increase was substantially less when the test meal contained meat, and a large dose of vitamin c taken with breakfast did not affect iron absorption from the noon or evening meal. at the surveyed average supplemental intake of 280 mg daily, the authors estimated a nearly 2-fold increase in the amount of iron absorbed daily if taken only with breakfast, and more than 3-fold if taken in divided doses with each meal. a semisynthetic test meal in fasting volunteers is the most favourable possible stage for the effect, and absorption is expressed as a relative ratio against a low baseline — a 9.57 ratio is not a 9.57-fold rise in anyone's whole-day iron uptake, as the same group's complete-diet study (carded below) later showed. the ratios, not absolute absorption percentages, are what this paper reports. cook jd, monsen er. vitamin c, the common cold, and iron absorption. the american journal of clinical nutrition. 1977. pmid: 835510. registry id: none in the record (pre-registration-era study). mesh: adolescent · adult · ascorbic acid/therapeutic use · common cold/prevention & control · diet · ferritins/blood · humans · intestinal absorption/drug effects · iron/blood · iron/metabolism · male · stimulation, chemical

cards.headline: Hallberg 1986 (299 subjects, real meals): the enhancement was largest in meals rich in inhibitors, food vitamin C matched synthetic, and about 50 mg per main meal was judged enough for optimum effect
cards.summary: Hallberg 1986 (299 subjects, real meals): the enhancement was largest in meals rich in inhibitors, food vitamin C matched synthetic, and about 50 mg per main meal was judged enough for optimum effect
cards.type: Radioisotope meal-absorption studies across meal types (Hallberg, Brune & Rossander 1986)
cards.people: 299 subjects; different meals in which the nonheme iron was labelled with two different radio-iron isotopes were served with and without ascorbic acid to the same subjects, including meals containing foods with a known high content of ascorbic acid and studies giving different amounts of synthetic ascorbic acid with different meals.
cards.result: Marked differences in the enhancement of iron absorption were seen between meals: the most pronounced effects of ascorbic acid were found in meals with a high content of ligands known to inhibit iron absorption, such as phytates and tannins. Crystalline (synthetic) ascorbic acid and native ascorbic acid in foods appeared to have the same effect in promoting absorption of iron. The authors concluded that ascorbic acid has a key physiologic role in facilitating the absorption of nonheme iron from the diet and that about 50 mg of the vitamin in each main meal is desirable for optimum effect.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports the pattern across meals rather than a per-dose table — the fine-grained dose numbers live in Cook & Monsen's semisynthetic-meal work and in the reviews. 'About 50 mg in each main meal' is the authors' practical reading of a curve whose steepest gains come early; it is a meal-level statement, not a supplement-dose recommendation.
cards.source: Hallberg L, Brune M, Rossander L. Effect of ascorbic acid on iron absorption from different types of meals. cards.headline: Hallberg 1989: phytate inhibited absorption dose-dependently (by 18% relative at 2 mg, 64% at 25 mg, 82% at 250 mg) — and ascorbic acid significantly counteracted the inhibition
cards.summary: Hallberg 1989: phytate inhibited absorption dose-dependently (by 18% relative at 2 mg, 64% at 25 mg, 82% at 250 mg) — and ascorbic acid significantly counteracted the inhibition
cards.type: Controlled clinical trial of phytate dose and ascorbic acid counteraction (Hallberg, Brune & Rossander 1989)
cards.people: Volunteers served wheat rolls containing no phytates and rolls to which sodium phytate was added at seven dose levels between 2 and 250 mg (expressed as phytate phosphorus), the iron in the two kinds of rolls labelled with two radioisotopes (55Fe and 59Fe) and the rolls served on alternate days; the counteracting effects of ascorbic acid and of meat were also tested.
cards.result: The inhibition of iron absorption was strongly related to the amount of phytate added: 2 mg inhibited absorption by 18% (p less than 0.001), 25 mg by 64% (p less than 0.001), and 250 mg by 82% (p less than 0.001) — all relative reductions in absorption of the labelled meal iron. The addition of ascorbic acid significantly counteracted the inhibition, whereas the corresponding effect of meat was less well defined and only seen at the highest phytate level.
cards.watchOut: This card measures the inhibitor's dose-response more precisely than the rescuer's: the abstract states that ascorbic acid 'significantly counteracted' the phytate inhibition without printing the ascorbic acid dose or the size of the rescue, so no number for the counteraction is claimed here.
cards.source: Hallberg L, Brune M, Rossander L. Iron absorption in man: ascorbic acid and dose-dependent inhibition by phytate. The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 1989. PMID: 2911999. cards.headline: Lynch & Cook 1980 (review): enhancement from vegetable meals is directly proportional to the quantity of ascorbic acid present, and ascorbic acid can reverse the inhibiting effect of tea and calcium/phosphate
cards.summary: Lynch & Cook 1980 (review): enhancement from vegetable meals is directly proportional to the quantity of ascorbic acid present, and ascorbic acid can reverse the inhibiting effect of tea and calcium/phosphate
cards.type: Narrative review of the vitamin C and iron interaction (Lynch & Cook 1980)
cards.people: Review of the human absorption literature: food iron is absorbed from two separate pools, heme and nonheme iron; the nonheme pool is the major dietary pool and the one whose absorption is greatly influenced by meal composition.
cards.result: Ascorbic acid is a powerful enhancer of nonheme iron absorption and can reverse the inhibiting effect of such substances as tea and calcium/phosphate, though its influence may be less pronounced in meals of high iron availability — those containing meat, fish, or poultry. The enhancement of iron absorption from vegetable meals is directly proportional to the quantity of ascorbic acid present. The absorption of soluble inorganic iron added to a meal increases in parallel with the absorption of nonheme iron, but ascorbic acid has a much smaller effect on insoluble iron compounds, such as ferric oxide or ferric hydroxide. The mechanism given: ascorbic acid facilitates iron absorption by forming a chelate with ferric iron at acid pH that remains soluble at the alkaline pH of the duodenum.
cards.watchOut: A 1980 narrative review — carded for the dose-proportionality framing and the mechanism, not as independent data; the primary studies on this shelf carry the numbers. Its stated obstacles to ascorbic acid use (high cost, instability during food storage) concern fortification programmes, not a patient taking a supplement.
cards.source: Lynch SR, Cook JD. Interaction of vitamin C and iron. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences. 1980. PMID: 6940487. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era review).
