cards.headline: Teucher 2004 (review): the dose-response rises steeply to an ascorbic acid-to-iron molar ratio of about 7.5 (roughly a 3-fold relative increase), then flattens; meals with low-to-medium inhibitors need a molar ratio of 2:1
cards.summary: Teucher 2004 (review): the dose-response rises steeply to an ascorbic acid-to-iron molar ratio of about 7.5 (roughly a 3-fold relative increase), then flattens; meals with low-to-medium inhibitors need a molar ratio of 2:1
cards.type: Review of enhancers of iron absorption (Teucher, Olivares & Cori 2004)
cards.people: Review of the human absorption literature on ascorbic acid and other organic acids, including the dose-response relationship obtained from a semisynthetic meal containing 4.1 mg iron with ascorbic acid in doses ranging from 25 to 1,000 mg.
cards.result: Ascorbic acid, with its reducing and chelating properties, is the most efficient enhancer of nonheme iron absorption. The promotion of absorption is more pronounced in meals containing inhibitors of iron absorption: meals containing low to medium levels of inhibitors require the addition of ascorbic acid at a molar ratio of 2:1 (for example, 20 mg ascorbic acid to 3 mg iron), and to promote absorption in the presence of high levels of inhibitors, ascorbic acid needs to be added at a molar ratio in excess of 4:1, which may be impractical. The dose-response from the semisynthetic meal is best described by a steep linear response up to a 7.5 molar ratio of ascorbic acid to iron, followed by a less pronounced linear dose-response above 7.5; at the 7.5 molar ratio the increase in iron absorption was about 3-fold (relative). Other organic acids may only be effective at ratios in excess of 100 molar. The review also cautions that the long-term effect of high ascorbic acid intake on iron status may be less than predicted from single-meal studies.
cards.watchOut: The 'about 3-fold at a 7.5 molar ratio' and Cook & Monsen's '9.57 ratio at 1,000 mg' come from the same semisynthetic-meal programme but are not interchangeable numbers: the ratio depends on the meal and on its baseline absorption, which is why this shelf reports each study's own figures rather than one pooled multiplier.
cards.source: Teucher B, Olivares M, Cori H. Enhancers of iron absorption: ascorbic acid and other organic acids. International Journal for Vitamin and Nutrition Research. 2004. PMID: 15743017. cards.headline: Von Siebenthal 2023 (modern supplement trial): 80 mg of ascorbic acid raised fractional absorption of a 100 mg iron dose by 30% relative; 500 mg added nothing further; coffee cut absorption by 54% relative
cards.summary: Von Siebenthal 2023 (modern supplement trial): 80 mg of ascorbic acid raised fractional absorption of a 100 mg iron dose by 30% relative; 500 mg added nothing further; coffee cut absorption by 54% relative
cards.type: Crossover stable-isotope absorption trial in iron-depleted women (von Siebenthal 2023)
cards.people: 34 iron-depleted women (median serum ferritin 19.4 μg/L) at ETH Zurich; each woman received 100 mg iron doses as ferrous fumarate labelled with 54Fe, 57Fe or 58Fe under six conditions — (1) water in the morning (reference), (2) 80 mg ascorbic acid, (3) 500 mg ascorbic acid, (4) coffee, (5) breakfast including coffee and orange juice (containing about 90 mg ascorbic acid), and (6) water in the afternoon — 204 doses in all, with fractional iron absorption calculated from erythrocyte incorporation of the isotopic labels.
cards.result: Compared with the reference condition, 80 mg ascorbic acid increased fractional iron absorption by 30% (relative; p<0.001) but 500 mg ascorbic acid did not further increase it (p=0.226). Coffee decreased fractional absorption by 54% (relative; p=0.004), and coffee with breakfast decreased it by 66% (relative; p<0.001) despite the presence of about 90 mg of ascorbic acid in the orange juice. Serum hepcidin was higher (p<0.001) and fractional absorption was 37% lower in the afternoon compared with the morning (p=0.059). Compared with consuming the 100 mg dose in the morning with coffee or breakfast, consuming it with orange juice alone resulted in about a 4-fold increase in iron absorption, providing about 20 mg more absorbed iron per dose.
cards.watchOut: The percentages are relative changes in fractional absorption of a single 100 mg supplement dose in young iron-depleted women — the cleanest modern answer to how much the vitamin C dose matters alongside a supplement, and its answer is a modest relative gain that is already maximal at 80 mg. It measures absorption of single doses, not anaemia recovery; the clinical-outcome cards are Li 2020 and Deng 2024 below.
cards.source: von Siebenthal HK, Moretti D, Zimmermann MB, Stoffel NU. Effect of dietary factors and time of day on iron absorption from oral iron supplements in iron deficient women. cards.headline: Cook & Reddy 2001 (the whole-diet test): across complete diets with vitamin C intakes of 51 to 247 mg/day, mean iron absorption did not differ significantly between dietary periods
cards.summary: Cook & Reddy 2001 (the whole-diet test): across complete diets with vitamin C intakes of 51 to 247 mg/day, mean iron absorption did not differ significantly between dietary periods
cards.people: 12 subjects; iron absorption from a complete diet was measured during 3 separate dietary periods by having the subjects ingest a labelled wheat roll with every meal for 5 days — the diet freely chosen for the first period, then altered to maximally decrease or increase the dietary intake of vitamin C in the second and third periods.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in mean iron absorption among the 3 dietary periods despite a range of mean daily intakes of dietary vitamin C of 51–247 mg/day. When absorption values were adjusted for differences in iron status and the 3 absorption periods were pooled, multiple regression analysis indicated that iron absorption correlated negatively with dietary phosphate (P=0.0005) and positively with ascorbic acid (P=0.0069) and animal tissue (P=0.0285). The authors concluded that the facilitating effect of vitamin C on iron absorption from a complete diet is far less pronounced than that from single meals, and that these findings may explain why several prior studies did not show a significant effect on iron status of prolonged supplementation with vitamin C.
cards.watchOut: Twelve subjects and self-selected diets — the null is a small study's null, and the authors' own adjusted analysis keeps a positive ascorbic acid signal. What the card establishes is narrower and important: the large single-meal ratios do not survive translation into whole diets at ordinary vitamin C intakes.
cards.source: Cook JD, Reddy MB. Effect of ascorbic acid intake on nonheme-iron absorption from a complete diet. The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2001. PMID: 11124756. cards.headline: Li 2020 (the clinical test, 440 patients): iron plus 200 mg vitamin C every 8 hours was equivalent to iron alone — haemoglobin difference 0.16 g/dL at 2 weeks, ferritin difference 1.27 ng/mL at 8 weeks
cards.summary: Li 2020 (the clinical test, 440 patients): iron plus 200 mg vitamin C every 8 hours was equivalent to iron alone — haemoglobin difference 0.16 g/dL at 2 weeks, ferritin difference 1.27 ng/mL at 8 weeks
cards.type: Single-centre, open-label, equivalence randomised clinical trial (Li 2020)
cards.people: 440 adults with newly diagnosed iron-deficiency anaemia at Huashan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai (220 in each group; 426 women [96.8%]; mean [SD] age 38.3 [11.7] years), randomly assigned to a 100-mg oral iron tablet (ferrous succinate) plus 200 mg of vitamin C or a 100-mg iron tablet alone, every 8 hours daily for 3 months; all 440 were assessed for the primary outcome and 432 (98.2%) completed the trial.
cards.result: From baseline to the 2-week follow-up, the mean (SD) change in haemoglobin level was 2.00 (1.08) g/dL in the oral iron plus vitamin C group and 1.84 (0.97) g/dL in the iron-only group (between-group difference, 0.16 g/dL; 95% CI, −0.03 to 0.35 g/dL), thus meeting the criteria for equivalence against the prespecified 1 g/dL margin. The mean (SD) change in serum ferritin level from baseline to 8 weeks was 35.75 (11.52) ng/mL in the vitamin C plus iron group and 34.48 (9.50) ng/mL in the iron-only group (between-group difference, 1.27 ng/mL; 95% CI, −0.70 to 3.24 ng/mL; P=0.21). There were no significant differences between the groups in adverse events (46 [20.9%] vs 45 [20.5%]; difference, 0.4%; 95% CI, −6.7% to 8.5%; P=0.82), and no patient withdrew because of adverse events. The authors concluded that oral iron supplements alone were equivalent to oral iron supplements plus vitamin C, and that on-demand vitamin C supplements are not essential to take along with oral iron supplements for patients with iron-deficiency anaemia.
cards.watchOut: An equivalence trial answers 'is iron alone as good' — at a generous 1 g/dL margin — but the confidence interval for the haemoglobin difference (−0.03 to 0.35 g/dL) also excludes any large hidden benefit of adding vitamin C at this dose and schedule. Open-label and single-centre, and almost entirely women; it is nonetheless the only large randomised clinical-outcome test of the exact advice patients are routinely given, and it is concordant with the meta-analysis beside it.

cards.headline: Deng 2024 (meta-analysis of the clinical trials): the pooled advantage of adding vitamin C was 0.14 g/dL of haemoglobin and 3.23 μg/L of ferritin — statistically significant, and 'small and likely clinically insignificant' by the authors' own judgement
cards.summary: Deng 2024 (meta-analysis of the clinical trials): the pooled advantage of adding vitamin C was 0.14 g/dL of haemoglobin and 3.23 μg/L of ferritin — statistically significant, and 'small and likely clinically insignificant' by the authors' own judgement
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Deng 2024)
cards.people: 10 randomised controlled trials (n=1,782) and 1 prospective cohort study (n=148), comprising 1,930 patients with iron-deficiency anaemia, comparing oral iron supplements with versus without vitamin C; databases searched from inception to July 2023; the review protocol was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42023435260) before data collection.
cards.result: Vitamin C supplementation was associated with a significant increase in serum haemoglobin level (mean difference, 0.14 g/dL; 95% CI, 0.08 to 0.20; P<0.01; 10 studies, 1,490 patients) and serum ferritin level (mean difference, 3.23 μg/L; 95% CI, 1.63 to 4.84; P<0.01; 9 studies, 1,682 patients) in the iron plus vitamin C group compared with the iron-only group. The authors state that the addition of vitamin C was associated with a small and likely clinically insignificant increase in serum haemoglobin, and that the results do not support routine supplementation of oral iron therapy with vitamin C in the treatment of iron-deficiency anaemia.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are mostly small and vary in iron formulation, vitamin C dose, and population, and the pooled estimate leans on them collectively rather than on the one large rigorous trial (Li 2020, equivalence) — read the two cards together: at most a tenth-of-a-gram haemoglobin advantage against a prespecified equivalence finding. The PubMed record for this article carries no MeSH terms.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a real, graded absorption effect at the meal — and a clinical effect too small to find where it matters
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real, graded absorption effect at the meal — and a clinical effect too small to find where it matters
cards.people: Nine sources: the classic radioiron meal studies (Cook & Monsen 1977; Hallberg 1986, 299 subjects; Hallberg 1989), two reviews (Lynch & Cook 1980; Teucher 2004), a modern supplement isotope trial (von Siebenthal 2023, 34 women), a complete-diet study (Cook & Reddy 2001, 12 subjects), and the clinical-outcome evidence in iron-deficiency anaemia (Li 2020, 440 patients; Deng 2024, 1,930 patients pooled).
cards.result: Absorption from single meals: vitamin C increases nonheme iron absorption in proportion to dose — relative absorption ratio 1.65 at 25 mg and 9.57 at 1,000 mg from a semisynthetic meal (Cook & Monsen 1977); steepest gains up to an ascorbic acid-to-iron molar ratio of about 7.5, at roughly a 3-fold relative increase (Teucher 2004); the effect is largest in inhibitor-rich meals, where ascorbic acid significantly counteracts phytate (Hallberg 1989), and about 50 mg per main meal was judged desirable for optimum effect (Hallberg 1986). Absorption from a supplement dose: +30% relative fractional absorption at 80 mg, with no further gain at 500 mg (von Siebenthal 2023). Whole diet: no significant absorption difference across vitamin C intakes of 51–247 mg/day (Cook & Reddy 2001). Anaemia outcomes: equivalence for iron with versus without 200 mg vitamin C every 8 hours (Li 2020); pooled advantage 0.14 g/dL of haemoglobin (Deng 2024). PROPOSED SPLIT — the absorption claim is strong, replicated physiology at the single meal that fades with dose saturation, whole diets, and time; the treatment claim (add vitamin C to oral iron to correct anaemia faster) is (the treatment made no difference) on the clinical evidence.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict: absorption is a process measure rather than a hard outcome, and the shelf's two halves point in different directions. Nothing here concerns heme iron from meat, fish, or poultry, which meal composition affects far less, or intravenous iron. The same enhancing physiology would be expected to raise dietary iron absorption in iron-overload states — the mirror-image concern — which is outside this shelf's question and is not carded here.

shelves.title: Zinc and pneumonia in nursing-home residents (observational only for the outcome): normal serum zinc was associated with lower pneumonia incidence, almost 50% fewer antibiotic prescriptions and shorter pneumonia — but no completed trial has tested supplementation against pneumonia
shelves.question: In older adults living in nursing homes, does zinc supplementation reduce the incidence and duration of pneumonia versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Boston · Cause of Death · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Female · Homes for the Aged · Humans · Incidence · Male · Nursing Homes · Nutritional Status · Pneumonia · Time Factors · Vitamin E · Vitamins · Zinc
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the pneumonia outcome, printed on the face. The slated anchor is not a supplementation trial: Meydani 2007 (PMID: 17921398) is an observational analysis nested in a vitamin E trial, in which residents with normal serum zinc (70 µg/dL or above) had lower pneumonia incidence, almost 50% fewer new antibiotic prescriptions and shorter pneumonia than residents with low zinc. The only carded randomised supplementation trial (Barnett 2016, PMID: 26817502) tested 30 mg/day for 3 months in zinc-deficient residents and measured serum zinc and T-cell function, not pneumonia. A registered pilot for a pneumonia-outcome trial (NCT05527899) had reported no results as of its 2024 protocol (PMID: 38450236), whose authors state causality could not be inferred from the earlier work. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: adequate serum zinc is associated with less pneumonia; whether supplementation causes that benefit is untested in a completed trial.

cards.headline: Meydani 2007: nursing-home residents with normal serum zinc had lower pneumonia incidence, almost 50% fewer new antibiotic prescriptions, and shorter pneumonia than residents with low zinc — an observational analysis, not a supplementation trial
cards.summary: Meydani 2007: nursing-home residents with normal serum zinc had lower pneumonia incidence, almost 50% fewer new antibiotic prescriptions, and shorter pneumonia than residents with low zinc — an observational analysis, not a supplementation trial
cards.type: Observational analysis nested in a randomised vitamin E trial (Meydani 2007)
cards.people: Residents of 33 nursing homes in Boston, Massachusetts, who participated in a 1-year randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled vitamin E supplementation trial; all participants were given daily doses of 50% of the recommended dietary allowance of essential vitamins and minerals, including zinc. Serum zinc was measured at baseline (n = 578) and at the final visit (n = 420); low zinc was defined as under 70 µg/dL and normal as 70 µg/dL or above.
cards.result: Compared with subjects with low zinc concentrations, subjects with normal final serum zinc concentrations had a lower incidence of pneumonia, fewer (by almost 50%) new antibiotic prescriptions, a shorter duration of pneumonia, and fewer days of antibiotic use (P ≤ 0.004 for all, as printed in the record). Normal baseline serum zinc concentrations were associated with a reduction in all-cause mortality (P = 0.049). The authors conclude that zinc supplementation to maintain normal serum zinc concentrations in the elderly may help reduce pneumonia — a conclusion the design cannot by itself establish, as the record's own framing is an association between measured serum zinc and outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Serum zinc was measured, not randomised: residents who maintain normal zinc differ in diet, absorption, inflammation and overall health, and low zinc may be a marker of the same frailty that causes pneumonia rather than its cause.
cards.source: Meydani SN et al. Serum zinc and pneumonia in nursing home elderly. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2007. PMID: 17921398. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Barnett 2016: in the only carded randomised supplementation trial, 30 mg of zinc daily for 3 months raised serum zinc by a 16% greater change than placebo and increased T-cell numbers and proliferation — in 31 zinc-deficient residents (subgroup N on the face)
cards.summary: Barnett 2016: in the only carded randomised supplementation trial, 30 mg of zinc daily for 3 months raised serum zinc by a 16% greater change than placebo and increased T-cell numbers and proliferation — in 31 zinc-deficient residents (subgroup N on the face)
cards.people: 53 nursing-home elderly aged 65 years or older met eligibility criteria; 58% had a low serum zinc concentration (under 70 µg/dL), and these 31 were randomly assigned to zinc 30 mg/day (n = 16) or placebo 5 mg/day (n = 15) for 3 months in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Randomised subgroup N = 31.
cards.result: The difference in mean change in serum zinc was significantly higher, by 16%, in the zinc group than in the placebo group (P = 0.007) after controlling for baseline zinc; controlling for C-reactive protein, copper or albumin did not change the results. However, supplementation of participants with serum zinc of 60 µg/dL or below failed to raise their concentration to 70 µg/dL or above. Zinc supplementation also significantly increased anti-CD3/CD28- and phytohemagglutinin-stimulated T-cell proliferation and the number of peripheral T cells (P < 0.05); when proliferation was expressed per T cell, the between-group differences were lost, suggesting the enhancement was mainly due to more T cells.
cards.watchOut: This trial proves supplementation moves the blood level and a laboratory immune measure — it measured no pneumonia or infection outcome, and its randomised zinc-deficient subgroup is 31 people, so it cannot answer the clinical question on this shelf.
cards.source: Barnett JB et al. Effect of zinc supplementation on serum zinc concentration and T cell proliferation in nursing home elderly: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2016. PMID: 26817502. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ortega 2024: the definitive supplementation trial does not yet exist — a registered pilot (NCT05527899) is testing 30 versus 60 mg/day doses, and its protocol states plainly that causality could not be inferred from the earlier work
cards.summary: Ortega 2024: the definitive supplementation trial does not yet exist — a registered pilot (NCT05527899) is testing 30 versus 60 mg/day doses, and its protocol states plainly that causality could not be inferred from the earlier work
cards.people: Protocol for a randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind pilot trial of zinc supplementation in elderly nursing-home residents with low serum zinc, designed to choose between 30 and 60 mg/day elemental zinc doses and establish safety before a larger trial; pilot participant N not documented in the record. The protocol recounts the group's earlier finding that 29% of nursing-home residents had low serum zinc coinciding with a two-fold increase in pneumonia incidence and duration compared with residents with adequate levels.
cards.result: No outcome results are reported — this is a study protocol. Its stated rationale is that the earlier serum-zinc association could not establish causality and necessitates a double-blind clinical trial; the planned larger trial would test zinc supplementation in nursing-home elderly with low serum zinc on respiratory infections, antibiotic use and duration of sick days with pneumonia. The pilot also evaluates the correlation between serum zinc and pan-T-cell zinc levels.
cards.watchOut: A protocol card is evidence about the state of the science, not about zinc: it is carded so the shelf does not pretend the supplementation question has been answered, and it must never be cited as a trial result.

cards.headline: Synthesis: normal serum zinc is associated with less and shorter pneumonia in nursing-home residents, and supplementation reliably raises serum zinc and T-cell measures — but no completed randomised trial has tested supplementation against pneumonia itself
cards.summary: Synthesis: normal serum zinc is associated with less and shorter pneumonia in nursing-home residents, and supplementation reliably raises serum zinc and T-cell measures — but no completed randomised trial has tested supplementation against pneumonia itself
cards.people: The carded evidence: one observational analysis of serum zinc and pneumonia (baseline n = 578, final n = 420, within a vitamin E trial), one small randomised supplementation trial measuring serum zinc and T-cell function (53 eligible; 31 zinc-deficient residents randomised), and one registered pilot-trial protocol with no results (NCT05527899). Total carded participants across the outcome and laboratory studies exceed 600, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the randomised clinical-outcome evidence is absent, which is a different limitation and is printed here.
cards.result: Residents with normal final serum zinc had lower pneumonia incidence, almost 50% fewer new antibiotic prescriptions and shorter pneumonia than residents with low zinc (Meydani 2007). Supplementation at 30 mg/day for 3 months raised serum zinc (16% greater change than placebo) and increased T-cell numbers and proliferation, without bringing the most deficient residents (60 µg/dL or below) up to the normal threshold (Barnett 2016). The field's own next step is a dose-finding pilot for a pneumonia-outcome trial that has not yet reported (Ortega 2024). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the pneumonia outcome.
cards.watchOut: The honest gap on this shelf is causal: everything favourable about pneumonia comes from comparing people by their measured zinc level, and the one randomised trial measured blood and laboratory outcomes only.

synthesis the carded evidence: one observational analysis of serum zinc and pneumonia (baseline n = 578, final n = 420, within a vitamin e trial), one small randomised supplementation trial measuring serum zinc and t-cell function (53 eligible; 31 zinc-deficient residents randomised), and one registered pilot-trial protocol with no results (nct05527899). total carded participants across the outcome and laboratory studies exceed 600, so no small-n stamp labelling applies; the randomised clinical-outcome evidence is absent, which is a different limitation and is printed here. residents with normal final serum zinc had lower pneumonia incidence, almost 50% fewer new antibiotic prescriptions and shorter pneumonia than residents with low zinc (meydani 2007). supplementation at 30 mg/day for 3 months raised serum zinc (16% greater change than placebo) and increased t-cell numbers and proliferation, without bringing the most deficient residents (60 µg/dl or below) up to the normal threshold (barnett 2016). the field's own next step is a dose-finding pilot for a pneumonia-outcome trial that has not yet reported (ortega 2024). proposed possible (benefit) — observational only for the pneumonia outcome. the honest gap on this shelf is causal: everything favourable about pneumonia comes from comparing people by their measured zinc level, and the one randomised trial measured blood and laboratory outcomes only. synthesis of meydani sn et al. american journal of clinical nutrition. 2007 (pmid: 17921398); barnett jb et al. american journal of clinical nutrition. 2016 (pmid: 26817502); ortega ef et al. frontiers in nutrition. 2024 (pmid: 38450236).

shelves.title: High-dose vitamin D and falls (PARTIAL completion of live #30's annual-bolus question): no fall prevention at 1,000-4,000 IU/day, with significantly more serious and fracture falls at higher doses in STURDY
shelves.question: Does high-dose vitamin D increase falls in older adults compared with standard dose?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Aged · Bayes Theorem · Dietary Supplements · Drug Dosage Calculations · Female · Humans · Male · Vitamin D · Vitamin D Deficiency · Vitamins
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — regular high-dose vitamin D does not reduce falls, and the one dose-ranging trial raises harm signals rather than benefit. In STURDY, 688 adults aged 70 and over at elevated fall risk with serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D of 25-72.5 nmol/L (10-29 ng/mL) were randomised to 200 IU/day (control) or 1,000, 2,000 or 4,000 IU/day: in the confirmatory stage, the best dose (1,000 IU/day) did not differ from 200 IU/day on time to first fall or death (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.76-1.15), while falls with adverse outcomes were more frequent with the best dose (serious fall HR 1.87; fall with hospitalisation HR 2.48), and dose-finding event rates were higher at 2,000 and 4,000 IU/day than at 1,000 (Appel 2021). STURDY's fall-type analysis found the pooled higher doses (≥1,000 IU/day) carried a greater risk of a first fall with fracture than 200 IU/day (HR 2.66) (Wanigatunga 2021). The large VITAL trial (25,871 adults, 2,000 IU/day versus placebo for a median 5.3 years) found no fall reduction at all (2 or more falls in 9.8% versus 9.4%; OR 0.97) — a standard-versus-nothing comparison that rules out a hidden benefit the dose-ranging trial might have missed (LeBoff 2020). PARTIAL completion: live shelf #30 covers the single annual 500,000-IU bolus (Sanders), a different exposure entirely; this shelf covers regular daily high-dose versus standard-dose supplementation. The accurate summary is not 'high-dose vitamin D increases all falls' — overall fall rates were not significantly higher — but 'high-dose vitamin D does not prevent falls, and serious and fracture falls were significantly more frequent at higher doses in the one trial that ranged doses'. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm).

cards.headline: Appel 2021 (STURDY): 1,000 IU/day did not beat 200 IU/day on first fall or death (HR 0.94), serious falls were more frequent on the higher dose (HR 1.87), and 2,000/4,000 IU/day fared worse than 1,000 in dose-finding
cards.summary: Appel 2021 (STURDY): 1,000 IU/day did not beat 200 IU/day on first fall or death (HR 0.94), serious falls were more frequent on the higher dose (HR 1.87), and 2,000/4,000 IU/day fared worse than 1,000 in dose-finding
cards.people: Response-adaptive randomised trial at 2 US community-based research units: 688 participants aged 70 and over with elevated fall risk and serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D of 25-72.5 nmol/L (10-29 ng/mL, converted at 2.5 nmol/L per ng/mL), randomised to 200 IU/day (control), 1,000, 2,000 or 4,000 IU/day of vitamin D3. In stage 1 the best non-control dose was selected; in the confirmatory stage, participants with experience on the best dose (1,000 IU/day; n = 308) were compared with those randomised to 200 IU/day (n = 339) over 2 years.
cards.result: During dose-finding, primary-outcome rates were higher for the 2,000- and 4,000-IU/day doses than for 1,000 IU/day, which was selected as best (posterior probability 0.90). In the confirmatory stage, event rates did not differ significantly between the best-dose group and 200 IU/day (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.76-1.15; P = 0.54) — for falls overall, the higher dose made no difference. But falls with adverse outcomes were more frequent with the best dose: serious fall HR 1.87 (95% CI 1.03-3.41) and fall with hospitalisation HR 2.48 (1.13-5.46). The authors conclude doses of 1,000 IU/day or higher did not prevent falls versus 200 IU/day and that several analyses raised safety concerns at 1,000 IU/day or higher.
cards.watchOut: The control was 200 IU/day, not placebo, and the response-adaptive design means the harm signals come from secondary analyses of a trial whose dose-finding stage ended before its prespecified thresholds — signals to take seriously, printed as signals, not as a powered primary result.
cards.source: Appel LJ et al. The Effects of Four Doses of Vitamin D Supplements on Falls in Older Adults : A Response-Adaptive, Randomized Clinical Trial. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2021. PMID: 33284677. Registry ID: NCT02166333. cards.headline: Wanigatunga 2021 (STURDY fall types): pooled doses of 1,000 IU/day or more carried a higher risk of a first fall with fracture than 200 IU/day (HR 2.66)
cards.summary: Wanigatunga 2021 (STURDY fall types): pooled doses of 1,000 IU/day or more carried a higher risk of a first fall with fracture than 200 IU/day (HR 2.66)
cards.people: Secondary analysis of the STURDY randomised trial: the same 688 participants aged 70 and over with elevated fall risk and baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D of 10-29 ng/mL (25-72.5 nmol/L), randomised to 200, 1,000, 2,000 or 4,000 IU/day of vitamin D3; outcomes included repeat falls and falls that were consequential, injurious, required emergency care, caused fracture, or occurred indoors or outdoors.
cards.result: After adjustment for multiple comparisons, the risk of fall-related fracture was greater in the pooled higher-dose group (1,000 IU/day or more) than in the 200-IU/day control group (HR 2.66, 95% CI 1.18-6.00). Time to first outdoor fall appeared lower at 1,000 IU/day (HR 0.61) and 2,000 IU/day (HR 0.60) before multiple-comparison adjustment, but not after (adjusted P = 0.222). The authors conclude doses of 1,000-4,000 IU/day might increase the risk of first falls with fractures and that replication is warranted given the possibility of type 1 error — a caution this card keeps attached to the number.
cards.watchOut: A secondary analysis of the same 688-person trial as the first card — one trial programme, not two — with few fracture-fall events behind a wide interval (1.18-6.00); it sharpens the harm signal's location (fracture falls) without independently confirming it.
cards.source: Wanigatunga AA et al. The effects of vitamin D supplementation on types of falls. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2021. PMID: 34118059. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: LeBoff 2020 (VITAL): in 25,871 adults, 2,000 IU/day for a median 5.3 years did not reduce falls versus placebo — 2 or more falls in 9.8% versus 9.4% (OR 0.97)
cards.summary: LeBoff 2020 (VITAL): in 25,871 adults, 2,000 IU/day for a median 5.3 years did not reduce falls versus placebo — 2 or more falls in 9.8% versus 9.4% (OR 0.97)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, falls analysis (VITAL, LeBoff 2020)
cards.people: Nationwide double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial (VITAL): 25,871 adults (men 50 and over, women 55 and over; mean age 67.1 years) without cancer or cardiovascular disease at baseline, randomised in a 2x2 factorial design to vitamin D3 2,000 IU/day and/or omega-3 fatty acids 1 g/day or placebos, treated for a median 5.3 years. Mean baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D was 77 nmol/L (about 31 ng/mL).
cards.result: The numbers of participants with 2 or more falls were similar between vitamin D and placebo (9.8% versus 9.4%). Over 5 years there were no differences in 2 or more falls (OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.90-1.05; P = .50), falls resulting in a doctor visit (OR 1.03, 0.94-1.13) or falls resulting in a hospital visit (OR 1.04, 0.90-1.19). Results did not differ by baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D below versus at or above 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) or other cut points. The authors conclude this large trial does not indicate supplemental vitamin D should be used for primary prevention of falls in the US population.
cards.watchOut: VITAL compared 2,000 IU/day with placebo in generally healthy, mostly vitamin-D-replete adults — it answers 'does this dose prevent falls?' (no), not 'is this dose worse than 200 IU/day in fall-prone, low-vitamin-D elders?', which is STURDY's question; the two trials' populations differ as much as their comparisons.
cards.source: LeBoff MS et al. VITamin D and OmegA-3 TriaL (VITAL): Effects of Vitamin D Supplements on Risk of Falls in the US Population. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2020. PMID: 32492153. Registry ID: NCT01747447 (also NCT01704859, as printed in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: high-dose vitamin D does not prevent falls at any tested dose, and the dose-ranging trial found significantly more serious and fracture falls at 1,000 IU/day and above
cards.summary: Synthesis: high-dose vitamin D does not prevent falls at any tested dose, and the dose-ranging trial found significantly more serious and fracture falls at 1,000 IU/day and above
cards.people: The carded evidence: the STURDY dose-ranging trial and its fall-type analysis (688 participants, one programme) and the VITAL falls analysis (25,871 participants). Total carded participants exceed 26,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: STURDY: best dose versus 200 IU/day HR 0.94 for first fall/death, with serious-fall HR 1.87 and fracture-fall HR 2.66 at higher doses (Appel 2021; Wanigatunga 2021). VITAL: 2,000 IU/day versus placebo OR 0.97 for recurrent falls (LeBoff 2020). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — no fall benefit, with harm signals for serious falls from a single trial programme, which is why the stamp stops at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge this shelf with the annual-bolus shelf (#30): a single 500,000-IU dose, monthly mega-doses and daily 1,000-4,000 IU are different exposures, and the harm pattern here (serious/fracture falls, overall falls unchanged) is not the bolus pattern (all falls up).
cards.source: Synthesis of Appel LJ et al. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 33284677); Wanigatunga AA et al. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2021 (PMID: 34118059); LeBoff MS et al. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2020 (PMID: 32492153).

shelves.title: Folic acid in pregnancies exposed to antiseizure medication (PARTIAL completion of live #48): the direct studies find no demonstrated reduction in birth defects — guidelines recommend it anyway, by extrapolation
shelves.question: Does folic acid supplementation reduce birth defects in women taking antiseizure medication?
shelves.mesh: Abnormalities, Drug-Induced · Adult · Cleft Palate · Dietary Supplements · Drug Utilization · Epilepsy · Female · Folic Acid · Follow-Up Studies · Guidelines as Topic · Heart Defects, Congenital · Humans · Hypospadias · Infant, Newborn · Male · Neural Tube Defects · Pregnancy · Prospective Studies · Registries · United Kingdom · Vitamins · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — printed on the face, and the evidence is observational throughout. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #48 homes periconceptional folic acid preventing neural tube defects in the general population (the MRC recurrence trial and the Hungarian trial). This shelf asks the separate question for women taking antiseizure medication, whose drugs raise malformation risk and several of which are folate antagonists. The direct evidence does not show the protection seen in the general population. In the UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register (Morrow 2009), major congenital malformations were actually more frequent in women who took folic acid before conception than in those who took it late or not at all (3.9% vs 2.2%), and neural tube defects were near-identical (0.4% vs 0.34%) — confounding by indication (higher-risk women are likelier to be prescribed folate) may explain the direction, but no protective effect is visible. In the Slone case-control data (Hernández-Díaz 2000), folic-acid multivitamins blunted the harm of dihydrofolate-reductase inhibitors but did not diminish the adverse effects of antiepileptic drugs. A third direct register analysis (Australian Register, Vajda 2021, PMID 33272896) is already carded elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here; it likewise found no folic-acid dose effect. Against this, the 2024 AAN/AES/SMFM guideline still recommends at least 0.4 mg of folic acid daily before and during pregnancy for anyone on an antiseizure medication — a recommendation resting on extrapolation from the general population and on possible neurodevelopmental benefit, not on demonstrated malformation prevention in this population. Supplement note (clarification exception): none of the carded publications names a specific tested brand or manufacturer — the exposures are generic folic acid preparations (0.4 mg daily in the 2024 recommendation; higher doses are commonly prescribed in this population but were not shown to work better), so no product can be endorsed from this evidence. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): folic acid has not been shown to reduce birth defects in antiseizure-medication-exposed pregnancies; it is recommended anyway, and this shelf reports both halves of that sentence.

cards.headline: UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register 2009: preconception folic acid showed no protection — major malformations 3.9% with it versus 2.2% with late or no folic acid; neural tube defects 0.4% versus 0.34%
cards.summary: UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register 2009: preconception folic acid showed no protection — major malformations 3.9% with it versus 2.2% with late or no folic acid; neural tube defects 0.4% versus 0.34%
cards.people: Women with epilepsy enrolled prospectively in the UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register before the outcome of pregnancy was known: 1,935 pregnancies in women reported to have taken folic acid before conception, compared with 2,375 pregnancies in women who took folic acid only later in pregnancy (n = 1,825) or not at all (n = 550); outcomes were analysed against folic acid exposure, malformation type and drug group for the commonest monotherapy antiseizure medications.
cards.result: In the preconception-folic-acid group, 76 major congenital malformations occurred (3.9%, 95% CI 3.1–4.9), including 8 neural tube defects (0.4%, 95% CI 0.2–0.8). In the late-or-no folic acid group there were 53 major malformations (2.2%, 95% CI 1.7–2.9) and 8 neural tube defects (0.34%, 95% CI 0.2–0.7). Preconception supplementation was therefore not associated with fewer malformations of either kind — the treatment made no demonstrated difference. The authors conclude that extrapolating the general-population folate results to women with epilepsy may be questionable, and that the increased malformation risk in this group may act through mechanisms other than folic acid metabolism.
cards.watchOut: Observational and wide open to confounding by indication: women at highest risk (for example those taking valproate, or with a previously affected pregnancy) are the most likely to be prescribed preconception folate, which can make a neutral exposure look harmful — this card shows absence of demonstrated benefit, not proof of harm.
cards.source: Morrow JI et al. Folic acid use and major congenital malformations in offspring of women with epilepsy: a prospective study from the UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register. Journal of neurology, neurosurgery, and psychiatry. 2009. PMID: 18977812. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hernández-Díaz 2000: folic-acid multivitamins offset the defects linked to folate-blocking drugs such as trimethoprim — but did not diminish the adverse effects of antiepileptic drugs
cards.summary: Hernández-Díaz 2000: folic-acid multivitamins offset the defects linked to folate-blocking drugs such as trimethoprim — but did not diminish the adverse effects of antiepileptic drugs
cards.people: Case-control analysis from a US birth-defects surveillance programme: infants with cardiovascular defects (3,870), oral clefts (1,962) or urinary tract defects (1,100) compared with 8,387 control infants with malformations whose risk is not reduced by vitamin supplementation; mothers were interviewed within 6 months after delivery about medication use — including antiepileptic drugs such as carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital and primidone — and supplement use.
cards.result: Exposure to antiepileptic drugs in early pregnancy was associated with relative risks of 2.2 (95% CI 1.4–3.5) for cardiovascular defects, 2.5 (95% CI 1.5–4.2) for oral clefts and 2.5 (95% CI 1.2–5.0) for urinary tract defects. Use of multivitamin supplements containing folic acid diminished the adverse effects of dihydrofolate-reductase inhibitors (whose own relative risks were 3.4, 95% CI 1.8–6.4, for cardiovascular defects and 2.6, 95% CI 1.1–6.1, for oral clefts), but not those of antiepileptic drugs — for the antiseizure-exposed pregnancies on this shelf, folic acid made no demonstrated difference.
cards.watchOut: The outcomes here are cardiovascular, oral-cleft and urinary-tract defects rather than neural tube defects specifically; exposure was recalled after delivery; and supplement use meant multivitamins containing folic acid, not folic acid alone at the higher doses often prescribed alongside antiseizure medication.

cards.headline: AAN/AES/SMFM guideline 2024: despite the null direct studies, clinicians should prescribe at least 0.4 mg of folic acid daily before and during pregnancy to every patient on an antiseizure medication
cards.summary: AAN/AES/SMFM guideline 2024: despite the null direct studies, clinicians should prescribe at least 0.4 mg of folic acid daily before and during pregnancy to every patient on an antiseizure medication
cards.type: Practice guideline with systematic review (AAN/AES/SMFM, Pack 2024)
cards.people: Practice guideline of the American Academy of Neurology, the American Epilepsy Society and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine, built on a systematic review of evidence through August 2022 on antiseizure medications and folic acid supplementation in people with epilepsy of childbearing potential; recommendations integrate the systematic review with structured rationales, related evidence and inferences.
cards.result: On folic acid, the guideline states that clinicians should prescribe at least 0.4 mg of folic acid supplementation daily preconceptionally and during pregnancy to any patient of childbearing potential treated with an antiseizure medication, to decrease the risk of neural tube defects and possibly improve neurodevelopmental outcomes in the offspring. The same guideline directs clinicians to avoid valproic acid, if clinically feasible, to minimise major congenital malformations and neural tube defects — that is, its firmest birth-defect lever is drug choice, not folate dose. No specific folic acid brand or manufacturer is named; the recommendation is for generic folic acid.
cards.watchOut: FLAG: this card is a guideline, not a study — it is carded because only two free direct studies exist for this slice (the third, the Australian Register analysis, is already carded elsewhere). Its folic-acid recommendation is an extrapolation from the general-population evidence homed on live shelf #48 plus possible neurodevelopmental benefit, and it must not be quoted as if a study in this population had shown malformations falling.

cards.headline: Synthesis: in this population folic acid's benefit is assumed, not shown — the register and case-control data are null, and the guideline recommendation rests on extrapolation
cards.summary: Synthesis: in this population folic acid's benefit is assumed, not shown — the register and case-control data are null, and the guideline recommendation rests on extrapolation
cards.people: The carded evidence: two direct observational studies in antiseizure-medication-exposed pregnancies (UK Register, 4,310 pregnancies; Slone case-control study, over 15,000 infants) and one practice guideline with systematic review. A third direct register analysis (Australian Register, Vajda 2021, PMID 33272896) exists but is already carded elsewhere in the library and is fenced off this shelf.
cards.result: In this specific population, folic acid's benefit is assumed, not shown: the UK Register found malformation rates no lower (and nominally higher) with preconception folate, the Slone data found folate offset other folate-blockers' harm but not antiepileptic drugs', and the Australian analysis found no dose effect. Guidelines nonetheless recommend at least 0.4 mg daily — a low-risk intervention extrapolated from the general population, where the randomised evidence homed on live shelf #48 is strong. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): whether folic acid reduces birth defects in women taking antiseizure medication is unproven on the direct evidence; the recommendation to take it stands on extrapolation, and avoiding valproate where feasible is the better-evidenced protective step.
cards.watchOut: Nothing on this shelf argues against taking folic acid — it is inexpensive and safe, and the general-population neural-tube-defect evidence is strong; the shelf's point is narrower: in antiseizure-medication-exposed pregnancies, the malformation reduction itself has never been demonstrated.
cards.source: Synthesis of Morrow JI et al. Journal of neurology, neurosurgery, and psychiatry. 2009 (PMID: 18977812); Hernández-Díaz S et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2000 (PMID: 11096168); Pack AM et al. Neurology. 2024 (PMID: 38748979).

shelves.title: Vitamin D alone in adults not selected for deficiency (PARTIAL completion of live #56): two large trials and an 81-trial pool all found no fracture prevention
shelves.question: In adults without vitamin D deficiency, does vitamin D supplementation prevent fractures?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cholecalciferol/therapeutic use · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Fatty Acids, Omega-3/therapeutic use · Female · Fractures, Bone/epidemiology,prevention & control · Hip Fractures/epidemiology,prevention & control · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoporosis · Vitamin D Deficiency
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — for vitamin D ALONE in adults not selected for deficiency, the slice live shelf #56 leaves open (its home question is calcium plus vitamin D in healthy adults). Two large placebo-controlled trials of vitamin D alone agree: VITAL (25,871 US adults not recruited for deficiency, low bone mass or osteoporosis; vitamin D3 2000 IU daily for a median 5.3 years) found total fractures in 769 of 12,927 on vitamin D versus 782 of 12,944 on placebo (HR 0.98), with no effect on nonvertebral (HR 0.97) or hip fractures (HR 1.01) and no modification by baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D level; D-Health (20,326 Australians aged 60–84; 60,000 IU monthly for up to 5 years) found fractures in 5.6% versus 5.9% (HR 0.94). The 81-trial pool (Bolland 2018; 44,790 participants in the total-fracture analysis) gives a relative risk of exactly 1.00 for total fracture, and trial sequential analysis crossed the futility boundary for even a 5% relative reduction. Correcting deficiency is a different question, and institutionalised deficient older women are homed elsewhere (live #1498); the annual mega-dose harm signal is homed on live #30 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: VITAL 2022: in 25,871 adults not selected for vitamin D deficiency, vitamin D3 2000 IU daily did not reduce total, nonvertebral or hip fractures over 5.3 years (HR 0.98, 0.97 and 1.01)
cards.summary: VITAL 2022: in 25,871 adults not selected for vitamin D deficiency, vitamin D3 2000 IU daily did not reduce total, nonvertebral or hip fractures over 5.3 years (HR 0.98, 0.97 and 1.01)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, fracture ancillary study (VITAL, LeBoff 2022)
cards.people: 25,871 US men aged 50 or older and women aged 55 or older (50.6% women) in the VITAL trial's fracture ancillary study, randomised in a two-by-two factorial design to vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) 2000 IU per day or placebo (with n-3 fatty acids as the second factor); participants were not recruited on the basis of vitamin D deficiency, low bone mass, or osteoporosis; median follow-up 5.3 years, with fractures adjudicated by central medical-record review.
cards.result: Total fractures occurred in 769 of 12,927 participants on vitamin D and 782 of 12,944 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.08; P=0.70) — the treatment made no difference. Nonvertebral fractures: HR 0.97 (95% CI 0.87 to 1.07); hip fractures: HR 1.01 (95% CI 0.70 to 1.47). There was no modification of the treatment effect by baseline characteristics, including serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels, and no substantial between-group differences in adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The publication names the preparation only as vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) 2000 IU daily and does not name a brand or manufacturer, so no specific tested product can be identified from the record — current products are the same generic compound, but the record itself is silent on brand. A minority of participants were frankly deficient at baseline; the trial's own subgroup analysis found no benefit even by baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D level, but VITAL was not a trial of treating documented deficiency.
cards.source: LeBoff MS et al. Supplemental Vitamin D and Incident Fractures in Midlife and Older Adults. The New England journal of medicine. 2022. PMID: 35939577. cards.headline: D-Health 2023: monthly vitamin D3 60,000 IU for up to 5 years did not reduce fractures in 20,326 Australians aged 60–84 (5.6% vs 5.9%; HR 0.94)
cards.summary: D-Health 2023: monthly vitamin D3 60,000 IU for up to 5 years did not reduce fractures in 20,326 Australians aged 60–84 (5.6% vs 5.9%; HR 0.94)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, fracture outcome analysis (D-Health, Waterhouse 2023)
cards.people: 21,315 Australian adults aged 60–84 randomised to oral vitamin D3 60,000 IU per month or placebo for up to 5 years; 20,326 participants (vitamin D 10,154; placebo 10,172; 45.7% women; mean age 69.3 years) included in the fracture analysis, with fractures ascertained by linkage to administrative datasets over a median follow-up of 5.1 years. Participants were a general population sample, not selected for vitamin D deficiency.
cards.result: One or more fractures occurred in 568 of 10,154 (5.6%) on vitamin D and 603 of 10,172 (5.9%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.06) — the treatment made no difference. Non-vertebral fractures: HR 0.96 (95% CI 0.85 to 1.08); major osteoporotic fractures: HR 1.00 (0.85 to 1.18); hip fractures: HR 1.11 (0.86 to 1.45). The authors note the hazard ratio appeared to decrease with longer follow-up, a time pattern they flag as needing further research rather than an established effect.
cards.watchOut: Fractures were a tertiary outcome ascertained from administrative data rather than adjudicated records, and the monthly bolus schedule is not the daily dosing most people use — the trial answers the monthly-bolus version of the question and, reassuringly, found no sign that intermittent dosing increased fractures either.
cards.source: Waterhouse M et al. The effect of monthly vitamin D supplementation on fractures: a tertiary outcome from the population-based, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled D-Health trial. The lancet. cards.headline: Bolland 2018: pooling 81 randomised trials (53,537 participants), vitamin D alone had no effect on total fracture (relative risk 1.00) or hip fracture (relative risk 1.11), and trial sequential analysis crossed the futility boundary
cards.summary: Bolland 2018: pooling 81 randomised trials (53,537 participants), vitamin D alone had no effect on total fracture (relative risk 1.00) or hip fracture (relative risk 1.11), and trial sequential analysis crossed the futility boundary
cards.type: Systematic review, meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis of 81 randomised trials (Bolland 2018)
cards.people: 81 randomised controlled trials (53,537 participants) comparing vitamin D with untreated controls, placebo, or lower-dose vitamin D in adults over 18; trials co-administering calcium were eligible only where the groups differed solely by vitamin D use, so the pooled estimate isolates vitamin D's own effect. The total-fracture analysis covers 36 trials and 44,790 participants; hip fracture, 20 trials and 36,655 participants.
cards.result: Vitamin D had no effect on total fracture (relative risk 1.00, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.07 — a relative measure; the component trials' absolute rates are those of the VITAL and D-Health cards), hip fracture (relative risk 1.11, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.26), or falls (relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.02), with no difference between higher and lower doses and no clinically relevant bone-density effect at any site. For total fracture, the estimate lay within the trial-sequential futility boundary for relative risk reductions of 15%, 10%, 7.5% and 5% — reliable evidence that vitamin D does not reduce total fractures by even 5% in relative terms.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are heterogeneous in dose, schedule and population, including some older trials in institutional or deficient populations; the futility finding is about the average effect across such trials, and the two large modern trials on the preceding cards — both in non-deficient general populations — are the cleaner answer to this shelf's exact question.
cards.source: Bolland MJ et al. Effects of vitamin D supplementation on musculoskeletal health: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and trial sequential analysis. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2018. PMID: 30293909. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: vitamin D alone does not prevent fractures in adults who are not deficient — two large trials and the full trial pool agree
cards.summary: Synthesis: vitamin D alone does not prevent fractures in adults who are not deficient — two large trials and the full trial pool agree
cards.people: The carded evidence: two large placebo-controlled trials of vitamin D alone in general populations not selected for deficiency (VITAL, 25,871 participants; D-Health, 20,326 analysed) and one systematic review and meta-analysis of 81 trials (53,537 participants). Total carded participants exceed 45,000 in the trials alone, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Total fractures: HR 0.98 (VITAL) and HR 0.94 (D-Health); pooled relative risk 1.00 (Bolland 2018), with trial sequential analysis excluding a relative reduction of 5% or more. Hip fractures: HR 1.01, HR 1.11 and pooled relative risk 1.11 — no benefit in any analysis. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in adults without vitamin D deficiency, vitamin D supplementation does not prevent fractures. The combined calcium-plus-vitamin-D question stays homed on live shelf #56 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: This verdict is bounded by its population: adults not selected for deficiency. It does not speak to treating documented vitamin D deficiency, to institutionalised older people (live #1498), or to annual mega-dose regimens, whose harm signal is homed on live #30.
cards.source: Synthesis of LeBoff MS et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2022 (PMID: 35939577); Waterhouse M et al. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2023 (PMID: 37011645); Bolland MJ et al. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2018 (PMID: 30293909).

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology). The textbooks describe hepcidin as the liver's iron-regulatory hormone: when body iron stores rise, hepatocytes make more hepcidin; hepcidin binds ferroportin — the only iron exporter — on duodenal enterocytes (and macrophages), internalising and degrading it, so dietary iron taken into the enterocyte cannot reach the plasma and is shed with the cell, and stored iron stays locked in macrophages. The carded human studies show each limb of that account in people. Urinary hepcidin excretion was greatly increased in patients with iron overload and tracked serum ferritin (Nemeth 2003). A single oral iron dose of 60 mg or more raised serum hepcidin within 24 hours and cut fractional absorption of the next day's dose by 35% to 45% (Moretti 2015) — the stores signal acting on absorption in real time. And when transfusion raised haemoglobin and iron loading in thalassaemia major, hepcidin rose with ferritin and fell as erythropoiesis reasserted itself (Pasricha 2013), showing the stores signal competing with the erythropoietic signal exactly as the textbooks describe. The adjacent dosing shelf, live #1041, homes the alternate-day dosing consequence of this physiology and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Nemeth 2003: urinary hepcidin was greatly increased in iron overload and correlated with serum ferritin — the stores signal in humans
cards.summary: Nemeth 2003: urinary hepcidin was greatly increased in iron overload and correlated with serum ferritin — the stores signal in humans
cards.type: Human physiology study (urinary hepcidin in iron overload and inflammation, Nemeth 2003)
cards.people: Patients with iron overload, infections or inflammatory diseases, compared with controls; urinary hepcidin excretion was measured and set against serum ferritin, with complementary in-vitro work in primary human hepatocytes (subject numbers are not printed in the record — N not documented in the record).
cards.result: Urinary hepcidin excretion was greatly increased in patients with iron overload, infections or inflammatory diseases, and hepcidin excretion correlated well with serum ferritin — the marker of body iron stores. Interleukin-6 dramatically induced hepcidin messenger RNA in human hepatocytes in vitro (interleukin-1 and tumour necrosis factor alpha did not), identifying hepcidin as a type II acute-phase protein as well as a stores signal.
cards.watchOut: The iron-loading limb in patients is correlational (hepcidin against ferritin), and the interleukin-6 induction was shown in cultured human hepatocytes, not by infusion in volunteers — the card claims the human association, and the textbook supplies the causal frame.
cards.source: Nemeth E et al. Hepcidin, a putative mediator of anemia of inflammation, is a type II acute-phase protein. Blood. 2003. PMID: 12433676. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Moretti 2015: an oral iron dose of 60 mg or more raised hepcidin within 24 hours and cut the next dose's fractional absorption by 35% to 45%
cards.summary: Moretti 2015: an oral iron dose of 60 mg or more raised hepcidin within 24 hours and cut the next dose's fractional absorption by 35% to 45%
cards.type: Human physiology study (isotope-labelled iron absorption and hepcidin, Moretti 2015)
cards.people: 54 non-anaemic young women with plasma ferritin ≤20 µg/L in three studies: dose-finding with 40–240 mg of isotope-labelled iron as ferrous sulfate on one or two consecutive days (n=25 and n=16), and a study of three 60 mg doses within 24 hours (n=13).
cards.result: Twenty-four hours after doses of 60 mg or more, serum hepcidin was increased (P<.01) and fractional iron absorption was decreased by 35% to 45% (P<.01). A sixfold increase in dose (40 to 240 mg) produced only a threefold increase in iron absorbed (6.7 to 18.1 mg). Total iron absorbed from three doses in 24 hours was not significantly greater than from two morning doses — the hepcidin rise closes the absorptive gate behind each dose.
cards.watchOut: These were iron-depleted young women given supplement doses, not iron-loaded adults eating meals — the study demonstrates the hepcidin-absorption mechanism and its time course, while the stores-rise end of the axis is carried by the Nemeth and Pasricha cards.
cards.source: Moretti D et al. Oral iron supplements increase hepcidin and decrease iron absorption from daily or twice-daily doses in iron-depleted young women. Blood. 2015. PMID: 26289639. Registry ID: NCT01785407 and NCT02050932 (as given in the record). cards.headline: Pasricha 2013: in 31 adults with thalassaemia major, transfusion raised haemoglobin and hepcidin together — hepcidin tracked ferritin and opposed erythropoiesis
cards.summary: Pasricha 2013: in 31 adults with thalassaemia major, transfusion raised haemoglobin and hepcidin together — hepcidin tracked ferritin and opposed erythropoiesis
cards.type: Human physiology study (transfusion and hepcidin dynamics, Pasricha 2013)
cards.people: 31 chronically transfused adults with beta-thalassaemia major, sampled immediately before transfusion and 4 to 8 days after, in a longitudinal study of how suppressing erythropoiesis changes hepcidin.
cards.result: Pretransfusion hepcidin correlated positively with haemoglobin and ferritin and inversely with erythropoiesis, yet was relatively suppressed for the degree of iron loading (the hepcidin-ferritin ratio). After transfusion, haemoglobin and hepcidin increased while erythropoietin and growth differentiation factor-15 decreased. By multiple regression, hepcidin was associated positively with haemoglobin and ferritin and inversely with erythropoiesis, before and after transfusion.
cards.watchOut: Thalassaemia major is an extreme of ineffective erythropoiesis and transfusional iron loading, not ordinary iron repletion — its value here is that it separates the competing signals (stores raise hepcidin; erythropoietic drive lowers it) inside the same patients.
cards.source: Pasricha SR et al. Transfusion suppresses erythropoiesis and increases hepcidin in adult patients with β-thalassemia major: a longitudinal study. Blood. 2013. PMID: 23656728. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: rising stores raise hepatic hepcidin, hepcidin removes ferroportin, and absorption falls within a day
cards.summary: Synthesis: rising stores raise hepatic hepcidin, hepcidin removes ferroportin, and absorption falls within a day
cards.people: The carded evidence: urinary hepcidin against iron status in patients (Nemeth 2003, N not documented in the record), isotope absorption studies in 54 iron-depleted women (Moretti 2015), and a 31-patient longitudinal transfusion study (Pasricha 2013). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall; Ganong.
cards.result: The Guyton & Hall / Ganong account — liver hepcidin as the hormonal readout of body iron, acting by degrading ferroportin in enterocytes and macrophages — is what the human data show: hepcidin excretion greatly increased with iron overload and correlated with ferritin; a 60 mg iron dose raised hepcidin within 24 hours and reduced the next dose's fractional absorption by 35% to 45%; and hepcidin rose and fell with ferritin and erythropoietic drive in transfused patients. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Ferroportin internalisation itself was demonstrated in cell and animal systems (textbook context, labelled as such — no animal study is carded as evidence here); the human cards establish the hormone's behaviour and its absorptive consequence, which is the level at which the textbook claim is testable in people.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nemeth E et al. Blood. 2003 (PMID: 12433676); Moretti D et al. Blood. 2015 (PMID: 26289639); Pasricha SR et al. Blood. 2013 (PMID: 23656728). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology.

shelves.title: Why B12 needs intrinsic factor and a terminal ileum: the carrier-and-door physiology shown in human absorption studies
shelves.question: In adults, why does vitamin B12 absorption require intrinsic factor and an intact terminal ileum?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Celiac Disease · Clinical Trials as Topic · Humans · Ileum · Intestinal Absorption · Intestine, Small · Male · Middle Aged · Vitamin B 12
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbook account is a relay: food B12 is freed by acid and pepsin, rides first on R-protein, is handed to intrinsic factor — secreted by gastric parietal cells — when pancreatic enzymes digest the R-protein in the duodenum, and the intrinsic-factor–B12 complex is then taken up by specific receptors (the cubilin–amnionless complex) that exist only in the terminal ileum. Both requirements are therefore anatomical: no intrinsic factor, no protected carrier through the small bowel; no terminal ileum, no receptor to land on. The carded human studies show each requirement operating in people. Whole-body counting after a 5 µg dose of intrinsic-factor-bound labelled B12 put normal absorption at 20.4% and showed the ileum's absorptive capacity adapting upward when proximal bowel was lost (Mackinnon 1975). Patients with diseased or resected ileums had low B12 (and low B12 analogues, which share the ileal route), while pernicious-anaemia patients — whose defect is intrinsic factor, not ileum — had normal analogue levels (Shaw 1989). And Schilling testing after continent ileostomy showed absorption preserved where functioning ileal mucosa remained in circuit (Jagenburg 1975). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Mackinnon 1975: healthy adults absorbed 20.4% of a 5 µg dose of intrinsic-factor-bound B12 — and absorption rose above normal after proximal bowel resection, showing the ileum adapts
cards.summary: Mackinnon 1975: healthy adults absorbed 20.4% of a 5 µg dose of intrinsic-factor-bound B12 — and absorption rose above normal after proximal bowel resection, showing the ileum adapts
cards.type: Human physiology study (whole-body counting of IF-bound B12 absorption, Mackinnon 1975)
cards.people: Whole-body counting of intrinsic-factor-bound 58Co vitamin B12 absorption (7-day retention of a 5 µg dose) in 24 control subjects, 4 patients after proximal small-bowel resection, and 9 patients with adult coeliac disease, used as an index of ileal function because intrinsic-factor–B12 absorption is confined to the ileum.
cards.result: Control subjects absorbed 20.4% (± 1 SD 6.2%) of the administered dose. After proximal resection, absorption averaged 42.3% (range 32–61%) — above the normal range — and 2 of 9 coeliac patients (whose damage spares the ileum) also absorbed above normal (44.1% and 54%). The ileum is both the sole site of intrinsic-factor–B12 uptake and capable of functional adaptation.
cards.watchOut: A 5 µg labelled dose with intrinsic factor measures the receptor pathway's capacity, not absorption of an ordinary meal's B12; the percentage absorbed falls as dose rises, so 20.4% is a property of this test dose, not of dietary B12 in general.
cards.source: Mackinnon AM et al. Adaptive changes in vitamin B12 absorption in celiac disease and after proximal small-bowel resection in man. The American journal of digestive diseases. 1975. PMID: 1099899. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Shaw 1989: patients with diseased or resected ileums had low B12 and low B12 analogues, while pernicious-anaemia patients had normal analogue levels — separating the ileal requirement from the intrinsic-factor requirement
cards.summary: Shaw 1989: patients with diseased or resected ileums had low B12 and low B12 analogues, while pernicious-anaemia patients had normal analogue levels — separating the ileal requirement from the intrinsic-factor requirement
cards.type: Human physiology study (B12 and analogue levels by disease site, Shaw 1989)
cards.people: 93 patients with gastrointestinal diseases — pernicious anaemia, ileal resections, ileitis, Crohn's colitis, ulcerative colitis and irritable bowel syndrome — in whom serum vitamin B12 and non-cobalamin B12 analogues were measured.
cards.result: Patients with pernicious anaemia had normal analogue levels, unchanged or rising when B12 treatment stopped. Patients with irritable bowel syndrome, Crohn's colitis, ulcerative colitis and total colectomy had analogues in the normal range. Patients with diseased or resected ileums had low B12 and low analogues — the authors' reading: analogues are absorbed in the ileum by a mechanism independent of intrinsic factor, so ileal loss removes both pathways while intrinsic-factor loss removes only the cobalamin one.
cards.watchOut: Serum levels are a downstream readout, not a direct absorption measurement: low levels after ileal resection also reflect depleted stores and interrupted enterohepatic recycling of B12, which this cross-sectional design cannot separate from failed uptake.
cards.source: Shaw S et al. The ileum is the major site of absorption of vitamin B12 analogues. The American journal of gastroenterology. 1989. PMID: 2912026. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Anemia, Pernicious · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Gastrointestinal Diseases · Humans · Ileitis · Ileum · Vitamin B 12

cards.headline: Jagenburg 1975: Schilling tests stayed normal in most of 34 patients after continent ileostomy — absorption follows functioning ileal mucosa, wherever it sits
cards.summary: Jagenburg 1975: Schilling tests stayed normal in most of 34 patients after continent ileostomy — absorption follows functioning ileal mucosa, wherever it sits
cards.type: Human physiology study (Schilling tests after ileostomy, Jagenburg 1975)
cards.people: 34 patients studied 10 months to 6 years after construction of a continent ileostomy (an ileal reservoir), with Schilling tests of vitamin B12 absorption, repeated where the first test was low.
cards.result: A single Schilling test was normal (>10% excretion) in 21 of 34 patients; of the 13 initially below 10%, repeat testing was normal in 8, borderline (5–10%) in 4, and low (mean 4.5%) in 1 — one borderline patient had previously lost 80 cm of terminal ileum. Instilling the B12–intrinsic-factor complex directly into the reservoir in 3 patients showed the reservoir's ileal mucosa itself absorbed the vitamin. The authors conclude the reservoir does not add malabsorption risk.
cards.watchOut: The Schilling test's urinary-excretion readout depends on renal function and complete urine collection, one reason first tests were low and repeats normal in 8 patients; it is a test of the intrinsic-factor pathway as a whole, not of the ileum in isolation.
cards.source: Jagenburg R et al. Vitamin B12 absorption in patients with continent ileostomy. Scandinavian journal of gastroenterology. 1975. PMID: 1124347. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: intrinsic factor is the carrier, the terminal ileum is the only door — human studies show absorption failing when either is lost and adapting when ileum remains
cards.summary: Synthesis: intrinsic factor is the carrier, the terminal ileum is the only door — human studies show absorption failing when either is lost and adapting when ileum remains
cards.people: The carded evidence: whole-body absorption counting in 24 controls and surgical/coeliac patients (Mackinnon 1975), serum B12 and analogues across 93 patients grouped by disease site (Shaw 1989), and Schilling testing in 34 ileostomy patients (Jagenburg 1975). Textbook framing: Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep.
cards.result: Normal adults absorbed about a fifth of a small intrinsic-factor-bound test dose; absorption is confined to the ileum and can adapt upward (to ~42%) when proximal bowel is resected but ileum survives; ileal disease or resection lowers B12 while intrinsic-factor failure (pernicious anaemia) leaves the ileum-dependent analogue pathway intact. That is the Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep relay — gastric intrinsic factor as carrier, terminal ileal receptors as the single uptake site — demonstrated limb by limb in patients. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Very large oral B12 doses can cross by passive diffusion without intrinsic factor or ileum (about 1% of a pharmacological dose) — that exception is why high-dose oral therapy works, and it does not contradict the physiological pathway at dietary doses, which is what this shelf describes.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mackinnon AM et al. The American journal of digestive diseases. 1975 (PMID: 1099899); Shaw S et al. The American journal of gastroenterology. 1989 (PMID: 2912026); Jagenburg R et al. Scandinavian journal of gastroenterology. 1975 (PMID: 1124347). Textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology.

shelves.question: In older adults, does monthly high-dose vitamin D (e.g., 60,000 IU) increase or decrease falls and fractures versus daily standard dosing or placebo?

shelves.balance: SPLIT, by comparator — verified against the home shelves before building: the daily-dose falls shelf (pack 1491) cards daily 700–1,000 IU and fences the large daily trials in prose, the annual-bolus harm is live shelf #30 (Sanders, single 500,000 IU dose), pack 5987 covers daily high-dose versus standard-dose, and pack 6026 cards the D-Health fracture result (HR 0.94) under its non-deficiency fracture question. None of them asks the monthly intermediate-dose question, which is the slice carded here. Versus placebo, monthly dosing did nothing: in ViDA (Khaw 2017; 5,108 adults aged 50–84; 200,000 IU loading then 100,000 IU monthly for a mean 3.4 years), falls occurred in 52% on vitamin D versus 53% on placebo (adjusted HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.07) and non-vertebral fractures in 6% versus 5% (adjusted HR 1.19, 0.94 to 1.50; p = 0.15). In D-Health (Waterhouse 2021; 60,000 IU monthly for up to 5 years; falls analysis in 15,416 survey participants), vitamin D had no effect on falling in the past month (OR 1.02, 0.95 to 1.10), with a body-mass-index interaction: risk was increased in participants with BMI under 25 (OR 1.25, 1.09 to 1.43) and unchanged at BMI 25 or over (OR 0.95). Versus a lower monthly dose the direction flips to harm: in 200 prior fallers aged 70 or over (Bischoff-Ferrari 2016), 66.9% fell on 60,000 IU monthly versus 47.9% on 24,000 IU monthly over 12 months, with no benefit on lower-extremity function. PROPOSED SPLIT: monthly high-dose vitamin D neither prevents falls or fractures against placebo nor is it benign against a standard monthly dose in people who have already fallen.

cards.headline: Khaw 2017 (ViDA): monthly 100,000 IU did not prevent falls (52% versus 53%; HR 0.99) or non-vertebral fractures (6% versus 5%; adjusted HR 1.19, not significant) over a mean 3.4 years
cards.summary: Khaw 2017 (ViDA): monthly 100,000 IU did not prevent falls (52% versus 53%; HR 0.99) or non-vertebral fractures (6% versus 5%; adjusted HR 1.19, not significant) over a mean 3.4 years
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, secondary and post-hoc outcomes (ViDA)
cards.people: 5,110 healthy volunteers aged 50–84 years in Auckland, New Zealand (mean age 65.9 years; 58% men; mean baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D 63 nmol/L, about 25 ng/mL, with 30% below 50 nmol/L, about 20 ng/mL), randomised to an initial 200,000 IU dose then monthly 100,000 IU colecalciferol (n = 2,558) or matching placebo (n = 2,552); fracture analysis in 5,108, falls analysis in those returning questionnaires.
cards.result: During follow-up 2,638 participants reported a fall: 1,312 (52%) of 2,539 in the vitamin D group versus 1,326 (53%) of 2,517 on placebo (adjusted HR for falls 0.99, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.07; p = 0.82) — the treatment made no difference. Non-vertebral fractures were reported in 156 (6%) on vitamin D versus 136 (5%) on placebo (adjusted HR 1.19, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.50; p = 0.15). Deaths did not differ significantly (65 versus 58). The authors conclude monthly high-dose bolus vitamin D did not prevent falls or fractures in this healthy ambulatory population. Falls were a post-hoc outcome and fractures a secondary outcome of the trial.
cards.watchOut: Participants were healthy and mostly vitamin-D-replete at baseline; falls were post-hoc and self-reported by questionnaire, and the fracture confidence interval (0.94 to 1.50) cannot exclude moderate harm or small benefit.
cards.source: Khaw KT et al. Effect of monthly high-dose vitamin D supplementation on falls and non-vertebral fractures: secondary and post-hoc outcomes from the randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled ViDA trial. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2017. PMID: 28461159. Registry ID: ACTRN12611000402943. cards.headline: Waterhouse 2021 (D-Health): monthly 60,000 IU had no effect on falling overall (OR 1.02), but increased fall risk in participants with BMI under 25 (OR 1.25)
cards.summary: Waterhouse 2021 (D-Health): monthly 60,000 IU had no effect on falling overall (OR 1.02), but increased fall risk in participants with BMI under 25 (OR 1.25)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, falls analysis (D-Health)
cards.people: 21,315 Australians aged 60–84 years randomised to monthly 60,000 IU colecalciferol or placebo for up to 5 years (mean treatment duration 4.3 years); the falls analysis used annual-survey data from 15,416 participants and falls-diary data from 2,200, with mean on-trial 25-hydroxyvitamin D of 114.8 nmol/L (about 46 ng/mL) on vitamin D versus 77.5 nmol/L (about 31 ng/mL) on placebo.
cards.result: Vitamin D had no effect on falling in the past month (OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.10) — the treatment made no difference overall. There was an interaction with body mass index (p-interaction = 0.001): vitamin D increased fall risk in participants with BMI under 25 kg/m2 (OR 1.25, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.43) and had no effect at BMI 25 or over (OR 0.95, 0.87 to 1.04). Falls were a prespecified tertiary outcome of D-Health. The trial's fracture result is carded on pack 6026 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: The BMI interaction is a subgroup finding within an overall null result and should be read as a signal to check, not proof of harm in leaner older adults; the primary falls measure was falling in the month before an annual survey, not continuous fall counting.
cards.source: Waterhouse M et al. Vitamin D supplementation and risk of falling: outcomes from the randomized, placebo-controlled D-Health Trial. Journal of cachexia, sarcopenia and muscle. 2021. PMID: 34337905. Registry ID: ACTRN12613000743763. MeSH: *Accidental Falls/prevention & control · Aged · Australia/epidemiology · Dietary Supplements · Humans · *Vitamin D · Vitamins
