cards.headline: Bischoff-Ferrari 2016: in prior fallers, 66.9% fell on 60,000 IU monthly versus 47.9% on 24,000 IU monthly over 12 months, with no functional benefit
cards.summary: Bischoff-Ferrari 2016: in prior fallers, 66.9% fell on 60,000 IU monthly versus 47.9% on 24,000 IU monthly over 12 months, with no functional benefit
cards.type: Randomised double-blind clinical trial, three monthly-dose arms
cards.people: 200 community-dwelling men and women aged 70 years or older with a prior fall in Zurich, Switzerland (mean age 78 years; 67% women; 58% vitamin-D-deficient, under 20 ng/mL, at baseline), randomised for 1 year to monthly 24,000 IU vitamin D3, monthly 60,000 IU vitamin D3, or monthly 24,000 IU plus 300 micrograms of calcifediol.
cards.result: The higher monthly regimens reached 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels of at least 30 ng/mL more often (p = 0.001) but did not improve lower-extremity function (Short Physical Performance Battery; p = 0.26) — the treatment made no difference to function. Falls incidence differed significantly between groups (p = 0.048): 66.9% (95% CI 54.4 to 77.5) fell in the 60,000 IU group and 66.1% in the 24,000 IU plus calcifediol group versus 47.9% (35.8 to 60.3) in the 24,000 IU group; mean falls were 1.47 and 1.24 versus 0.94 (p = 0.09). The authors conclude higher monthly doses had no benefit on function and were associated with more falls.
cards.watchOut: Small (200 participants), single-centre, and the comparator is a lower monthly dose rather than placebo, so this card speaks to dose choice in prior fallers, not to whether any vitamin D helps. The calcifediol arm is a different compound and is reported here only as part of the trial's design.
cards.source: Bischoff-Ferrari HA et al. Monthly High-Dose Vitamin D Treatment for the Prevention of Functional Decline: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA internal medicine. 2016. PMID: 26747333. Registry ID: NCT01017354. cards.headline: Synthesis: monthly high-dose vitamin D — null against placebo in 26,000 randomised participants, harmful against a lower monthly dose in prior fallers — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: monthly high-dose vitamin D — null against placebo in 26,000 randomised participants, harmful against a lower monthly dose in prior fallers — SPLIT
cards.people: ViDA (5,108 analysed) and D-Health (15,416 in the falls analysis) against placebo; one 200-participant Zurich trial against a 24,000 IU monthly control in prior fallers.
cards.result: Against placebo the answer is consistent across two large trials and two monthly doses (60,000 and 100,000 IU): no reduction in falls, and no fracture reduction in ViDA (the D-Health fracture analysis, HR 0.94, is homed on pack 6026). Against a standard monthly dose, the one head-to-head trial found significantly more fallers at 60,000 IU. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) versus placebo; POSSIBLE (harm) versus lower monthly dosing. This shelf is distinct from the daily-dose falls shelf (pack 1491), the daily high-dose shelf (pack 5987) and the annual-bolus shelf (live #30).
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the three dosing worlds: daily standard dose, monthly high dose and the single annual 500,000 IU bolus have different evidence and different homes in this library.
cards.source: Synthesis of Khaw KT et al. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2017 (PMID: 28461159); Waterhouse M et al. Journal of cachexia, sarcopenia and muscle. 2021 (PMID: 34337905); Bischoff-Ferrari HA et al. JAMA internal medicine. 2016 (PMID: 26747333). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Calcium absorption: about a third of a typical 300–500 mg dose is absorbed — the fraction falls from ~64% at tiny loads to ~29% at 500 mg, rises about two-thirds when vitamin D status improves within the normal range, and is a stable personal trait
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what fraction of an oral calcium dose is absorbed, and how do dose size and vitamin D status change that fraction?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Calcium Radioisotopes · Calcium, Dietary/administration & dosage,blood,pharmacokinetics · Female · Humans · Intestinal Absorption · Middle Aged · Models, Biological
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The Heaney programme measured true fractional calcium absorption in healthy adults by isotopic-tracer methods over several decades, and its three determinants are consistent across reports: (1) the fraction absorbed at an ordinary load is roughly one third — 0.321 from milk and 0.409 from kale at a ~300 mg load; (2) the fraction is strongly load-dependent, falling from an average 64.0% at the smallest loads to 28.6% at 500 mg, inversely with the logarithm of load, so absorbed calcium rises with dose even as efficiency falls; and (3) vitamin D status matters well inside the laboratory reference range — absorption was 65% higher (relative) at a mean 25-hydroxyvitamin D of 86.5 nmol/L (34.6 ng/mL) than at 50.2 nmol/L (20.1 ng/mL) on identical 500 mg loads. A fourth finding frames all three: absorption is a consistent personal trait, correlated within individuals across loads, substances and years. Framing follows Ganong (vitamin-D-dependent active transport plus passive paracellular uptake), named as textbook framing. The library's calcium shelves ask supplementation outcomes (fractures, bone density); absorption physiology itself was uncovered.

cards.headline: Heaney & Weaver 1990: at a ~300 mg load, fractional absorption averaged 0.321 from milk and 0.409 from kale in 11 healthy women
cards.summary: Heaney & Weaver 1990: at a ~300 mg load, fractional absorption averaged 0.321 from milk and 0.409 from kale in 11 healthy women
cards.type: Human absorption study (intrinsic isotopic labelling, paired foods), Am J Clin Nutr 1990
cards.people: Eleven normal women, each absorbing intrinsically labelled calcium from kale and from milk in paired tests at an average test load of 300 mg. N = 11 — printed plainly; a small classic absorption study by modern standards.
cards.result: Fractional calcium absorption from kale averaged 0.409 ± 0.101 and from milk 0.321 ± 0.089 (P < 0.025) in the same subjects — i.e. about a third of a typical dietary load is absorbed, with the food matrix shifting the fraction by several points (kale, a low-oxalate vegetable, absorbed better than milk; the programme's earlier spinach work, cited in the report, absorbed poorly because of oxalate).
cards.watchOut: N = 11, women only, single ~300 mg load size; the animal MeSH tag in the record reflects the journal's indexing of the research programme, but the carded measurements are the human paired tests described in the abstract.
cards.source: Heaney RP, Weaver CM. Calcium absorption from kale. Am J Clin Nutr. 1990. PMID: 2321572. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). MeSH: Adult · Animals · Biological Availability · Calcium/metabolism · Female · Humans · Intestinal Absorption/physiology · Middle Aged · Milk/metabolism · Vegetables/metabolism

cards.headline: Heaney 1990 load study: fractional absorption fell from 64.0% at the smallest loads to 28.6% at 500 mg, inversely with the logarithm of load
cards.summary: Heaney 1990 load study: fractional absorption fell from 64.0% at the smallest loads to 28.6% at 500 mg, inversely with the logarithm of load
cards.type: Human absorption study (isotopic tracer across graded loads), J Bone Miner Res 1990
cards.people: Healthy adult women studied under meal conditions at calcium loads ranging from 15 to 500 mg, true absorption measured by isotopic tracer. The record does not print a participant number in its abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Fractional absorption was highly inversely correlated with the logarithm of the ingested load (P < 0.001): absorption averaged 64.0% at the lowest loads and 28.6% at the highest (500 mg). The fitted relationship permits calculation of absorbed calcium for dosing strategies: doubling a dose does not double absorbed calcium, because the absorbed fraction falls as load rises — the quantitative basis for splitting calcium doses.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record, printed on the face per the labelling rule. Loads above 500 mg were not tested in this report; extrapolation of the log relationship beyond the studied range is the reader's, not the paper's.
cards.source: Heaney RP et al. Influence of calcium load on absorption fraction. J Bone Miner Res. 1990. PMID: 2270776. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). MeSH: Adult · Calcium Radioisotopes · Calcium, Dietary/administration & dosage,blood,pharmacokinetics · Female · Humans · Intestinal Absorption · Middle Aged · Models, Biological

cards.headline: Heaney 2003: on identical 500 mg loads, calcium absorption was 65% higher (relative) at 25-hydroxyvitamin D 86.5 nmol/L (34.6 ng/mL) than at 50.2 nmol/L (20.1 ng/mL) — both inside the reference range
cards.summary: Heaney 2003: on identical 500 mg loads, calcium absorption was 65% higher (relative) at 25-hydroxyvitamin D 86.5 nmol/L (34.6 ng/mL) than at 50.2 nmol/L (20.1 ng/mL) — both inside the reference range
cards.type: Human absorption study (randomised controlled trial design, pharmacokinetic AUC method), J Am Coll Nutr 2003
cards.people: Middle-aged women in two spring experiments one year apart: one pretreated with 25-hydroxyvitamin D (mean serum level 86.5 nmol/L, 34.6 ng/mL) and one untreated (mean 50.2 nmol/L, 20.1 ng/mL), each receiving 500 mg oral calcium loads with a standard low-calcium breakfast and 10–12 hours of serial blood sampling. The record does not print a participant number in its abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Relative absorption, estimated from the area under the curve of the load-induced rise in serum calcium, was 3.63 ± 0.234 mg·h/dL in the pretreated experiment versus 2.20 ± 0.240 mg·h/dL untreated (P < 0.001) — absorption 65% higher in relative terms at the higher vitamin D level, an absolute AUC difference of 1.43 mg·h/dL. The authors concluded that absorptive performance is already reduced at the low end of the then-current 25-hydroxyvitamin D reference range.
cards.watchOut: Absorption here is a serum-AUC proxy for true fractional absorption, not the double-isotope measurement of the other cards, and the comparison is between two experiments a year apart rather than a within-person crossover as indexed; N not documented in the record, printed on the face. The 65% figure is relative and is labelled relative, with the absolute AUC values beside it.
cards.source: Heaney RP et al. Calcium absorption varies within the reference range for serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D. J Am Coll Nutr. 2003. PMID: 12672710. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Heaney 1990 consistency study: absorption is a stable personal trait — a woman's fraction correlated with itself across loads, substances and up to 5 years (216 women)
cards.summary: Heaney 1990 consistency study: absorption is a stable personal trait — a woman's fraction correlated with itself across loads, substances and up to 5 years (216 women)
cards.type: Human absorption study (repeated isotopic-tracer measurements), J Bone Miner Res 1990
cards.people: Seventy-four premenopausal and 142 postmenopausal women (216 total), each measured two or three times under conditions predicted to alter absorptive performance — differing loads, differing intervals, and substances of differing intrinsic absorbability.
cards.result: Absorption under one test condition correlated significantly with the same woman's absorption under differing conditions, accounting for up to 60% of the variance typically found in cross-sectional studies; correlations for the same substance at differing loads over 8 weeks ranged from +0.773 to +0.849 (P < 0.001), and remained significant over intervals as long as 5 years (r = +0.487, P < 0.001). Between-person differences in absorptive efficiency are therefore real and durable, not measurement noise — the double-isotope method itself carries only about 10% within-person variability (the programme's companion variability report).
cards.watchOut: Women only, and consistency of a trait does not fix its level: the same woman's fraction still moves with load size and vitamin D status, as the other cards show.
cards.source: Heaney RP et al. Calcium absorptive consistency. J Bone Miner Res. 1990. PMID: 2270777. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Synthesis: expect about one third of an ordinary calcium dose to be absorbed — less per unit as the dose grows, more when vitamin D status is higher, and consistently more or less in a given person
cards.summary: Synthesis: expect about one third of an ordinary calcium dose to be absorbed — less per unit as the dose grows, more when vitamin D status is higher, and consistently more or less in a given person
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded Heaney-programme human studies above (1990–2003), framed by Ganong's account of vitamin-D-dependent active transport and passive paracellular absorption.
cards.result: The quantitative picture is concordant across three decades of tracer work: fractional absorption ≈ 0.32–0.41 at a ~300 mg food load; 0.64 at very small loads falling to 0.286 at 500 mg along a log-load relationship; a 65% relative improvement in absorption between 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels of 50.2 nmol/L (20.1 ng/mL) and 86.5 nmol/L (34.6 ng/mL) on identical loads; and within-person stability of the trait (r up to +0.85 over 8 weeks). The Ganong framing — a saturable, calcitriol-driven active pathway dominant at low loads plus a non-saturable paracellular pathway — predicts exactly the load curve the tracers measure, and is presented as textbook framing, not as a carded result. Practical corollaries the data support: split large doses, and treat low-normal vitamin D status as an absorption problem, not only a bone problem.
cards.watchOut: All carded measurements are in women, mostly middle-aged or older, by tracer or AUC methods; men's fractions and children's are not established by these cards. Two cards rest on records whose abstracts print no participant number (labelled on their faces).
cards.source: Synthesis of Heaney RP, Weaver CM, Am J Clin Nutr 1990 (PMID: 2321572); Heaney RP et al., J Bone Miner Res 1990 (PMID: 2270776); Heaney RP et al., J Am Coll Nutr 2003 (PMID: 12672710); Heaney RP et al., J Bone Miner Res 1990 (PMID: 2270777). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Cutaneous vitamin D synthesis: one minimal erythemal dose raises serum vitamin D3 to ~26 ng/mL — abolished by sunscreen, more than halved by ageing, and needing ~6× the dose in heavily pigmented skin
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how much vitamin D does whole-body sun exposure synthesise in skin, and how do ageing, pigmentation and sunscreen change that yield?
shelves.mesh: 4-Aminobenzoic Acid · Adult · Cholecalciferol · Female · Humans · Osmolar Concentration · Photosynthesis · Skin · Sunlight · Sunscreening Agents · Ultraviolet Rays
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology — UV-B photolyses epidermal 7-dehydrocholesterol to previtamin D3, which thermally isomerises to vitamin D3; continued exposure photodegrades previtamin D3 to inert isomers, so synthesis self-limits and sun alone does not cause vitamin D toxicity). The textbook account commonly equates one whole-body minimal erythemal dose with a large oral dose (on the order of 10,000–25,000 IU) — that equivalence is a textbook account, not a value measured in the carded studies; the carded measurements are serum responses to defined doses. One minimal erythema dose raised mean serum vitamin D3 from 1.5 to 25.6 ng/mL in unprotected subjects, while through an SPF-8 sunscreen there was no rise at all (Matsuoka 1987, N = 8). Ageing attacks the substrate: epidermal 7-dehydrocholesterol falls with age and skin from 77–82-year-olds made less than half the previtamin D3 of skin from 8–18-year-olds under the same UV (MacLaughlin & Holick 1985). Pigmentation gates the photons: 1 minimal erythemal dose raised serum vitamin D up to 60-fold in lightly pigmented volunteers but not significantly in heavily pigmented volunteers, one of whom needed a sixfold dose to reach the same level (Clemens 1982, N = 5). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the skin is a high-capacity vitamin D source whose yield is set by UV-B reaching epidermal 7-dehydrocholesterol — sunscreen, age and melanin each cut it, by the amounts carded.

cards.headline: Matsuoka 1987: one minimal erythema dose of UV raised serum vitamin D3 from 1.5 to 25.6 ng/mL in unprotected subjects, but barely moved it (5.6 to 4.4 ng/mL) through SPF-8 sunscreen
cards.summary: Matsuoka 1987: one minimal erythema dose of UV raised serum vitamin D3 from 1.5 to 25.6 ng/mL in unprotected subjects, but barely moved it (5.6 to 4.4 ng/mL) through SPF-8 sunscreen
cards.type: Human physiology study (controlled UV exposure with and without sunscreen, Matsuoka 1987)
cards.people: 8 normal subjects, 4 protected with the sunscreen para-aminobenzoic acid (sun protection factor 8) and 4 unprotected, each exposed to one minimal erythema dose of UV radiation, with serial serum vitamin D3; parallel in-vitro human skin-slice photoisomerisation experiments. N = 8 — a small classic study, labelled plainly.
cards.result: Mean serum vitamin D3 rose from 1.5 ± 1.0 to 25.6 ± 6.7 ng/mL in the unprotected subjects. In the sunscreen-protected subjects it was 5.6 ± 3.0 ng/mL before and 4.4 ± 2.4 ng/mL after exposure — no rise. Para-aminobenzoic acid also prevented photoisomerisation of 7-dehydrocholesterol to previtamin D3 in human skin slices in vitro. Sunscreen that blocks UV-B blocks cutaneous vitamin D3 synthesis.
cards.watchOut: N = 8 and an SPF-8 PABA preparation from 1987 — the direction and near-completeness of the block are the findings; modern higher-SPF products were not tested here. Serum vitamin D3 (the parent compound) is the acute synthesis readout, not 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
cards.source: Matsuoka LY et al. Sunscreens suppress cutaneous vitamin D3 synthesis. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1987. PMID: 3033008. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: MacLaughlin & Holick 1985: ageing more than halved the skin's capacity to make previtamin D3 — epidermal 7-dehydrocholesterol falls with age across skin from donors aged 8–92
cards.summary: MacLaughlin & Holick 1985: ageing more than halved the skin's capacity to make previtamin D3 — epidermal 7-dehydrocholesterol falls with age across skin from donors aged 8–92
cards.type: Human physiology study (ex-vivo human skin UV exposure across ages, MacLaughlin & Holick 1985)
cards.people: Surgically obtained human skin from donors aged 8–92 years; epidermal provitamin D3 (7-dehydrocholesterol) concentration measured by age, and skin samples exposed to UV radiation with previtamin D3 formation measured in epidermis and dermis.
cards.result: There was an age-dependent decrease in epidermal 7-dehydrocholesterol concentration. The epidermis was the major site of previtamin D3 formation in both young and older skin, accounting for more than 80% of the total produced. Comparing skin from the 8- and 18-year-old subjects with skin from the 77- and 82-year-old subjects, ageing decreased the capacity of the skin to produce previtamin D3 by more than twofold.
cards.watchOut: Ex-vivo skin, not whole-person sun exposure — it isolates the skin's intrinsic capacity from behaviour (older people also expose less skin). The twofold figure compares the youngest with the oldest samples, not a per-decade rate.
cards.source: MacLaughlin J et al. Aging decreases the capacity of human skin to produce vitamin D3. The Journal of clinical investigation. 1985. PMID: 2997282. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Clemens 1982: one minimal erythemal dose raised serum vitamin D up to 60-fold in lightly pigmented volunteers but not significantly in heavily pigmented volunteers, who needed a sixfold dose
cards.summary: Clemens 1982: one minimal erythemal dose raised serum vitamin D up to 60-fold in lightly pigmented volunteers but not significantly in heavily pigmented volunteers, who needed a sixfold dose
cards.type: Human physiology study (controlled UV exposure by skin pigmentation, Clemens 1982)
cards.people: 2 lightly pigmented and 3 heavily pigmented healthy volunteers exposed to a single standard dose of UV radiation (1 minimal erythemal dose), with circulating vitamin D measured over 24–48 h; one heavily pigmented subject was re-exposed to a dose six times larger. N = 5 in total — a very small classic study, labelled plainly.
cards.result: In the lightly pigmented subjects, 1 minimal erythemal dose increased serum vitamin D concentrations by up to 60-fold at 24–48 h. The same dose did not significantly change serum vitamin D in the heavily pigmented subjects. Re-exposure of one heavily pigmented subject to six times the dose raised circulating vitamin D to concentrations similar to those in the lightly pigmented subjects after the lower dose — melanin competes for UV-B and raises the exposure needed, it does not abolish synthesis.
cards.watchOut: N = 5 (2 + 3) — among the smallest studies on any physiology shelf, carded because it is the primary human demonstration and its N is printed on the face. Terminology for the volunteer groups is modernised in this card; the measurement is what is carded.
cards.source: Clemens TL et al. Increased skin pigment reduces the capacity of skin to synthesise vitamin D3. Lancet (London, England). 1982. PMID: 6119494. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: 8 + 5 volunteers in the in-vivo studies, plus human skin from donors aged 8–92 years.
cards.result: Whole-body-scale UV exposure is a potent vitamin D source: a single minimal erythemal dose raised serum vitamin D3 to 25.6 ng/mL in unprotected skin and up to 60-fold in lightly pigmented volunteers. The yield is gated by exactly the three factors in the question — an SPF-8 sunscreen essentially abolished the rise, ageing more than halved the skin's synthetic capacity, and heavy pigmentation required about a sixfold larger dose for the same rise. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: The in-vivo studies are very small (N = 8 and N = 5) classic experiments; effect directions are large and concordant, but precise magnitudes in modern populations rest on these small samples plus the ex-vivo ageing series.
cards.source: Synthesis of Matsuoka LY et al., The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism 1987 (PMID: 3033008); MacLaughlin J et al., The Journal of clinical investigation 1985 (PMID: 2997282); Clemens TL et al., Lancet (London, England) 1982 (PMID: 6119494).

shelves.question: In healthy people, what are the distributions and reference intervals for serum vitamin B12 and its functional marker methylmalonic acid — by age, sex and ancestry — how common are low and borderline B12 values in apparently healthy populations, and why does methylmalonic acid need age-specific ranges?

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, gastrointestinal absorption / haematology sections (framing brief — rests chiefly on the primary population and reference-interval literature, and says so). The B12 distribution itself is well described: NHANES III (n=11,851 with serum B12) centres the US mean at 518 pg/mL (382 pmol/L), with only ≈3% below 200 pg/mL (148 pmol/L). The emerging limb is the functional marker: in NHANES 2011–2014, serum methylmalonic acid rose across its whole distribution in vitamin-B12-replete older adults with normal renal function — especially at ≥70 years — so MMA needs AGE-SPECIFIC reference intervals, and its intervals in a B12-replete, normal-renal-function subpopulation were considerably narrower than in the overall population (Mineva 2019). B12 assays are notoriously non-harmonised: a directly established Chinese interval on a second-generation Roche ECLIA was 250.8–957.1 pg/mL (185–706 pmol/L) in 391 healthy adults (Jiang 2020), carded with its assay generation, not as a universal range. Cross-points: pack #6150 (B12 absorption MECHANISM — no intervals) and pack #2039 (metformin-associated B12 deficiency — a monitoring question) are not re-carded here. The folate limb of the NHANES III report is carded inside this shelf (one home); no separate folate-distribution shelf is spawned from the same dataset.

cards.headline: NHANES III national estimates (n=11,851 with serum B12): mean serum vitamin B12 518 pg/mL (382 pmol/L), only ≈3% below 200 pg/mL (148 pmol/L); mean serum folate 7.2 ng/mL and red-cell folate 196 ng/mL (Wright 1998)
cards.summary: NHANES III national estimates (n=11,851 with serum B12): mean serum vitamin B12 518 pg/mL (382 pmol/L), only ≈3% below 200 pg/mL (148 pmol/L); mean serum folate 7.2 ng/mL and red-cell folate 196 ng/mL (Wright 1998)
cards.type: Primary physiology / population distribution study (NHANES III)
cards.people: The third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (1988–94), US civilian non-institutionalised population aged ≥4 years: 23,378 participants with serum folate data, 23,082 with red-cell folate data and 11,851 with serum vitamin B12 data.
cards.result: Mean serum and red-cell folate were 7.2 and 196 ng/mL respectively, and mean serum vitamin B12 was 518 pg/mL (382 pmol/L). Non-Hispanic white people had higher mean serum and red-cell folate than non-Hispanic black or Mexican American people. Serum B12 was lowest in older adults, and non-Hispanic black people had HIGHER serum B12 than non-Hispanic white individuals. Only approximately 3% of the population had a serum B12 below 200 pg/mL (148 pmol/L).
cards.watchOut: Pre-fortification (1988–94) data, collected before the US folic-acid fortification the authors were anticipating: the folate distributions in particular describe a population that no longer exists nutritionally.
cards.source: Wright JD et al. Blood folate and vitamin B12: United States, 1988-94. Vital and health statistics. Series 11, Data from the National Health Survey. 1998. PMID: 10222835. primary physiology / population distribution study (nhanes iii) the third national health and nutrition examination survey (1988–94), us civilian non-institutionalised population aged ≥4 years: 23,378 participants with serum folate data, 23,082 with red-cell folate data and 11,851 with serum vitamin b12 data. mean serum and red-cell folate were 7.2 and 196 ng/ml respectively, and mean serum vitamin b12 was 518 pg/ml (382 pmol/l). non-hispanic white people had higher mean serum and red-cell folate than non-hispanic black or mexican american people. serum b12 was lowest in older adults, and non-hispanic black people had higher serum b12 than non-hispanic white individuals. only approximately 3% of the population had a serum b12 below 200 pg/ml (148 pmol/l). pre-fortification (1988–94) data, collected before the us folic-acid fortification the authors were anticipating: the folate distributions in particular describe a population that no longer exists nutritionally. wright jd et al. blood folate and vitamin b12: united states, 1988-94. vital and health statistics. series 11, data from the national health survey. 1998. pmid: 10222835. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adult · age distribution · aged · child · child, preschool · erythrocytes/chemistry · ethnicity · female · folic acid deficiency/blood,epidemiology · humans · infant · male · middle aged · nutrition surveys · population surveillance · prevalence · racial groups · sex distribution · socioeconomic factors · united states/epidemiology · vitamin b 12 deficiency/blood,epidemiology

cards.headline: NHANES 2011–2014: methylmalonic acid rises with age across its whole distribution — widest central 95% intervals at ≥70 years — so age-specific MMA intervals are needed even in B12-replete adults with normal renal function (Mineva 2019)
cards.summary: NHANES 2011–2014: methylmalonic acid rises with age across its whole distribution — widest central 95% intervals at ≥70 years — so age-specific MMA intervals are needed even in B12-replete adults with normal renal function (Mineva 2019)
cards.type: Primary physiology / reference-interval study (NHANES 2011–2014, B12 and MMA)
cards.people: US adults in NHANES 2011–2014 with serum vitamin B12 (electrochemiluminescence assay) and serum methylmalonic acid (isotope-dilution liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry); age-specific MMA intervals were estimated in a healthy subpopulation with replete B12 status and normal renal function.
cards.result: Age, race/Hispanic origin and B12 supplement use were generally significantly associated with both serum B12 and MMA. MMA increased with age, particularly at ≥70 years; non-Hispanic white persons had lower B12 and higher MMA than non-Hispanic black persons. Shorter fasting times and impaired renal function were associated with higher MMA but not, after covariate control, with B12. Central 95% reference intervals for both analytes were widest at ≥70 years; MMA intervals in the B12-replete, normal-renal-function subpopulation were considerably narrower than in the overall population but still age-dependent. B12 showed little, MMA notable, increase with impaired renal function. The fetched record prints no numeric interval limits, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: MMA is confounded by renal function and fasting time in a way B12 is not: an 'age-specific' MMA interval applied without the renal-function condition this study built in misreads the data.
cards.source: Mineva EM et al. Age-specific reference ranges are needed to interpret serum methylmalonic acid concentrations in the US population. The American journal of clinical nutrition. 2019. PMID: 31127807. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Directly established Chinese B12 interval on a second-generation Roche ECLIA (391 healthy adults aged 21–80): 250.8–957.1 pg/mL (185–706 pmol/L), with no significant age (P = 0.07) or sex (P = 0.2002) partitioning (Jiang 2020)
cards.summary: Directly established Chinese B12 interval on a second-generation Roche ECLIA (391 healthy adults aged 21–80): 250.8–957.1 pg/mL (185–706 pmol/L), with no significant age (P = 0.07) or sex (P = 0.2002) partitioning (Jiang 2020)
cards.type: Primary physiology / reference-interval study (direct CLSI establishment, single assay generation)
cards.people: 580 serum samples collected for method verification on the Roche Cobas E602 second-generation electrochemiluminescence kit, of which 391 samples from healthy Chinese adults aged 21–80 (groups 21–40, 41–60, 61–80) were used to establish the reference interval per CLSI guidelines; the interval is the nonparametric 2.5th–97.5th percentile range.
cards.result: Kit performance complied with laboratory requirements. Serum B12 was non-Gaussian. Harris-Boyd testing did not indicate partitioning by age or gender, and there was no significant difference between age groups (P = 0.07) or gender groups (P = 0.2002). The established reference interval for healthy Chinese adults was 250.8–957.1 pg/mL (185–706 pmol/L).
cards.watchOut: The authors call this a preliminary study and the interval belongs to one assay generation (second-generation Roche ECLIA): B12 assays are not harmonised, so these limits must not be printed as a universal B12 range.
cards.source: Jiang W et al. A preliminary study for the establishment of a reference interval for vitamin B12 in China after performance verification of a second-generation ECLIA kit. Journal of clinical laboratory analysis. 2020. PMID: 31907976. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: B12 centres near 518 pg/mL (382 pmol/L) in the US population with ≈3% below 200 pg/mL (148 pmol/L), while its functional marker methylmalonic acid climbs with age and needs age-specific intervals — the still-emerging half of this shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: B12 centres near 518 pg/mL (382 pmol/L) in the US population with ≈3% below 200 pg/mL (148 pmol/L), while its functional marker methylmalonic acid climbs with age and needs age-specific intervals — the still-emerging half of this shelf
cards.people: All datasets carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (absorption / haematology) — framing brief; the shelf rests on the population literature. NHANES III gives the national B12 (and, in the same report, folate) distributions; NHANES 2011–2014 (Mineva) shows MMA rising with age even in B12-replete adults with normal renal function, with intervals narrowing considerably once renal impairment and B12 deficiency are excluded; the Chinese direct study (Jiang) shows what one modern assay's interval looks like (250.8–957.1 pg/mL (185–706 pmol/L)) and why assay generation must travel with the number. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the B12 distribution is settled, but age-specific MMA intervals are a stated need, not yet standard laboratory practice, and B12 intervals remain assay-bound.
cards.watchOut: An MMA value in an older adult must be read against age and renal function together; reading it against a young-adult interval manufactures B12 deficiency that the distribution data do not support.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
